exp20v2-craft.interview.product.sense:
Product Sense Rounds: Design, Improve, Critique

How to answer "design an X" without sounding rehearsed, and how to tell the difference.

1. The Friday review

On Friday 25 September 2026, Lavanya Subbaraman, Head of Product at Mashal Commerce Network, opened a spreadsheet she had been avoiding. Mashal is a Pune-based marketplace on which neighbourhood kirana stores order stock from distributors; it was hiring product managers for its ordering flows. The summer hiring cycle had begun with 240 applicants. Sixty were given a phone screen, which is 25 per cent. Twenty-four of those 60 were invited to the on-site loop, which is 40 per cent. Six received offers, which is 25 per cent of 24, and 2.5 per cent of the original 240.

The spreadsheet concerned one round of that loop, the product sense round: a 45-minute conversation in which the interviewer says "design a feature for X" or "improve Y" and watches how the candidate thinks. Nine of the 24 on-site candidates had passed it, which is 37.5 per cent. Six of the nine became offers. Each hire carried an annual cost to company of ₹45 lakh, so six offers committed ₹270 lakh, or ₹2.7 crore, a year.

What troubled Lavanya was a pair of recordings. Madan Gokhale, her senior product manager, had passed candidate nine, Mihir Kapadia, with the comment "textbook structure". Candidate seventeen, Meenal Kharat, had failed with the comment "wandered". Yet when Lavanya replayed them, Mihir had spent eight minutes reciting a seven-step acronym before touching a single user, while Meenal had asked whether the users who abandon reorders most were being served at all, a question no one else in the loop had raised. Lavanya had to decide, before the October cycle opened, whether to change what the round rewarded. If she kept the rubric, Mashal would go on hiring fluent reciters; if she changed it carelessly, judgements would grow noisier.

Exhibit 1 shows how little room there is for error: one interviewer's reading of one 45-minute conversation helps decide who among 24 is paid ₹45 lakh a year. The argument of this page follows: a product sense round is product deconstruction performed under time pressure, and the person on either side of the table does well only if they treat it as reasoning on display, not method on display.

2. The idea

A product sense round is an interview in which a candidate is given an open product problem and is assessed on the quality of judgement they show while working it. It takes three common forms. In a design prompt the candidate invents something ("design a reorder feature for a grocery app"). In an improve prompt they take an existing product and make it better ("improve a metro ticketing app"). In a critique prompt they evaluate a product's choices ("what do you think of this checkout?").

The round exists because a résumé cannot show how someone chooses among plausible options. Large technology employers formalised such questions in the 2000s; interview guides then turned the pattern into acronyms. Lewis Lin's Decode and Conquer (2013) popularised CIRCLES: comprehend the situation, identify the customer, report their needs, cut through prioritisation, list solutions, evaluate trade-offs, summarise. The acronym stopped candidates freezing, then taught them to recite.

The sentence Lavanya could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib is this: the round does not test whether you have a method; it tests whether your choices about whom to serve, which problem to solve and what to give up are good, and whether you can say why. A method is scaffolding for that judgement. It was never a substitute for it.

3. How it actually works

Take a prompt Madan uses: "Improve the reorder experience in a grocery delivery app." The mechanics have six steps, and the unwritten ones matter most.

Clarify. The candidate asks questions that change the answer: for whom, in which city, towards what company goal. Segment. The candidate names two or three distinct groups of users and says how they differ. Choose a pain. They pick one segment and one problem, and, here is the implicit step, state what they are leaving out and why. Generate. They offer several solutions that differ in kind, not in decoration. Trade off. They pick one, name what it costs, and say what evidence would change their mind. Close. They summarise in a sentence a busy executive could act on.

Two things stay unwritten. The interviewer is a collaborator whose reactions carry information, and the candidate must hold a hypothesis and update it; one who finishes with the user they began with has probably not listened. Exhibit 3 shows how Mashal's 45 minutes divide.

Notice that 22 of the 45 minutes sit before any solution appears. Mihir reached solutions at minute 24, leaving 21 minutes against the 23 allowed. His structure was visible; his judgement was thin.

4. A worked example

Lavanya had the two recordings scored on four dimensions, each from 1 to 5. Under the old rubric, problem framing carried 40 per cent; her proposed weights move emphasis to user insight. The pass mark is a weighted score of 3.75.

Exhibit 4. Rubric weights and scores. Old: Mihir 0.40×5 + 0.10×2 + 0.30×4 + 0.20×3 = 2.00 + 0.20 + 1.20 + 0.60 = 4.00; Meenal 1.20 + 0.40 + 1.50 + 0.60 = 3.70. New: Mihir 1.25 + 0.60 + 1.00 + 0.60 = 3.45; Meenal 0.75 + 1.20 + 1.25 + 0.60 = 3.80. Pass mark 3.75.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Framework versus judgement

A framework lists what is worth considering; judgement decides which items matter here. Interviewers blur the two when they reward the checklist because it is easy to see.

Structure is necessary but not discriminating

Almost every prepared candidate is structured, so structure tells you nothing among them. The evidence lies in what they chose and refused to include.

What the round cannot tell you

Forty-five minutes cannot show execution, stakeholder handling or behaviour in the third month of a stalled project. Treat a pass as one reading, not a verdict.

Familiarity bias

A candidate who uses a product daily sounds insightful; one who has never used it sounds naive. Interviewers should ask whether they are scoring thinking or acquaintance.

The interviewer is a variable

Two interviewers can differ by a full point on one dimension. Independent scoring before discussion reduces this; it does not remove it.

Ritual questions versus working questions

"Who is the user?" is ritual if the answer never changes the plan. A working question sends the candidate down a different path depending on the reply.

Numbers as scaffolding

Estimates in the round are not forecasts; they show that the candidate can size a trade-off and spot the assumption carrying the weight, as Exhibit 6 did.

Questions before relying on it

Ask what the round predicts, over what horizon, and whether you have ever checked. Few firms compare round scores with performance a year later.

6. How it looks in different settings

The round changes with the product being discussed and with the company asking.

Mashal's own round is a marketplace round, so a good answer must name the distributor's side: a faster reorder that floods distributors with small loss-making orders is no improvement.

7. Common mistakes

Reciting the acronym. From outside, the candidate announces each step by name and the answer sounds identical to the last one the interviewer heard. The misunderstanding is that visible structure is the product. Diagnostic: strip the labels from the transcript and see whether reasoning remains.

Solving before choosing. The candidate reaches features within five minutes. They believe ideas impress; interviewers want to see why this user and this problem. Diagnostic: check at minute ten whether a user and a pain have been named.

The kitchen-sink answer. Seven features, no ranking. The mistake is confusing breadth with judgement. Diagnostic: ask "which one would you drop first?"; a candidate who cannot answer never chose.

Interviewer error: scoring fluency. Interviewers pass the smoothest speaker. The misunderstanding is that confident delivery signals quality. Diagnostic: score before discussing, and compare scores with the written rubric, as Lavanya did.

8. What good looks like

Return to Meenal's answer. She began by asking whether "reorder" meant the same basket or a fresh one, and whether the interviewer cared about orders or margin. She named three segments in under a minute, picked seniors, and said she was leaving flatmates alone because their abandonment was lowest. She proposed three different solutions (a one-tap repeat, a voice reorder, a family member's shared basket), chose the second, named its cost (speech recognition in regional languages is imperfect), and said that a two-week test on 5,000 users would change her mind.

A good answer shows a chosen path, the visible cost of that choice, a named uncertainty and responsiveness to the interviewer. It looks more specific, not more polished.

9. What Lavanya decided

Lavanya adopted the new weights, kept the 3.75 pass mark, and added two rules: two interviewers score independently before talking, and every score of 4 or 5 must cite a sentence the candidate said. She also replaced the open prompt with one anchored in an artefact, a real screen from a kirana store's ordering flow, so that familiarity with consumer apps mattered less. Re-scoring the 24 recordings under the new weights passed 11 (about 46 per cent), not 9. Seven of the original nine, 78 per cent, stayed. A rubric that reverses two recordings on weights alone was uncalibrated, so she would run the new version for one cycle and compare scores with six-month reviews.

For the candidate, the lesson mirrors hers. Prepare a method so that you do not freeze, but spend your practice on choosing: pick a segment, say what you drop, name the assumption that would flip your answer. To go further, study product deconstruction, because the round is that skill compressed, and then study why memorised frameworks fail, which this page has argued without naming.

Two questions to sit with. If the same performance can pass or fail on rubric weights alone, what is a pass score actually measuring? And if you were the candidate, which assumption in your last answer would, if wrong, have changed what you chose, and did you say so?
exp40v2-craft.interview.product.sense:
Product Sense Rounds: Design, Improve, Critique

What the round measures, what it costs, and why the part candidates rehearse carries almost none of the signal.

1. Two decisions, eleven days apart

On Friday 11 September 2026, sixty-seven days into a cycle that opened on Monday 6 July, Vrinda Umralkar opened a year of interview records in Bengaluru. She is Director of Product at Upkram Systems, which sells warehouse-execution software to Indian third-party logistics operators. It was hiring seven product managers; the cycle drew 2,880 applications.

Of the 216 who reached the product-sense round — sixty minutes of design this, improve that, what do you make of this — 81 passed, a rejection of 62.5 per cent imposed by one person's reading of one hour. Vrinda had to submit the 2027 design before the next cycle opened on Monday 11 January 2027, while the six-month reviews of her seven new hires land between May and July 2027 — after that deadline. She would price the round without ever seeing it predict anything.

Eleven days later, on Tuesday 22 September, Ujjwal Vanarse did the mirror arithmetic in Mumbai. Twenty-six months an associate product manager at Vachan Audio Collective, a consumer app for Indian-language podcasts, he wanted a full product title elsewhere. Since Monday 13 July he had logged 24 practice rounds across seventy-one days. His first real round, at the freight marketplace Vinimay Freight Network, fell on Thursday 15 October, twenty-three days away. He had eighteen hours of preparation left and four targets. Uday Vernekar, his former manager, said those hours were not the decision, and refused to say what was.

Both ask one question from opposite sides of a table, and this page argues one answer: the round samples selection behaviour, not method, and nearly all its power to discriminate sits in what a candidate declines out loud — segments abandoned, features dropped, the assumption named as load-bearing.

2. The idea, and the four camps

Precisely: a product-sense round is a time-boxed, scored work sample in which an assessor poses an under-specified product problem and observes selection behaviour — which users and problems the candidate attends to, discards, and defends when pressed. The prompt type changes the starting material, not the object of measurement: a design prompt withholds the product, an improve prompt the goal, a critique prompt the author's intent.

It has three ancestors and a defect from each. From the consulting case interview it takes structured ambiguity and estimation aloud, and the habit of rewarding whoever narrates confidently. From the studio design critique it takes the discipline of judging an artefact against its stated intent, and the critic's licence to substitute taste for argument. From the work-sample tradition in selection research, which since the 1980s has found structured samples to predict performance better than open conversation, it takes the rubric — and the temptation to make it so specific it stops touching the job.

The problem it solves is real. Product management produces few attributable artefacts: a shipped feature has twenty parents, and a CV line claiming it is unfalsifiable. India's hiring surge of 2021 and 2022 sharpened that, since title inflation ran ahead of scope. Firms needed an independent read, and an hour was cheapest.

3. Mechanics, and the steps nobody writes down

The visible choreography of a strong hour is unremarkable: establish what is really being asked, name the groups it could serve, choose one group and one problem, generate options differing in kind, price one, close with a recommendation an executive could repeat. Every prepared candidate in India can do this, which is why it carries so little information.

First solution proposedminute 19minute 8

Exhibit 3. Median minute of each marker, 216 sixty-minute rounds, Upkram 2026. Failing candidates stated no exclusion in 96 of 135 cases (71.1 per cent) and gave no estimate in 88 of 135 (65.2 per cent).

Read row four against the first three. Candidates who passed reached their first solution at minute 19 — eleven minutes later than those who failed, and 31.7 per cent into the hour. They spent the opening third doing what the two absent rows show the failures skipping. They were not short of structure but of subtraction.

Upkram scores seven dimensions from 1 to 5 and passes at an equally weighted mean of 3.60. The gap between the two groups is 1.23 points, decomposed below.

Structure and sequencing — the thing every acronym teaches and every candidate rehearses — accounts for 3.5 per cent of the difference between those Upkram hired and those it turned away. Subtraction and pricing account for 59.3 per cent.

Four steps are almost never written down. First, the prompt is a scored instrument with a known answer space: the interviewer has heard forty answers and the forty-first obvious one is worth nothing. Second, the clock is managed aloud — "twenty minutes left, so one segment properly rather than three thinly" scores. Third, an intervention names an under-evidenced dimension, not an error, so the reply is evidence, not retreat. Fourth, the candidate is drafting the interviewer's write-up: no committee hears the round, it reads two hundred words written from memory, and memory of an hour is dominated by its last ten minutes.

4. When the round is worth running, and when it misleads

ConditionUpkram (Vrinda, assessing)Ujjwal's four targets
1. Weekly choices among defensible optionsHolds: picker speed against stock accuracy every sprint.Holds for two; doubtful where the roadmap is set a year out.
2. Judgement visible in sixty minutes without unavailable domain knowledgeFails: putaway economics take three months, so the prompt scores consumer-app familiarity.Favours him on consumer and marketplace prompts, penalises him on enterprise.
3. Two independent scorers, later checked against performanceHalf holds: four raters calibrated on 24 rounds, no score ever compared.Unverifiable from outside, but askable.

Exhibit 5. The case for the round as four testable claims. Condition 2's failure drives Vrinda's eventual decision.

Three situations make the round actively misleading. The first is an execution-shaped role, where the manager inherits a roadmap and the work is sequencing; testing invention selects the wrong person. The second is urgent headcount: once a vacancy has been open five months the decision is made on availability, and theatre is worse than nothing. The third is seniority: for a director the question is whether they can read a profit-and-loss statement and name the line to starve.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

SettingWhat breaksWhat mature firms do
Multi-product group (Vanijya Retail Group)Answers cannibalise a sister unit, unremarked: the interviewer does not own it.Score "asked what else we sell"; seed a prompt whose answer is "not here".
Two-sided marketplace (Vinimay Freight Network)A faster match for one side wrecks the other's economics.Give both sides' unit economics; see whether they are read.
Regulated services (Ullas Care Group)Licensing and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 are invisible, so good answers look naive.State the binding constraint; designing within it is the job.
Hardware plus software (Vritta Devices Works)Proposals carry eighteen-month tooling lead times.Give component cost and the next revision date.

Exhibit 6. In each setting the fix is the same: move information out of the interviewer's head and into the prompt.

The internal seams do comparable damage. Recruiters calibrate on throughput and product managers on taste, so the pool arriving is not the one the rubric was written for. Interviewing is unpriced: Upkram's 216 rounds consumed 288 hours of senior product time with no roadmap adjusted for it, which is why write-ups get written in corridors. And the rubric drifts by accretion until it measures compliance.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Structure is the entry fee, not the test

Competent interviewers reward visible structure because it is easy to see and defend in a debrief; Exhibit 4 prices it at 0.3 points of 8.6. The tell is a write-up whose strongest praise is "very structured". Structure did signal rigour in 2014, when half the pool froze; coaching ended that, and nobody retuned the rubric.

The clarifying question that changes nothing

Strong and weak candidates both ask questions early; what differs is whether the answer alters the path. Listen for conditionality. Someone who asks "orders or margin?" and answers the same either way has performed a ritual, and never pauses after the reply.

Revision under argument versus capitulation under expression

Some candidates fold at a raised eyebrow, others only at a reason. In a transcript these look identical and are opposite in value, so the expert objects once wrongly and watches. Whoever drops a sound position against a weak objection will drop a roadmap against a loud stakeholder.

Familiarity in the costume of insight

A candidate who uses the product daily sounds brilliant; one who never has sounds thin. At Upkram this cut the other way: nobody has used warehouse-execution software, so the open prompt silently became a consumer-app prompt. The tell is an insight that is a product fact, not a user fact; product facts are an evening's work.

Numbers in the round rank; they do not forecast

Competent candidates estimate to show they can multiply. Experts estimate to establish an ordering, then hunt the input that would reverse it — Section 8 has one assumption moving a segment from 59.4 per cent of the prize to 31.7. The tell is "this holds only while X exceeds Y".

Agreement is not accuracy, and checklists buy the first by spending the second

This nuance costs the most money. Exhibit 7 shows four calibrated raters scoring one set of 24 recorded rounds.

Exhibit 7. One shared sample of 24 rounds, 96 scorings; the spread between the most and least generous rater is 33.3 percentage points. Each rater scored exactly 24 rounds, so the average of the four means is the exact pooled mean: 3.54 + 3.21 + 3.04 + 2.88 = 12.67, over four, is 3.1675, shown as 3.17. All four agreed on 13 rounds — 5 unanimous passes, 8 unanimous fails — leaving 11 split; the unanimous passes supply 20 of the 42 passes, so the 11 split rounds gave 22 of 44, exactly half.

For a candidate near the line, the interviewer's identity matters more than anything done in the hour. The standard response is a tighter checklist. It works — on agreement. Section 8 shows the cost.

Predictive validity is almost never measured, because the break-even is too low to bother

A principal product manager at Upkram costs ₹60 lakh a year: over 2,000 hours, ₹3,000 an hour, and at a 1.6 loading ₹4,800. Each round plus write-up runs 80 minutes, so 216 rounds cost 288 hours, or ₹13.82 lakh — ₹1.97 lakh per accepted hire. A mis-hire leaving at eleven months on a ₹52 lakh package costs ₹47.67 lakh in salary plus that ₹1.97 lakh: ₹49.64 lakh. The round pays for itself by preventing 13.82 ÷ 49.64 = 0.278 mis-hires across 7 hires, a reduction of 3.98 percentage points. Nobody audits an instrument that need only beat nothing by four points.

Prompt leakage turns judgement into recall

India has the deepest product-interview coaching market anywhere, and a popular prompt has a published answer within a month. The sign is three candidates in a week naming the same three segments in the same order. The fix is not harder prompts, which leak too, but prompts anchored in an artefact nobody has seen.

7. Across product types and company stages

TypeWhat a strong answer must establishTrap

Exhibit 9. Differences that are real. Omitted as folklore: "consumer needs creativity, enterprise needs rigour". Both need both.

Stage changes the round more than type does. A seed-stage firm of eleven has no pool and cannot afford a wrong hire, so its round is long, informal and really a test of tolerability at 10 p.m. on a Saturday. A growth-stage firm hiring twelve managers a year — Upkram's position — needs an instrument that survives people who are not the founder, which is when checklists appear and misfire. A scaled firm could measure validity and does not, because those who would run the study are the ones it would audit.

8. Three worked examples

One: Ujjwal at Vinimay, and the assumption that reversed his answer

Vedika's write-up quoted one sentence: "Medium haul — not where the waste is, but where the matchable waste is. Check the 12 per cent feasibility first: if it is really 25 the answer changes."

Two: his preparation, and why it barely matters

Of his 24 logged rounds, 14 were design prompts, 6 improve and 4 critique, though he expected real prompts to split roughly 35, 45 and 20 per cent. He modelled skill as a floor plus returns per round practised: 0.20 points for each of the first four rounds on a type, 0.10 for rounds five to eight, 0.05 thereafter. Floors of 2.30, 2.10 and 1.60 then reproduce his peer-scored means of 3.80, 3.10 and 2.40.

The allocation hardly matters: every plan gains 0.275 to 0.315 points, and best beats worst by 0.040. In Exhibit 7 the most and least generous rater differ by 0.66 points of mean score — 16.5 times that whole range. Uday Vernekar's refusal has an answer: the lever is how many loops he enters, not how he spends eighteen hours.

His guess of 12 per cent for Upkram's offer rate after a pass was close: the true figure was 9 of 81, or 11.1 per cent. Candidates mis-estimate the other factor, fearing the product-sense round as the bottleneck when at Upkram it passed 81 people for 7 seats.

Three: the checklist that worked, and the failure it caused

In 2025 Vrinda's predecessor faced this spread and did the textbook thing: a fixed prompt and a fourteen-item checklist, one point each, pass at nine. It worked as designed. The pass rate across 180 rounds rose to 54.4 per cent, rater pairs agreed 86 per cent of the time, and nobody argued in debriefs.

The failure appeared eleven months later. Of the 12 managers hired in 2025, five earned a six-month rating of 4 or better — 41.7 per cent — against five of the eight hired in 2024, or 62.5 per cent. The checklist items were defensible and collectively lethal: asks two clarifying questions, names three segments, proposes three solutions, states one metric. Each rewarded production, none subtraction.

The recovery is the part worth copying. Vrinda did not restore the open prompt; she rebuilt the instrument around the three dimensions carrying 59.3 per cent of the discrimination, required every 4 or 5 to quote a sentence the candidate said, and accepted that agreement would fall — it fell to 71 per cent. She also stopped treating the 2024-to-2025 comparison as evidence, which is why the memo was believed.
