PositionStrongest formWhat would make it wrong
ConstructJudgement about users is general; managers transfer across domains successfully.That domain knowledge dominates, as condition 2's failure suggests.
ProxyDefending a contested choice under challenge is the job, so fluency is signal.That fluency is trained and separable from the choice beneath it.
Work-sampleOnly days on a real artefact reveal product sense; use a paid exercise whose output is inspectable.That paid exercises select for free time, and reasoning with an interlocutor is what is needed.
NoiseA 33.3-point rater spread swamps whatever is measured; the round is ceremony until it predicts something.That the break-even really is 3.98 points, in which case a noisy instrument still pays.

Exhibit 15. Upkram's data refutes none of the four, which is why the argument does not resolve.

These are not flavours of one view. The work-sample school would abolish the round; the noise school would keep it only with two raters and a validity study; the construct school would resist domain-specific prompts — which Vrinda is about to overrule.

11. What mastery looks like

On the assessor's side mastery is rarer. An expert interviewer can say unprompted what their prompt cannot reveal; knows whether their pass rate makes them Vikrant or Varad; writes during the hour; objects once weakly to separate revision from capitulation. Above all they hold a pass lightly — a cheap filter on an hour, not a prediction about a year — and are the only ones who ever check.

12. What each of them decided

Vrinda submitted her 2027 design on 19 December 2026. She kept the judgement rubric and refused the obvious fix: a second scorer on all 216 rounds would double product-sense cost from ₹13.82 lakh to ₹27.65 lakh, and so double the effect the round must produce to break even, from 3.98 to 7.96 percentage points — and she had no evidence it achieved even four. She bought double-scoring only where disagreement lives. Sixty-two rounds, 28.7 per cent of the 216, scored within half a point of the 3.60 pass mark, and Exhibit 7's split rounds cluster there. Second-scoring those 62 costs 82.67 hours, or ₹3.97 lakh, lifting the total to ₹17.79 lakh and the required effect to 5.12 points rather than 7.96. She also replaced the open prompt with an anonymised putaway screen from a customer, so condition 2 might finally hold.

Ujjwal made the cheaper and more uncomfortable decision. He took Plan B, pouring all twelve remaining rounds into improve prompts while conceding in his notes that this bought 0.040 points. Then he did the thing that mattered: he raised his target list from four loops to eight, accepting that eight loops cost roughly 48 hours of interviews and leave against 18 hours of practice, and asked each recruiter what the round is scored on and whether more than one person scores it. Three answered. He walked into Vinimay on 15 October knowing Vedika Ullal would be his only scorer.

Three questions. First: the round need only cut mis-hires by four percentage points to pay for itself, and Vrinda has no evidence it does — is positive expected value under a wide prior enough to keep an instrument that rejects 62.5 per cent of those who reach it? Second: if the interviewer's identity is worth 0.66 points of mean score and a candidate's whole preparation allocation 0.040, what should a business school teach here? Third: when agreement and validity point in opposite directions and validity cannot be measured until the next cohort's reviews land, which do you optimise?

13. Going deeper

PM interviews places this round in the loop; without that map, over-preparing one round is the default error. Product deconstruction is the same skill without a clock, and practising it is how the in-round version stops sounding rehearsed. Why memorised frameworks fail generalises Exhibit 4 into roadmap reviews. A PM's operating system supplies the habits that make exclusions natural. Continuous learning as a PM addresses decay: sense built on one domain ages badly. Building a PM portfolio and narrative offers the evidence the work-sample school wants. Transitioning into product management matters because internal mobility bypasses this round. Your first 90 days in a PM role is where a pass meets reality. Confidence, doubt and judgement is hardest: holding a position firmly, a pass lightly.
case40v1-craft.interview.product.sense:
The Round That Cannot Agree With Itself

Ekagra Commerce Works and the product-sense interview, Pune, October 2026

1. Sunday night

At twenty past eleven on Sunday, 11 October 2026, Urmi Ekbote sat at her dining table in Baner, Pune, with three printouts spread across it. The board's people committee met at half past nine the next morning; on Thursday 15 October, notice would have to reach Gurugram if Ekagra Commerce Works did not mean to renew the contract that supplied its product-sense rubric.

The printouts did not agree. One showed that the product-sense round was the heaviest-weighted gate in a loop that had cost ₹1.66 crore in the nine months to September. One showed that two trained interviewers watching the same candidate often reached opposite verdicts. One showed that candidates who scored highest on the rubric were performing slightly worse on the job than those who scored lowest. Urmi, vice-president of product, had scored sixty-four of these rounds herself, and had written at the top of the first page: Is this round measuring anything, or is it measuring us?

2. The company, and a promise made in 2024

Ekagra Commerce Works was founded in Pune in 2018 by Umang Edulji and two classmates to sell order-management and settlement software to consumer brands that had outgrown spreadsheets. By September 2026 it ran catalogue, pricing and GST e-invoicing for about 2,300 brands and distributors, had annualised revenue of ₹478 crore and employed 1,850 people, 62 of them product managers. In November 2025 it launched an ONDC seller application.

The decision that constrains everything was taken in March 2024. The 2023 product cohort had gone badly: of 11 people hired, 6 left or were managed out inside twelve months, a figure of 54.5 per cent that Umang had not enjoyed explaining. His response was to buy objectivity. Ekagra licensed a structured product-sense rubric from Unnayan Talent Exchange of Gurugram, and Umang told the committee that product hiring would henceforth be “externally validated and rubric-scored”. The committee liked the sentence enough to adopt share of product hires rubric-scored as a standing metric, which had read 100 per cent at every meeting since January 2025. The rubric was no longer only an instrument; it was a commitment on a slide.

3. The industry

Indian commerce software in 2026 was crowded. Brands could buy pieces of Ekagra's stack from Shopify's Indian partners, from Unicommerce or from Razorpay's merchant suite, or build on ONDC directly; the protocol's spread, plumbed through UPI rails that NPCI kept extending, had commoditised integration faster than Ekagra's 2023 plan assumed. Reliance Retail and Tata Digital pulled volume into their own systems; Flipkart, Meesho and Zepto changed seller terms often enough to generate reactive work every quarter.

The same firms competed for its people: a product manager with three years' experience could expect ₹45 lakh to ₹52 lakh fixed in Bengaluru against Ekagra's Pune band of ₹38 lakh. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 made candidate work samples personal data, with a purpose limitation and a retention schedule.

Design sat in Dublin, customer success in Seoul, growth in Warsaw, data science in Santiago. The largest overseas account was a convenience-store operator in Osaka whose requirements had little in common with a Surat textile brand's on ONDC. Interviewers came from all five offices, which is how a hiring question became a question about what Ekagra wanted product sense to mean.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The rubric arrived in April 2024 as version three, thirty points and six criteria; a two-day workshop trained nine interviewers. In January 2025 Unnayan shipped version five: forty points, eight criteria, adding commercial framing and critique quality on the argument that version three rewarded candidates who could generate ideas but not judge them. Ekagra rescaled existing scores by four-thirds so the two years could be compared; a version-three score of 21 became 28.

Through 2025 nobody looked hard at the loop. In June 2025 Urvish Enjeti, a mechanical engineer who had spent four years building dispatch tooling for a two-wheeler fleet, scored 21 of 40 from Ela Udwadia and was rejected at the first gate. In November 2025 Utsah Mobility Network shipped a returns-and-reverse-pickup flow that Ekagra's sales team began citing in competitive deals, and Urvish was the product manager named on it. Eshan Upadhye circulated the story as a curiosity; nobody filed it as evidence.

The doubt began mechanically. In February 2026 Urmi started a quiet double-scoring pilot: a second interviewer watched a recording and scored it blind. It is Exhibit 4. In June, Uma Eranna matched rubric scores to twelve-month ratings for the 2024 and 2025 hires, producing Exhibit 6a, which pointed the wrong way. In August, Ujjwal Search Services traced the rejected candidates; that is Exhibit 6b.

Three things believed in 2025 had turned out to be wrong, or at least unsupported. First, that scores were comparable across interviewers: Exhibit 5 shows pass rates from 14.6 to 44.3 per cent on pools recruiting had always called equivalent. Second, that candidates were allocated at random; scheduling went by calendar availability, and a Dublin evening slot is a late-night slot in India, which filled with working engineers rather than students. Third, Unnayan's validity evidence: its report cited a correlation of 0.41 with manager satisfaction across 2,900 placements at 60 client firms, but on version three and against a six-month measure.

Then, on Monday 28 September, at the quarterly calibration workshop, two senior panellists scored the same recorded forty-minute answer 36 and 19 — a gap of 17 points. The pilot's largest observed gap was 14.

5. The people

Umang Edulji, co-founder and chief executive, Mumbai and Pune. The rubric stays until something demonstrably better exists, and “demonstrably” means a study, not an anecdote. Incentive: a Series D in which hiring governance is a line item. Not saying: he made the 2024 promise and must unmake it himself.

Eshan Upadhye, head of talent, Pune. Thirty-six product hires to make across the twelve months of FY27, against 24 in the nine months to September, 29 of them in India. The round is cheap and the only part of the loop that scales; his 2 October memo puts its cost at “about ₹35.7 lakh a year of interviewer time” and the pass rate at “a stable 28 per cent, in line with last year”. Not saying: he is measured on offers accepted by 31 March.

Ela Udwadia, director of design, Dublin. The lowest pass rate of any scorer, unrepentant: candidates perform a method instead of exercising judgement, and the eight criteria reward the performance. Not saying: she had never seen her colleagues' rates and assumed hers were normal.

Eknath Ugale, engineering director, Bengaluru. The highest pass rate, 44.3 per cent; the round is theatre and the weight belongs on technical depth. Not saying: in two of the last three quarters he approved product managers whose specifications his team rewrote.

Uma Eranna, staff data scientist, Santiago. She produced Exhibit 6a and insists on its weakness: 26 observations, ratings between 3.0 and 4.5, no way to distinguish a correlation of 0.41 from one of −0.2. Not saying: she scored 22 of 40 on this rubric in a March 2026 transfer attempt.

Euna Eom, customer-success lead, Seoul. Her complaint is categorical: whatever the round measures, it is not the ability to sit with a merchandising head for three hours and find which of eleven stated requirements is real. Not saying: she wants a product manager for her region.

Eshita Ubhayakar, founder of Unnayan Talent Exchange, Gurugram. Renewal is offered at ₹52 lakh, or ₹61 lakh with quarterly double-blind calibration; she notes accurately that Ekagra never ran the recommended re-calibration for all sixteen internal scorers in Exhibit 5. Not saying: version six, in beta, drops two of version five's criteria.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the arithmetic of the commitment: the round takes 1,116 of 2,325 interviewer hours, 48.0 per cent of all interviewing time. In Exhibit 2, applications grew 31.0 per cent while hires went from 20 to 24, so applications per hire rose from 710 to 775. In FY26, 186 of 744 rounds (25.0 per cent) passed, against 171 of 612 (27.9 per cent) in FY25; 31 of 186 (16.7 per cent) got offers and 24 of 31 (77.4 per cent) accepted.

The loop cost ₹6.92 lakh per accepted offer. Charging the round its 1,116 hours at the blended rate, ₹35.71 lakh, plus the whole ₹46.00 lakh licence, gives ₹81.71 lakh for one gate, or 49.2 per cent of total hiring cost. Eshan's memo quotes only the first figure.

Exhibit 4 was the hardest printout to put down: if 11 of 40 pairs (27.5 per cent) agree within two points and a third disagree about the verdict, the heaviest gate in the loop is settled by which calendar a candidate landed on.

Read naively, Exhibit 6a says the rubric is inverted and Exhibit 6b that the round discards people the market later calls product managers. Neither says either: the top band's best outcomes may be the people who left, and a product title at an unnamed firm is not a performance rating.

7. Voices

“If two of us watch the same person and land seventeen points apart, we are not disagreeing about the candidate. We are disagreeing about the instrument, and the instrument is the thing we told the board we had.”

Urmi Ekbote, calibration workshop, 28 September 2026

“Ela fails five of six. Eknath passes two of five. We tell candidates the process is standardised. At some point that becomes a thing we are saying rather than a thing that is true.”

Ewa Urbanek, internal chat, 7 October 2026

“Stop asking whether the correlation is negative. Twenty-six observations with ratings between 3.0 and 4.5 cannot tell you the sign. If you want to know whether the round works, run it as an experiment — and that means hiring some people it rejected.”

Uma Eranna, email to Urmi Ekbote, 9 October 2026

“We ask people to design a product they have never seen for users they have never met. My merchandising head in Osaka changed his mind four times in one meeting. Which criterion is that?”

Euna Eom, product leadership review, 6 October 2026

8. The options, as Urmi sees them

A. Renew and calibrate properly. Take Eshita's ₹61 lakh package, up ₹15 lakh on ₹46 lakh, and calibrate every scorer quarterly. Exhibit 4 may measure Ekagra's failure to calibrate, not the rubric's failure to discriminate. Against: version six drops two of the criteria Ekagra is about to pay to be calibrated on.

B. Replace it with a paid take-home deconstruction. Send every recruiter-screen pass a two-hour written deconstruction of a live product at an honorarium of ₹8,000, read blind by two reviewers. At FY26 volumes that is ₹59.52 lakh of honoraria plus 558 reviewing hours, ₹17.86 lakh, for ₹77.38 lakh in all, against the ₹81.71 lakh the round costs today. Year one also carries about ₹9 lakh of one-time legal work for consent, purpose limitation and retention under the DPDP Act, making it dearer by ₹4.67 lakh and cheaper after.

C. Rebuild the round in-house. Drop the licence and the eight criteria; run a sixty-minute live deconstruction of Ekagra's own product with two internal scorers on every round. At FY26 volumes the increment is two-part: the 180 panel-scored rounds come in-house at Exhibit 1's 1.5 hours a round, 270 hours, and a second scorer joins all 744, a further 1,116 hours. That is 1,386 extra interviewer hours, ₹44.35 lakh at ₹3,200 an hour, against the ₹46.00 lakh licence it saves — a net saving of ₹1.65 lakh. Designing it first costs five of fourteen senior product managers four hours a week for a quarter, 260 hours or ₹8.32 lakh once, so year one is dearer by ₹6.67 lakh — with the ONDC returns module already slipped from August to November, and no external validation left.

D. Leave the round and move the weight. Cut product sense from 35 per cent to 15, raise execution to 30 and technical depth to 25. Costs nothing, keeps the metric, satisfies Eknath. Does nothing about Exhibit 4, and the minimum-use clause means Ekagra keeps paying the licence while it runs the round.

All four share a premise: that the problem is measurement. None asks what Ekagra wants a product manager to be able to do, or whether that is one thing or two. Nor has anyone asked why three of the strongest scorers are among those who left. If the answer is the job rather than the gate, all four options are argued at the wrong end of the funnel.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The Unnayan agreement renews automatically on 1 November 2026 unless notice reaches Gurugram by Thursday 15 October. A minimum-use clause applies: below 600 rubric-scored rounds in a year, 60 per cent of the licence falls due regardless — ₹27.60 lakh on ₹46 lakh, ₹31.20 lakh on the renewal price. The committee has approved ₹1.80 crore for the twelve months of FY27 against a plan of 36 hires. Exhibit 3a's ₹1.66 crore covers only January to September 2026, so the nine-month rate annualises to about ₹2.21 crore: on a full-year basis the approval is a cut of roughly ₹41 lakh, not an increase. Per hire it is ₹5.00 lakh against this year's ₹6.92 lakh, a reduction of 27.7 per cent. Fourteen senior product managers are available as interviewers, and the three with the deepest ONDC context are the three whose roadmap has slipped. Campus offers must be out by the third week of March, and the reported metric has read 100 per cent at seven consecutive meetings.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 4 establish, and what does it not? Separate uncalibrated scorers from an incoherent thing being scored.
  2. Exhibit 5 shows pass rates from 14.6 to 44.3 per cent. List every explanation consistent with the data, and what evidence would separate them.
  3. Exhibit 6a appears to show an inverted rubric and Exhibit 6b costly false negatives. Argue that each shows nothing at all.
  4. Eshan's memo puts the round's cost at ₹35.7 lakh; Exhibit 3a supports ₹81.71 lakh. What does that choice reveal about who bears the cost?
  5. Uma's test — hire some of the people the round rejected — is the only one that would settle it. What would it cost in money, in time, and in what Umang must tell the board?
  6. It is Monday, half past nine. What does Urmi do, what does she sign by Thursday, and what does she tell the committee about a metric reading 100 per cent for seven meetings?

At a quarter to one Urmi turned the printouts face down and wrote two lines on the back of Exhibit 4. The first was Ela's: they perform a method. The second was Uma's: you cannot tell the sign. Both could not be acted on at once, and she was no longer sure either was about the candidates.
case20v1-craft.interview.product.sense:
Eleven Days Before the Product Sense Round

A decision case on how a candidate prepares for the interview that tests judgement

1. Opening

At 9:40 on the night of Monday, 5 October 2026, Chinmay Bhosale closed his laptop in his room at the ISB campus in Hyderabad and wrote a single line on the whiteboard above his desk: Friday 16 October, 11:00, Chandan, round one. He had eleven preparation days, about thirty-five usable hours, and one decision to take before he slept: how to spend them.

Chinmay was a four-year software engineer from Pune who had come to ISB to move into product management. Chandan Kirana Network, a Bengaluru company he admired, had shortlisted him for one of three associate product manager seats. The first of its five interview rounds was a forty-five-minute product sense round. He had already failed to impress in practice. The question was whether to practise harder at what he was doing, or to change what he was practising.

2. Company background

Chandan Kirana Network, founded in 2019 in Bengaluru, sells software and a shared ordering app to neighbourhood grocery stores. In 2026 it served about 18,000 kirana stores across nine cities, letting shoppers order from a store within two kilometres of their home, with part of its catalogue also discoverable through ONDC. Its annualised gross merchandise value was about ₹410 crore. Its rivals were large: Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart delivered from dark stores in minutes, JioMart worked through Reliance Retail's reach, and BigBasket leaned on Tata's backing. Chandan's argument was that a store the shopper already trusts, who gives credit and knows the family's brand of atta, is not easily replaced by an app.

The company hired associate product managers once a year. In 2026 it had received about 1,800 applications, interviewed 90 people, and would make three offers, so roughly one interviewee in thirty would be hired. The fixed pay was ₹34 lakh a year.

3. The situation

Chinmay's preparation so far had been methodical. Over ten days he had memorised a seven-step answer structure from a popular interview guide: clarify the goal, name the users, list their pain points, brainstorm solutions, pick one, define metrics, summarise. He had completed four mock rounds, each scored by his mock interviewer against four criteria out of five. Exhibit 1 sets out the results.

The pattern was plain. Communication averaged 4.75 and never fell below 4, while product judgement averaged 2.25. User insight, which began at 4, was down to 2 by the fourth mock, the most heavily rehearsed. Chinmay read this as noise. Falguni, his fourth interviewer, did not.

The loop at Chandan is shown in Exhibit 2. The product sense round carries the largest single weight, 30 per cent of the final score. Florencia Duarte, Chandan's design lead in Lisbon, writes the prompts. She had told colleagues she looks for candidates whose answers could not have been given about any other company.

4. The people

Falguni Ranade, an associate product manager at Chandan in Bengaluru, passed the same loop two years earlier and agreed to run mock four. Her note was short: “You answered every step and said nothing I could not have heard from fifty other people. I never learned what you would actually do.”

Charudatta Kher, director of product at Chandan in Bengaluru, runs the final panel. He is blunt about frameworks. To him a candidate who announces a framework is borrowing a method instead of showing judgement, and he scores accordingly. He wants hires who will argue with him usefully by their second day.

Cyrus Fernandes, Chinmay's classmate, is on exchange in Amsterdam and has run two mocks over video at 9 p.m. in Hyderabad, which is 5:30 p.m. there. He scored the first two mocks generously because he liked the structure.

Fatima Qureshi, a career coach on campus, has seen two cohorts through product interviews. She offers a six-session package outside ISB's own services at ₹15,000 a session, and believes that individual feedback, not additional reading, is what moves candidates.

5. The three options

Chinmay's hours do not stretch. Counting 2.5 hours on each of nine weekday evenings and 6 hours on each of the two weekend days, he has 34.5 hours. Exhibit 3 shows how each option would spend them, together with its cash cost.

Option A: drill the method harder. Chinmay would keep the seven steps and sharpen them against about 20 more prompts, each timed to forty-five minutes. The upside is fluency, and Exhibit 1 shows he is already fluent. The cost is that the weak scores sit in precisely the criteria that drilling does not train, and Charudatta penalises the visible scaffolding.

Option B: deconstruct Chandan and form views. He would spend the time on the product itself: use the app, visit eight or ten kirana stores near the Hyderabad campus to see how owners take orders, write a one-page teardown of three rivals and write down what he would change and what he would refuse to change. The upside is specific, defensible opinions, which is what Florencia and Charudatta are scoring. The cost is risk: the prompt may not concern grocery at all, and he would have only four hours of timed practice.

Option C: buy coaching. Fatima would review each answer live across six sessions. The upside is calibrated feedback from someone who is not a friend. The cost is ₹90,000, which is a considerable sum to him, and 24 of his 34.5 hours handed to a schedule he does not control, leaving only 5 hours to study the product.

6. Timeline

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Read Exhibit 1 closely. Which criteria are weak, which strong, and what does the fall in user insight from 4 to 2 suggest about the effect of the rehearsal?
  2. Why would a panel that scores product sense at 30 per cent of the total (Exhibit 2) penalise a visible framework even when every step is correct?
  3. Using Exhibit 3, which option best targets the weak criteria in the available hours, and what does each give up?
  4. If the prompt turns out not to concern grocery, what does Chinmay have in hand under each option? Which would you choose, and what would make you change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. A product sense round is product deconstruction under time pressure. The interviewer is not testing recall of steps; she is looking for a candidate who notices something about a real user, makes a trade-off and explains why. A framework is scaffolding, useful privately, but spoken aloud as a script it makes every answer sound like every other. Exhibit 1 is the evidence: the one thing rehearsal improved, communication, was already at the ceiling.

One defensible path. Option B, with two adjustments. First, Chinmay should spend the 22 hours of study on Chandan and its rivals, but not exclusively on grocery: the habit he is building, noticing a user's real constraint and committing to a view, transfers to any prompt, whether it concerns a refrigerator or a map. Second, he should not drop practice entirely. The four hours of timed answers should go to Falguni and Cyrus, with one instruction: score judgement and specificity, not structure.

Option A is the weakest because it trains the strongest criterion. Option C is not wrong in principle, but at ₹90,000 and 24 hours it buys feedback he could partly obtain free from Falguni, and it takes most of the time that Option B spends on the product. If the first Option B mock, around Saturday 10 October, still scores below 3 on insight, a single paid session with Fatima is a reasonable, bounded response. The test of success is simple: after the mock, could the interviewer say what Chinmay would do that another candidate would not?
case40v1-craft.levels.comp:
The Ladder Kosha Took Down

Levels, scope and compensation at Kosha Credit Network, Bengaluru. October 2026.

1. Sunday night, Indiranagar

On the evening of Sunday, 11 October 2026, Kshama Potdar sat at her dining table in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with three documents open and a fourth she had not written: a five-level product ladder her team had spent eight weeks building; a Kalanidhi Benchmark Partners study putting her product managers at the seventeenth percentile of the market; Khagol Payments Exchange's signed offer to a candidate she wanted; and, unwritten, her recommendation to Kosha Credit Network's compensation committee at nine next morning.

Kshama had joined as Chief Product Officer on Monday, 2 February 2026, after eleven years in payments and lending, hired partly to fix what everyone called “the levels problem”. She had found four or five problems sharing a vocabulary. Nineteen product managers held four titles; the titles did not map to scope, the bands did not map to the titles, five people had resigned in twelve months with three mentioning levels on the way out, and a clause written three years earlier meant most of what the ladder implied could not lawfully be done. Her husband asked what the decision was. She could not say it in one sentence.

2. Kosha Credit Network

Kosha Credit Network was founded in Bengaluru in 2018 to lend working capital to small merchants against their digital transaction history: a kirana store accepting UPI payments generates a cash-flow record no bank statement captures, and that record can underwrite a ninety-day ₹40,000 loan profitably. By FY26 Kosha employed about 640 people, had disbursed ₹4,120 crore to some 2.3 lakh merchants, held assets under management of ₹1,180 crore and reported total income of ₹412 crore.

The decision that constrained Kshama's Monday was taken in March 2023, when Kosha ran an eight-level ladder inherited from the founders' previous employer. The complaint, voiced at an all-hands, was that it had become a status machine: people negotiated for a level rather than a problem. Leadership collapsed it to four — Associate PM, Product Manager, Lead PM, Head of Product — one wide band each, and wrote into every appointment letter then on the rolls a clause promising no employee's fixed pay or title would be reduced by any future restructuring of levels. Eleven of the nineteen on the rolls in October 2026 were covered.

The flattening worked, in that nobody argued about levels. It also meant that for three and a half years the word “Lead” went to anyone a manager wanted to retain. By 2026 ten of the nineteen were Lead Product Managers: two owned a single feature, one a product line generating a quarter of Kosha's income.

3. The industry around it

Kosha competed for merchant attention with the distribution arms of PhonePe, Paytm and Razorpay, and for good merchants with banks and NBFCs whose cost of funds was lower. Its surface sat on NPCI's UPI rails and the account aggregator framework; the RBI's digital-lending directions had pushed disclosure and recovery-conduct deep into product work, the DPDP Act had made consent architecture a product feature, ONDC a second channel. What mattered here was the effect on scope: between January 2025 and June 2026 Kosha created three wholly regulatory product teams, staffing them from commercial surfaces.

Its exposure was also no longer only Indian. A cross-border merchant-lending pilot had opened out of Nairobi in 2025, with its principal designer in Lisbon on a local contract and its senior data scientist in Seoul. A single rupee band for a level is a claim about one labour market, and Kosha was hiring in four.

4. How the question arrived

Figure 1 sets out the sequence. The levelling project began in Kshama's second month and was meant to be dull: write five levels, describe what each owns, grade the nineteen, publish. The panel — Kshama, Pushpa Karnik of People, Preeti Khandekar of Engineering — finished grading on Monday, 10 August 2026.

Three things then went wrong. First, the grading produced a distribution nobody expected: of the ten Lead Product Managers, three graded to PM-4 Group Product Manager, five to PM-3 Senior Product Manager, two to PM-2. Seven would be told the word they had carried for years described a larger job than theirs. Second, Kalanidhi's benchmark of 15 September put Kosha's senior product managers at the seventeenth percentile of a forty-one-company sample. Third, on 28 September Kosha signed six ISB campus offers at a flat ₹29.00 lakh base, a number set by the placement market and not by its bands.

In February the levels problem had looked like a clarity problem; by October clarity was the cheap part. Kshama had also believed Kosha badly underpaid, until she rebuilt Kalanidhi's arithmetic herself in early October. She was no longer sure.

5. The people

Kshama Potdar, Chief Product Officer, Bengaluru. Wants a published ladder with scope definitions, having no other way to run promotion cases. Incentive: a product organisation she can grow to forty by FY28. Not saying: the levels were written before the scope definitions, still a draft paragraph each.

Pushpa Karnik, Chief People Officer, Bengaluru. Commissioned the Kalanidhi study; wants an eighteen per cent uplift to all band midpoints approved on Monday, the ladder being unpublishable without a market position behind it. Incentive: a quarterly attrition number. Not saying: she has already shown the draft ladder to three Lead PMs.

Kartik Poojary, Chief Financial Officer, Mumbai. Has approved an FY27 increment pool of ₹42.00 lakh for product and will not move it. Incentive: a Series D in the first quarter of FY28 and a board instruction to cut cost-to-income fifteen per cent. Not saying: he regards the 2023 clause as the most expensive sentence anyone at Kosha has written.

Kritika Pendse, Lead Product Manager, Bengaluru. Three years at Kosha, base ₹44.00 lakh, graded PM-3, protected by the clause on pay and title. Position: the ladder is a demotion in the costume of clarity. Incentive: a promotion case two cycles in the making. Not saying: she is in a third-round process elsewhere.

Pranav Katyal, Senior Product Manager at Kanthi Lending Works, Bengaluru. Wants to join Kosha as PM-4 running the merchant-credit surface; the panel graded him PM-3. Holds a Group PM offer from Khagol Payments Exchange. Not saying: the Khagol role has no engineers assigned yet.

Preeti Khandekar, Vice-President of Engineering, Pune. Runs a six-level engineering ladder stable since 2021 and wants product mapped onto it level for level. Incentive: her ladder's credibility, weakened whenever a PM negotiates outside it. Not saying: three of her engineering managers out-earn the product managers they work with, and she has used that in retention talks.

Karan Pethe, Head of Lending Partnerships, Nairobi. Wants a Group PM hired locally and says Bengaluru bands make no sense in Kenya. Incentive: a pilot that must show a portfolio by March 2027. Not saying: he has already told a Nairobi candidate the role is a Group PM role.

Prerna Kabra, board observer and partner at Kritya Growth Collective, Melbourne. Wants levels tied to a documented ladder, so Series D diligence is not a conversation about nineteen negotiated packages. Incentive: a clean data room. Not saying: another of her fund's companies has hired two Kosha product people this year.

Two more mattered without being in the room: Keshav Patodia, Principal Designer, Lisbon, on ₹78.00 lakh equivalent, 1.44 times Kosha's PM-4 midpoint, and Kaveri Puranik, Staff Data Scientist, Seoul, on ₹92.00 lakh, 1.23 times the PM-5 midpoint.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the proposed ladder, its bands, and where the nineteen sit against it. Compa-ratio means base over the midpoint of the level's band, so 1.00 is paid at the midpoint.

Two readings were circulating. Pushpa's: PM-4 and PM-5 are underpaid at 0.97 and 0.93, and that is where the leadership pipeline lives. Kshama's: at an overall compa-ratio of 1.02 Kosha pays above the midpoints of its own bands, and the dispersion inside PM-2 — seven bases running from ₹21.00 lakh to ₹33.00 lakh, a spread of 57.1 per cent over the lowest — is a legacy of three years without levels, not a market gap. Figure 2 draws the same data.

Exhibit 2 is the Kalanidhi benchmark, set out twice. Kalanidhi defines total compensation as base plus target bonus plus the full four-year grant value; Kosha annualises equity by dividing the grant by four. Against Kalanidhi's annualised median, Kosha's PM-3 cohort is 5.8 per cent behind. Against Kalanidhi's median as printed, 31.3 per cent behind.

Exhibit 3 costs the four things the committee could approve. The ordering surprised Kshama: raising every band eighteen per cent and bringing everyone to the new floor costs ₹11.42 lakh, while leaving the bands and bringing everyone to the existing midpoint costs ₹28.00 lakh. Both together cost ₹116.43 lakh, 2.77 times the pool.

That footnote was the figure Kshama kept returning to. At ₹29.00 lakh each January joiner enters at a compa-ratio of 1.14 against the PM-2 midpoint, out-earning five of the seven already graded PM-2: those at ₹21.00, ₹23.50, ₹25.00, ₹26.00 and ₹28.00 lakh. Exhibit 4 puts the candidate problem in the same currency — including a PM-3 grant of ₹24.00 lakh written for Pranav Katyal alone, against the ₹20.00 lakh every sitting PM-3 holds.

Two further figures circulated without agreement on what they meant. Of the eleven who joined before March 2023, six had a title change in the forty-two months to September 2026: 54.5 per cent, about 15.6 per cent a year crudely annualised. Of the eight who joined later, one had a title change over a mean tenure of seventeen months: 12.5 per cent, about 8.8 per cent a year on the same basis. Pushpa's memo quoted 54.5 against 12.5; Kshama's margin note read different windows; not comparable; HR did not retain effective dates for four of the eleven. Attrition, separately, ran at 25.6 per cent — five leavers in the twelve months to 30 September 2026 against an average headcount of 19.5.

7. Voices

“I am not asking for money. I am asking you not to take a word off a card I have carried for three years. If PM-3 is what the grading says, put me at PM-3 and keep calling me Lead. You wrote that promise.”

Kritika Pendse to Kshama Potdar, one-to-one, 6 October 2026

“Seventeenth percentile. Whatever the definitional argument, that is the number the board has seen, and a ladder published on top of it tells nineteen people how underpaid they are.”

Pushpa Karnik, leadership call, 8 October 2026

“Then let us not publish the bands. Publish the levels and the scope. Pay is a conversation with a manager; a level is a conversation with the company.”

Kartik Poojary, same call

“Engineering has had six levels since 2021 and nobody has resigned over a level since. Product has four and loses a person a quarter. The ladder is not your problem: you have four titles and nineteen different jobs.”

Preeti Khandekar, internal chat thread, 9 October 2026

“The Nairobi market for a PM with lending experience is about ₹34 lakh equivalent. Your PM-3 midpoint is ₹38 lakh. If the band is global I overpay and she becomes the highest-paid person in that office. If it is local I have two ladders by March. Tell me which before I call her back.”

Karan Pethe, email to Kshama Potdar, 9 October 2026

“If the letter says Senior Product Manager I will not sign it, and it is not the money — your PM-4 number beats Khagol's once I discount their paper. It is that I have been a Senior PM two years and will not do a third.”

Pranav Katyal, call with Kshama Potdar, 10 October 2026

“Decide it as a system. I have sat through a diligence where the answer to ‘how do you set levels’ was nineteen stories.”

Prerna Kabra, board note, 10 October 2026

8. The options as Kshama saw them on Sunday night

Option A. Publish the ladder, hold pay. Zero cost, the ₹42.00 lakh pool intact for April, two PMs red-circled above their ceilings with ₹4.00 lakh of excess frozen. Seven Lead PMs learn their level; five keep the title because the clause says so, two do not. Kritika Pendse probably resigns, probably taking someone with her.

Option B. Publish the ladder, lift everyone to the existing midpoint. ₹28.00 lakh, 4.05 per cent of payroll, inside the pool with ₹14.00 lakh spare. It gives something to those who move down in title, nothing to Kritika, already above her midpoint.

Option C. Raise the bands eighteen per cent, honour the new floors only. ₹11.42 lakh. It lets Pushpa take a market story to the board and costs less than Option B — elegant or a trick, depending on whether a band nobody is paid at is a real band.

Option D. Defer the ladder to April 2027 and make Pranav Katyal a PM-4 exception now. It buys six months. It also makes the new ladder's first use an exception to it, in writing, for an external hire — in the quarter six campus joiners arrive at ₹29.00 lakh.

All four options treat the ladder as the deliverable. Kshama had written one line at the foot of her notes and had not decided whether to say it aloud: the levels are drafted, the bands are drafted, the scope definitions are a paragraph each. Nothing in Exhibits 1 to 4 says what a Group Product Manager at Kosha owns — how much income, how many engineers, which decisions without escalation. Neither Pranav's grading nor Kritika's rested on a written definition of the thing graded, and no option answered Karan Pethe's question.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The committee met at nine on Monday, 12 October 2026, Prerna Kabra attending. Khagol's offer to Pranav Katyal lapsed on Wednesday, 14 October, three days after that Sunday night. The six ISB offers signed on 28 September were unconditional, at ₹29.00 lakh base, joining Tuesday, 5 January 2027 and adding 25.2 per cent to base payroll. The FY27 pool was ₹42.00 lakh, tied to a board instruction to cut cost-to-income fifteen per cent before a Series D in the first quarter of FY28. The March 2023 clause bound Kosha on eleven of the nineteen, on pay and title. Equity, worth ₹5.00 lakh to ₹12.00 lakh of annualised value across Exhibits 2 and 4, was priced at the November 2024 valuation of ₹1,850 crore, which the August 2026 secondary cleared 20.0 per cent below.

At about eleven Kshama drafted a message to Kritika Pendse, read it twice and did not send it. She had three slides, four costed columns and a candidate whose answer was due in seventy-two hours. What she did not have was a sentence beginning a Group Product Manager at Kosha is the person who — and she no longer knew whether that sentence was the first thing she owed the committee or a luxury.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Separate the four things this case keeps merging: title, level, band, scope. Which does Exhibit 1 measure?
  2. Exhibit 2 supports both “31.3 per cent behind” and “5.8 per cent behind”. Reconstruct each. Which would you take to a board, and what must you disclose with it?
  3. Option C costs ₹11.42 lakh and Option B ₹28.00 lakh. Why is the more generous-sounding option cheaper, and what does a published band actually commit a company to?
  4. Six campus joiners will out-earn five of the seven existing PM-2s. Is that a levelling, a pay or a hiring-market problem — and which option addresses it?
  5. Pranav Katyal says title matters more than money, and Exhibit 4 partly supports him. If you give him PM-4, what have you told the five Lead PMs graded PM-3? If you do not, what have you told the market?
  6. What should Kshama Potdar do before nine on Monday, and what exactly should she say to the committee — about the 2023 clause, Karan Pethe's question, and the scope definitions she has not written?
case20v1-craft.levels.comp:
Two Offers, One Ladder

A Product Management career case on levels, scope and compensation

1. Opening

On the evening of Monday, 12 October 2026, Gurleen Grewal sat on the floor of her ISB hostel room in Hyderabad with a laptop, two offer letters and a call booked for 9 p.m. with a mentor in Amsterdam. Both letters were for product management roles. Both would start in January 2027; both were due Friday, 16 October. Her spreadsheet said one offer paid more; her instinct said the other was the better job.

Gurleen was thirty-one. She had spent four years at Infosys as a consultant on banking implementations before the ISB MBA. Her father, Gurmeet Grewal, a retired bank manager in Ludhiana, had asked one question that morning: which letter said "Senior"? She wanted to answer the question underneath it: what each title would mean in the room where she worked.

2. Company background

The first offer came from Xamata Systems, a Pune company of about 900 people that sells payroll and statutory-compliance software to mid-sized Indian employers. Its product handles provident fund filings with the EPFO, ESIC contributions, TDS returns and the rule changes that follow the new labour codes. It competes with Zoho Payroll and RazorpayX Payroll, and had roughly ₹210 crore of annual recurring revenue.

The second offer came from Xipra Payments Network, headquartered in Mumbai, which runs merchant payment acceptance and UPI-based collection for several lakh small businesses. It sits in the same arena as PhonePe, Paytm and Razorpay, under NPCI's UPI rules and the RBI's directions on recurring mandates. It had about 2,400 employees and a product organisation of more than ninety people.

3. The situation

Gurleen received the Xamata letter on Thursday, 1 October and the Xipra letter on Monday, 5 October. Xamata extended its deadline to 16 October to match Xipra's. Figure 1 shows the sequence.

The two titles were not the same. Xamata offered "Product Manager", level P2 on a six-step ladder. Xipra offered "Senior Product Manager", level L4 on a ladder with eight steps. Figure 2 places both on one page, with the ladders as the companies shared them and the offered levels marked.

Gopal Ganguly, Xamata's Vice President of Product in Pune, had pitched plainly: she would own Statutory Filings, the product line that handles PF, ESI and TDS, with two engineering squads and a P&L that he called "yours to move". Gayatri Gadgil, a Group PM at Xipra in Mumbai, had offered a fast, well-funded team and a title that "will travel". Geetika Gulati, an ISB alumna working as a PM in Amsterdam, had warned her that title inflation is common, and that recruiters reading an Indian CV ask first how many people and how many rupees sit under it.

4. The people

Gurleen Grewal, Hyderabad, wants a role where her first PM year produces something she can defend in an interview: a number moved, a decision she made.

Gopal Ganguly, Pune, VP Product at Xamata, wants a PM who can run Statutory Filings unsupervised, since the previous owner left in August. He cannot hire above P2 but can shape the scope.

Gayatri Gadgil, Mumbai, Group PM at Xipra, wants to fill a vacancy on the mandate-disputes team quickly. Her team owns a feature area inside one large shared roadmap.

Geetika Gulati, Amsterdam, wants Gurleen to avoid choosing on the number alone, and is the one person who has sat on both sides of a hiring panel.

5. Exhibits

Figure 3 states the compensation as each letter defines it. Base is annual fixed pay. Bonus is the target variable payout as a percentage of base. Equity is the grant value stated in the letter, vesting evenly over four years, so one quarter of it counts each year. Annual total is base plus bonus plus one year of equity. All figures are in ₹ lakh.

Xipra's total was ₹10.55 lakh a year higher, and its cash was ₹7.55 lakh higher. On pay alone, the answer looked settled. But the bands in Figure 4, taken from each company's level guide, showed something her spreadsheet had hidden.

Xipra's "Senior" band starts at ₹38 lakh, only ₹2 lakh below the ceiling of Xamata's P2 band, yet its scope description is narrower. Figure 5 then set out what the two actual roles would hold, together with what Gurleen could learn from each firm's recent hiring history.

6. The options

Option A: accept Xipra's Senior PM offer. It brings the highest cash and equity, a title everyone understands and the Xipra brand. The cost is a narrow role, no revenue line and a historic chance of under one in three of promotion in three years.

Option B: accept Xamata's offer as written. It gives her a P&L of ₹62 crore ARR, fourteen engineers, direct customers and a likelier path to P3. The cost is ₹10.55 lakh a year in total pay compared with Xipra, a lower-sounding title and the risk of a first-year assignment that goes badly, since the line has just lost its owner.

Option C: negotiate with Xamata before answering. She would ask for a base at the top of the P2 band, ₹40.00 lakh, an equity grant of ₹56.00 lakh, and a written scope letter that names Statutory Filings, with a promotion review at twelve months. Xamata may refuse, so the request must go early in the week.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. From Figures 2 and 4, how would you explain the difference between a level, a title and a band? Which does a hiring manager control most easily?
  2. What does Figure 5 tell you about the real scope of each role? Which measures would you verify with a current employee?
  3. If Xipra's annual total is ₹10.55 lakh higher, what do you need to believe about the next three years for Xamata's role to be the better financial choice?
  4. What would you advise Gurleen to ask for in Option C, and in what order? What would you do if Gopal said no?

8. A note for the learner

The lens. Levels and bands are market facts before they are personal ones. A level is a company's claim about the scope a person can handle; a title is a label that companies fit to the level in different ways; a band is the pay range attached to the level. Candidates compare bands because they are numbers. The harder and more useful comparison is scope: how much money, how many people and how many decisions the role places under the person holding it. Scope is what a later employer will read.

One defensible path. Pursue Option C, and fall back to Option B if Xamata declines. The reasoning has three steps. First, the pay gap is real but narrower. If Xamata agrees to Gurleen's request, its annual total becomes ₹40.00 lakh base plus ₹4.00 lakh bonus (10% of base) plus ₹14.00 lakh equity (₹56.00 lakh divided by four), which is ₹58.00 lakh. That is ₹4.15 lakh below Xipra's ₹62.15 lakh, a gap of 6.7%, and ₹6.40 lakh above Xamata's first offer. Second, the promotion history in Figure 5 and the scope in the same exhibit both point the same way: a P2 who delivers on ₹62 crore ARR is a credible P3 candidate, while a Senior PM on a feature area with no revenue attached has little evidence to carry to the next interview. Third, her stated aim, to build a record she can defend, is better served by ownership than by a title, and Geetika's warning about European recruiters shows that scope is what travels.

The path carries risk: the line has just lost its owner, and equity is paper value until liquidity. It still holds because it keeps the larger scope, narrows the pay gap, and costs only a request she can make this week. A student who picks Xipra should say what scope they will seek within a year and who will confirm it in writing.
exp20v2-craft.levels.comp:
PM Levels, Scope and Compensation

Why the size of the problem you own matters more than the band attached to your title

1. Three offers in a week

On 9 March 2026, Meera Joglekar, a final-term student at the Indian School of Business in Hyderabad, held three written offers for her first product management role. She had spent four years in logistics operations before the MBA, and she had until 16 March, seven days, to answer. Rasdhar Payments Network, a large and listed payments company, offered the title Product Manager. Manjusha Freight Labs, a business-to-business software company in its Series C stage, offered Senior Product Manager. Jalsetu Marketplace Group, a young two-sided marketplace for regional produce, offered Product Lead.

The titles ran opposite to the money: Rasdhar paid most and named her most junior. Her mentor, Mrunal Raut, formerly six years in product at Flipkart, read the letters and asked a different question: what would she be responsible for on her first Monday, and what would she be allowed to decide?

The stakes were larger than one year's salary. A first job fixes the anchor later employers use: recruiters ask for current level and fixed pay. A narrowly scoped first role leaves a record of small things executed, which later negotiation cannot fully repair. This page follows Meera through the decision and uses it to build one argument: a level is a statement about scope, a band is a statement about price, and the first is the more durable asset.

2. The idea

Four terms need defining before any number is read. A level is a company's internal grade for a job, such as P2 or P3, defined by what the person is trusted to own. A band is the range of fixed annual pay the company will pay at that level. A title is the label printed on the offer and the business card, which the company can set freely and which therefore varies widely between firms. Scope is the size and difficulty of the problem a person owns, and it has four dimensions: surface (how much of the product), horizon (how far ahead the consequences of the decisions run), ambiguity (whether someone else has already defined the problem), and leverage (how many people's work the person directs without managing them).

The apparatus solved a pricing problem: large organisations needed to pay thousands of people consistently without negotiating each case afresh. Job evaluation systems, associated with the consultant Edward Hay from roughly the 1940s, scored jobs on know-how, problem solving and accountability, and attached pay ranges to the resulting grades. Technology companies later adopted the logic for engineers and, from roughly the 2000s, for product managers. Salary sites such as AmbitionBox and Levels.fyi now publish self-reported figures by level, so levels and bands are market facts before they are personal ones.

The sentence Meera could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: a level is a claim about the size of problem someone can be trusted with, and pay is only the price the market puts on that claim this year.

The change between rungs is not harder work or more vocabulary. The problem arrives less finished: at P1 someone hands over a defined task, at P3 the person decides which problems in a module are worth solving, and at P5 the person decides what the business is trying to become.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have four steps; practitioners leave the last two implicit. First, the company defines levels by scope. Second, it attaches a band to each, benchmarked against survey data. Third, it places each hire at a level by comparing the seat's scope with the candidate's evidence of past scope, not by comparing last salary with a band. Fourth, it places the hire within the band, where negotiation lives.

Jayant Rawool, Manjusha's head of product, shared his ladder when Meera asked; Table 1 gives its bands.

Table 1. Manjusha Freight Labs fixed-pay bands, ₹ lakh per year. Midpoint = (min + max) / 2; spread = (max - min) / min.
LevelTitleMinMaxMidpointSpread (%)
P1Associate PM14221857.1
P2Product Manager20302550.0
P3Senior PM28403442.9
P4Group PM38564747.4
P5Director52806653.8

Two features of the table matter. The bands overlap: a P2 at the top of the range earns ₹30 lakh, which is more than a P3 at the bottom, at ₹28 lakh. Pay alone tells an outsider little about level. And Meera's offer of ₹30 lakh fixed sits below the P3 midpoint. Her compa-ratio, defined as pay divided by band midpoint, is 30 / 34 = 0.88. Below 1.0 is normal for a new external hire.

Neighbouring levels share ₹20 to 22 lakh (P1, P2), ₹28 to 30 lakh (P2, P3), ₹38 to 40 lakh (P3, P4) and ₹52 to 56 lakh (P4, P5).

4. A worked example

Meera built one comparison in ₹ lakh per year. Equity vests evenly over four years, so the annual figure is the grant divided by four. The one-off joining bonus is excluded from steady state. Equity share is equity per year divided by steady-state total.

Table 2. The three offers, ₹ lakh per year. Year 1 total = fixed + variable + equity per year + joining bonus. Steady state excludes the bonus.
OfferFixedVariable (target)Equity grant (4 yrs)Equity per yearJoining bonusYear 1 totalSteady stateEquity share (%)
Rasdhar, Product Manager38448126605422.2
Manjusha, Senior PM30380200535337.7
Jalsetu, Product Lead26060150414136.6

On paper Rasdhar leads in year one by ₹7 lakh over Manjusha (60 minus 53). But paper equity is not the same as cash. Rasdhar's shares can be sold when they vest; Manjusha's and Jalsetu's cannot until a buyback or listing, and many private grants end at nothing. Meera therefore counted half of Manjusha's paper value and a quarter of Jalsetu's. These weights are judgements, not facts.

Table 3. Second pass: equity counted at a liquidity weight, ₹ lakh per year. Counted equity = paper equity per year × share counted.
OfferFixed + variableEquity per year (paper)Share counted (%)Equity countedRisk-adjusted steady state
Rasdhar42121001254
Manjusha3320501043
Jalsetu2615253.7529.75

Cash arithmetic favours Rasdhar; the question was whether anything it could not price justified ₹11 lakh a year. Meera tested one more chain. Rasdhar's fixed pay grows at 8 per cent a year for two cycles: 38 × 1.08 × 1.08 = 44.32 (precisely 44.3232). At Manjusha, a promotion to P4 is a plausible trajectory, with fixed pay rising 15 per cent and then 12 per cent: 30 × 1.15 × 1.12 = 38.64. The two rises compound to 28.8 per cent, not 27. The fixed-pay gap narrows from ₹8 lakh to about ₹5.68 lakh. It does not close. What no table shows is what each record would say in 2028.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Level is not title

"Senior" is the second rung at one firm, the fourth at another. Ask for the level code and band.

Scope is not headcount

A senior individual contributor who sets direction for four squads has more scope than a manager of two juniors.

Bands overlap, so pay is not rank

Table 1 showed it: ₹28 to 30 lakh is a P2 salary at one end and a P3 salary at the other.

Total compensation is a forecast

Fixed pay is a promise, variable pay a target, equity a probability-weighted claim. Adding them, as Table 2 does, is safe only when weights are stated, as in Table 3.

Promotion follows demonstrated scope, not tenure

Most ladders promote people already operating at the next level. Seats that cap scope stall careers whatever the band.

Market data lags and is self-reported

Sites such as AmbitionBox and Levels.fyi are self-reported and skew towards recent joiners and larger firms.

What this framework cannot tell you

It cannot tell you whether a manager will deliver the promised scope, or whether the company will survive.

Questions to ask before relying on a figure

Who defined this level, and when? What did the last two people in the seat own at month twelve?

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; early and large

In consumer products, scope is measured in users and a movable metric such as retention. At Rasdhar, Meera's seat was the saved-card flow, one of fourteen squads: wide reach, but small decisions reviewed by many hands.

In business-to-business products, scope is measured in accounts and contract value. At Manjusha, the dispatch and route-planning module carried an annual recurring revenue target of ₹18 crore, and Meera would work from the first quarter with named customers. In a marketplace, scope has two sides, supply and demand. Jalsetu's offer put her in charge of supplier onboarding for the whole supply side, with five colleagues: one designer, three engineers and one analyst.

Size changes everything else. In a large company levels are formal and scope grows through a defined process. In an early-stage company levels are loose, titles are generous because they cost nothing, and scope is the main thing on offer. A Product Lead at a young firm may own more than a Group PM at a large one, with less mentoring and a company that might not exist in three years.

7. Common mistakes

Anchoring on the headline fixed number

The symptom is a one-column spreadsheet; the misunderstanding is that cash this year equals career value. The cheapest diagnostic is rebuilding it as Table 3, plus a column for the evidence each seat adds to a résumé.

Reading the title as the level

The symptom is celebrating "Senior" unexamined; the misunderstanding is that titles compare across firms. The diagnostic: what is the level code and band?

Mistaking a large team for large scope

The symptom is choosing the seat with most reports; the misunderstanding is that leverage requires management. The diagnostic: what can the holder decide without permission, and what are they measured on?

Treating the band as fixed

The symptom is accepting the first placement in the band; the misunderstanding is that a band is one price. The diagnostic is the compa-ratio: Meera's 0.88 told her there was room to ask.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Meera's decision has a recognisable shape. The candidate converts every offer to one unit and one definition of total. She writes down the scope of each seat on four dimensions before she looks at the pay. She asks each manager for the level, the band, and what the last holder owned at month twelve. She applies liquidity weights openly and shows how the answer moves. And she treats the gap in cash as a price: she can say what she is paying ₹11 lakh a year to obtain, and she can name how she will know within six months whether she received it.

9. What Meera decided

On 14 March, two days before her deadline, Meera accepted Manjusha. Rasdhar paid ₹11 lakh a year more on a risk-adjusted basis, but its scope was one flow among fourteen, with a one-quarter horizon, and would leave her with a record of small, reviewed work. Jalsetu offered the widest scope but the lowest counted pay, ₹29.75 lakh, and no senior mentor. Manjusha sat between: a real module, an ₹18 crore target, a P3 level whose band she understood, and a manager who had shown her the ladder. She asked for the scope in writing, and for a review of her level after six months.

The decision is defensible rather than correct: if the promised scope fails to appear, she paid for it. What she learned is portable: price the seat, not the title.

The next topic is choosing between offers: how to weigh risk, learning and cash when the weights themselves are uncertain.

Two questions to sit with. First, if a company would not disclose the level and band for a seat, what would you infer? Second, think of the largest problem you have owned without being told how to solve it: which of the four dimensions of scope did it stretch, and what would an employer need to see to believe it?
exp40v2-craft.levels.comp:
PM Levels, Scope and Compensation

How bands are built and calibrated, what scope means mechanically, and why the size of the problem you own outranks the grade printed on the letter

1. Two desks, eight days apart

On 14 September 2026 Nupur Pendse, vice-president of product at Nirmiti Devices Industries, had sixteen days to put a product-management job architecture before her compensation committee. Nirmiti, founded in Pune in 2014, builds industrial smart meters and the platform that reads them: 1,180 employees, nine product managers in four grades she had never audited, hardware frozen eleven months before shipment and then resident on a wall for a decade. She also had an offer out to a candidate asking ₹5.0 lakh above budget, and a rewards head, Ulka Nerurkar, repeating the word "compression".

On 22 September, in Bengaluru, that candidate was doing his own arithmetic. Pranav Naravane, six years a product manager after three as an engineer, was a Senior PM at Nishaan Payments Network — listed, 14,000 people — where he owned the card-on-file flow. He held Nirmiti's offer at P5, titled Principal Product Manager; a second from Praroop Marketplace Collective, a Series B services marketplace, titled Group Product Manager; and a Nishaan counter-offer. His mentor Prerna Umrigar, five years in product at Flipkart, asked the question that separates these decisions: "In eighteen months, what will you be able to prove you decided?"

The two are one decision from opposite sides of the table: Nupur prices scope so it can be bought consistently, Pranav buys scope and pays in foregone cash. Levels and bands are market facts before they are personal ones, which is why both reason from the same survey. A band is a price; a level is a claim about the size of problem a person can be trusted with; only the second compounds.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A level is a company's internal grade for a job, defined by what the holder is trusted to own. A band is the range of fixed annual pay attached to it, described by a midpoint and a width. A title is a label the company sets at no cost. Scope is the size and difficulty of the problem owned, in four scorable dimensions: surface, how much of the product; horizon, how far forward consequences run; ambiguity, how much arrives already defined; leverage, how much work is redirected without managing the people doing it.

The apparatus was invented to price jobs, not to build careers. From the late 1940s Edward Hay and his successors built point-factor job evaluation: score a job on know-how, problem solving and accountability, group similar totals into a grade, attach one range to the grade. Survey houses — Mercer, Aon, WTW — priced grades against percentiles of reported pay. Technology firms extended it to product managers; Levels.fyi and AmbitionBox then made the results semi-public, which is why a candidate arrives knowing the band.

Four schools disagree about what follows. Market pricing: a band is a percentile of observed pay. Signs "we pay the 60th percentile of comparable firms"; refuses "our grades mean what theirs mean". Job architecture: internal consistency first, because unfairness between neighbours causes resignations. Signs "equivalent scope is paid within one band"; refuses "a scarce skill may be paid outside the structure". Scope first: the level states problem size and pay lags it. Signs "promote only people already at the next level"; refuses "a title may be granted to retain someone". Pay for person, associated with Netflix: no bands, one top-of-market number each. Signs "levels generate title-chasing"; refuses "consistency survives past a hundred people". Nupur held the third position, audited by the second.

3. Mechanics: how a band is actually constructed

The procedure has six steps, three usually left implicit. One: define levels by scope, not pay — five levels, P2 to P6, each described by what arrives undefined. Two: buy market data for one anchor level. Ulka's cut for P3 — India technology, Pune and Bengaluru, engineering-led firms of 500 to 2,000 employees — held 148 incumbents at a median of ₹28.5 lakh and a 75th percentile of ₹36.0 lakh. Three: choose a policy percentile and interpolate. Nirmiti's is the 60th: 28.5 + (10 ÷ 25) × (36.0 − 28.5) = ₹31.50 lakh, from which the rest derives.

Four: choose a midpoint progression — a widening ladder, 22 per cent from P2 to P3, then 24, 26 and 28, each midpoint computed from the rounded midpoint below and rounded to the nearest ₹0.5 lakh, which is why realised progressions differ from designed ones. Five: choose a width, (maximum ÷ minimum) − 1, widened from 40 per cent at P2 to 60 at P6; given midpoint M and width w, minimum = 2M ÷ (2 + w), maximum = minimum × (1 + w). Six: read the overlap and accept it.

Table 1. Nirmiti bands for 2027, ₹ lakh of fixed pay. Midpoint = (min + max) ÷ 2; width = (max ÷ min) − 1; realised progression = this midpoint ÷ the one below, − 1.
LevelTitleMinMidpointMaxWidth (%)Designed progression (%)Realised progression (%)

The overlap is the second-order effect, not a defect. Because each band is wide relative to the step between midpoints, neighbours share a zone: ₹25.7 to 30.3 lakh belongs to both P2 and P3, which is 4.6 ÷ 8.6 = 53.5 per cent of the P2 span; the same calculation gives 52.6 per cent at P3–P4, 53.8 at P4–P5 and 54.2 at P5–P6. A P5 at band minimum earns ₹38.4 lakh, a P4 at band maximum ₹46.8 lakh, so anyone inferring a level from a salary is reading noise.

Two placement statistics then govern everything, and experts never confuse them. Compa-ratio is pay ÷ midpoint; range penetration is (pay − minimum) ÷ (maximum − minimum). Pranav's ₹43.0 lakh gives 43.0 ÷ 49.0 = 0.878, a near miss, and (43.0 − 38.4) ÷ 21.2 = 21.7 per cent, the floor of the level. The first prices him against the market; the second is the firm's remaining headroom before it must promote him.

4. When the apparatus applies, and when it misleads

Three testable conditions. One: the level descriptions discriminate. If adjacent levels cannot be told apart by what arrives undefined, the structure pays for tenure. Nirmiti passes: P4 owns a module, P5 decides which modules exist. Praroop fails, which is Section 8. Two: the survey sample resembles the seat. Nupur's 148 incumbents come from engineering-led firms of similar size, so the cut prices a Nirmiti P3 fairly; it would misprice a PM holding a Bureau of Indian Standards certification window. Three: the equity is comparable. It is not: Nishaan's stock sells on an exchange, Praroop's options are a Series B claim, and they cannot share a column without a weight.

It misleads in three situations: below roughly fifteen PMs, where any structure encodes who was hired first; in a market repricing faster than the survey refreshes, as Indian product roles did in 2021 and 2022; and wherever a level is granted to retain someone.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

The clean ladder breaks in five places. Platform and multi-product. Prayukti Platform Group, a logistics software firm Nupur benchmarked against, levels platform PMs one grade below application PMs of equivalent surface because their customers are internal, and the roles became a tax. The fix counts migrations completed and dependent teams unblocked. Two-sided marketplaces. A PM who owns only supply owns half a loop, so scope is scored on whether the holder can commit both sides; Praroop's Group PM can. Regulated products. At Panah Insurance Services decisions pass a compliance gate the PM does not control, capping ambiguity whatever the title.

Hardware plus software inverts the usual pattern: software scope is reversible, a freeze eleven months before shipment followed by a decade on a wall is not. Nirmiti therefore scores horizon higher than a software firm would, and pays a P5 for work others call P4. AI-native products compress upward: at Udbhav Reasoning Labs nobody has ten years of relevant experience, the second product level is titled Staff, and its band maximum exceeds Nirmiti's P6 minimum. Bands there are set by scarcity.

At the seams, firms publish one ladder and run exceptions: the red circle, holding someone above band maximum flat until the band catches up; the VP-signed out-of-band offer; and the dual-ladder fiction, in which an individual-contributor P5 and a managing P5 share one band while Nupur's survey showed managers at median ₹50.5 lakh against ₹48.5 lakh for individual contributors — a 4.1 per cent premium Nirmiti absorbs.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Scope is four things, and they trade against each other

A competent practitioner says a role is bigger; an expert asks which dimension grew. A seat can widen surface while shrinking ambiguity — more product, fewer decisions — a demotion dressed as a promotion. The tell is a job description that lists systems owned and names no decision the holder makes.

The group compa-ratio is weighted; the average of averages is not

Nirmiti's nine PMs — one P2, three P3s, three P4s, two P5s — cost ₹313.5 lakh of fixed pay against band midpoints summing to ₹335.5 lakh: a group compa-ratio of 0.934. The unweighted mean of its four level ratios — 0.877 at P2, 0.970 at P3, 0.970 at P4, 0.872 at P5 — is 0.922. The gap decides budgets, because only the weighted figure is money.

Hiring below the midpoint funds next year's correction

Adding Pranav at ₹43.0 lakh takes the bill to ₹356.5 lakh against midpoints of ₹384.5 lakh, so the group ratio falls to 0.927. A falling ratio is the standard evidence for a larger merit pool, so a disciplined hire becomes next year's argument for money. The reading that a cheap hire is a saving misses a budget cycle.

Compression is a recurring liability; equity is not

Pranav asked for ₹48.0 lakh: compa-ratio 0.980, range penetration 45.3 per cent. Nirmiti's two existing P5s earn ₹41.5 and ₹44.0 lakh, so matching him meant lifting both — (48.0 − 41.5) + (48.0 − 44.0) = ₹10.5 lakh on a P5 fixed bill of ₹85.5 lakh, a 12.3 per cent increase recurring every year. Her alternative was a grant of ₹60.0 lakh against the standard P5 grant of ₹48.0 lakh: ₹3.0 lakh a year more of paper, ₹1.5 lakh at her own 50 per cent liquidity discount. Grants sit outside the band and salaries inside it — the asymmetry behind most refusals to move fixed pay.

Equity share is a design parameter, and offers drift from it

Nirmiti designed its P5 package at midpoint: ₹49.0 lakh fixed, variable at 15 per cent of fixed or ₹7.35 lakh, and ₹12.0 lakh annualised equity — ₹68.35 lakh in total, of which equity is 12.0 of the 68.35, or 17.6 per cent. Pranav's runs 43.0 + 6.45 + 15.0 = ₹64.45 lakh, of which equity is 15.0 of the 64.45, or 23.3 per cent. Equity as a share of total compensation is measured against total compensation, never fixed pay, where the same grant reads 34.9 per cent and flatters everyone.

Vesting changes the shape of a grant, not its size

An even four-year grant delivers a quarter a year; 10/20/30/40 delivers the same total and a very different first two years. It is a retention device: nobody who has drawn Figure 3 confuses "₹96 lakh of equity" with "₹24 lakh this year".

Variable pay is a target, and targets have a payout history

Nishaan has paid 92 per cent of target over three cycles, turning Pranav's ₹5.10 lakh into 5.10 × 0.92 = ₹4.69 lakh; Praroop paid 60 per cent last year, turning ₹3.80 lakh into ₹2.28 lakh. The expert question is who sets the target and whether the holder controls the metric.

A promotion increment and a market increment are different instruments

Staying at Nishaan, ₹34.0 lakh at 8 per cent for two cycles reaches 34.0 × 1.08 × 1.08 = ₹39.66 lakh, a compound rise of 16.6 per cent rather than 16; with a promotion in year two at 14 per cent instead, 34.0 × 1.08 × 1.14 = ₹41.86 lakh, a compound 23.1 per cent. Both are two-year figures, not comparable with a one-year survey movement. The ladder moves too: if the survey median rises 9 per cent in 2028 and 7.5 per cent in 2029, the P5 midpoint of ₹49.0 lakh becomes 49.0 × 1.09 × 1.075 = ₹57.42 lakh, a compound 17.2 per cent. A person at a constant compa-ratio is running to stay still.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

Scope is denominated differently, and that is the real difference. In consumer products it is users and a movable metric: Pranav's flow touches tens of millions of users and almost no decisions. In business software it is accounts and contract value; in enterprise, named deals and implementation risk, which raises a seat that looks small by surface. In platforms it is dependent teams; in marketplaces, both sides of the loop; in hardware, the freeze date, which is why Nupur scored horizon at the top of her scale. In AI products it is unsettled: evaluation sets and cost per inference are the emerging units.

Stage matters more than product type. Below about fifteen PMs, levels are theatre and scope is the only currency — Praroop's position, and why its title cost nothing. In a growth-stage firm the architecture arrives at an investor's request, painfully, because it prices what was free. In a listed firm levels drive grant sizes, approval limits and disclosure. The four dimensions are the same everywhere, so all three seats score on one rubric.

8. Three worked examples

Example one: scoring the seats before looking at the money

Prerna made Pranav score the seats first, on a point-factor plan in miniature: four factors, weights summing to one, each scored 1 to 5 against written anchors. Nishaan scores 2.20, the seat he holds; Nirmiti 4.05, lifted by a horizon nothing else matches; Praroop 4.50, lifted by ambiguity and by a Group PM who commands both sides of a marketplace and two PMs. Then the money, in Table 3.

Example two: the band Nupur did not widen

Nirmiti's 2027 merit budget is 9.0 per cent of the product fixed-pay bill — on the post-hire bill of ₹356.5 lakh, ₹32.09 lakh across ten people. Had Nupur met Pranav at ₹48.0 lakh, the ₹10.5 lakh compression fix would have taken 32.7 per cent of that pool for two incumbents, leaving ₹21.59 lakh for the other eight. She also declined to widen the P5 band, because a band widened for one candidate is no longer a price. The risk is explicit: at 21.7 per cent penetration Nirmiti must promote him within two years or the saving is a false economy.

Example three: where it failed, at Praroop

Praroop had eleven product managers in January 2026 and no levels, all titled Group Product Manager or above, titles being the founders' cheapest currency. At the Series B the board asked for a job architecture. Its consultant anchored at the market median rather than the 60th percentile, giving a P3 midpoint of ₹28.5 lakh and band maxima of ₹27.4, ₹33.7, ₹42.6 and ₹54.1 lakh at P2 to P5. Mapped against scope, seven of the eleven landed below their titles, as Table 5 shows.
