Four of the 11 PMs, 36.4 per cent, were red-circled above their new maximum, carrying ₹17.4 lakh of above-band pay against a bill of ₹418.0 lakh, or 4.2 per cent. The failure was not the arithmetic: Praroop had sold titles it never defined, and the architecture made that legible on one page. Three of the four resigned within seven months, by 31 August 2026, taking ₹133.6 lakh of the ₹418.0 lakh bill, 32.0 per cent, out of the door. The recovery, run by co-founder Ulhas Nene, rewrote the descriptions around what arrives undefined, promoted two internal P3s, and re-advertised the three seats with the scope rather than the title in the requisition — one of which is Pranav's offer.

9. Failure modes, warnings and the cost of late detection

Title inflation. Warning: a title granted in a retention conversation. Question: what changed in their scope that day? Late cost: Praroop's — 32.0 per cent of a payroll gone in seven months. Anchoring on fixed pay. Warning: a one-column comparison. Question: what is the four-year-average total, at what liquidity weight? Negotiating the band, not the placement. Warning: a candidate asking the firm to exceed its maximum. Question: what is my range penetration?

Ignoring compression. Warning: a new hire paid above two incumbents doing the same work. Question, Ulka's: what does this offer cost in year two, across everyone? Late cost: a third of a merit pool.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Wide bands against more levels. Nupur's 55 per cent band at P5 lets a person grow for five years without a promotion: humane to the job-architecture school, a trap to the scope-first school, because the only signal of progress is a number nobody else can see. The narrow-band camp would split P5 into two grades of 35 per cent width, citing attrition data in which resignations cluster in the fourth year in a level. It is wrong if promotion events are the problem.

Should equity sit in the band? The market-pricing school says no: equity is granted, repriced and forfeitable, and banding it converts a variable claim into a promise. The scope-first school replies that excluding it is how Nupur avoided paying Pranav properly — ₹3.0 lakh of paper against a ₹10.5 lakh cash liability is arbitrage, and the employee bears the variance. Both are right about the mechanism; only evidence on realised grant outcomes would settle who carries the risk, and private Indian firms do not publish it.

Can scope be scored at all? Table 2's rubric is defensible and also a construction: Pranav chose the weights, and moving ambiguity from 0.30 to 0.20 and leverage from 0.20 to 0.30 would have widened Praroop's lead. Sceptics say scope is judged, not measured, and a rubric merely launders the judgement. A written rubric at least exposes its weights.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this quotes a band. Someone who has internalised it asks, in the first fifteen minutes, for the level code, the band's minimum, midpoint and maximum, and what the last two holders of the seat decided without asking permission. They convert every offer to one unit and one definition of total, stating their weights aloud. They price an offer across the population in year two, and treat the cash gap as a price, not a verdict.

12. The two decisions

On 29 September 2026 Nupur signed the ladder in Table 1 unchanged, held the P5 offer at ₹43.0 lakh, raised the grant to ₹60.0 lakh and wrote a month-nine review of level and placement into the letter. Her reasoning: the ₹10.5 lakh compression liability was the real number in the room, not the ₹5.0 lakh gap.

On 1 October Pranav accepted Nirmiti — the less interesting seat by his own rubric, 4.05 against Praroop's 4.50, at an above-average ₹20.33 lakh for a marginal scope point in the wrong direction. What tipped it was the horizon: a decade-long consequence on a frozen platform was a decision he could not get elsewhere, and Praroop's three seats were open because three people had just left. The decision is defensible, not correct. If the promised scope has not appeared by month nine, he has paid for it.

Three questions for discussion. First, Nupur traded ₹3.0 lakh a year of paper against a ₹10.5 lakh cash liability — legitimate design, or risk pushed onto the person least able to price it? Second, Praroop's architecture was correct and cost 32.0 per cent of its product payroll in seven months; what should Ulhas Nene have done differently? Third, what evidence should a candidate demand before believing a scope promise?

13. Going deeper

The India PM market and how MBAs enter it supplies the structure behind Table 1: who the 148 respondents are. Choosing between offers takes up where Table 4 stops, when the weights are contested. PM interviews is where a scope claim is tested rather than asserted, and it decides the band. Building a PM portfolio and narrative assembles the evidence that lets the claim survive a panel. Transitioning into product management sets the anchor negotiation only partly repairs. Your first 90 days in a PM role is where Pranav learns whether his scope is real, a PM's operating system lets him hold it, and continuous learning as a PM keeps the claim credible as scope is redenominated.
case40v1-craft.specialise:
Jagruti Phadnis and the Recovery Requisition

Choosing a PM specialisation — an ambiguous case set in Bengaluru, November 2026

1. Sunday night, 15 November 2026

The Diwali lights were still strung along the balcony railing of Jagruti Phadnis's flat in Indiranagar, a week after anyone had switched them on. On the table were three printed documents: a debrief for a candidate named Jaswant Thube, a debrief for a candidate named Juhi Kanitkar, and a nomination form for the general manager of a new business line, with her own name typed into it by someone else and the signature box empty.

At ten the next morning, Monday 16 November, the board of Jaanch Systems would hold its half-yearly talent review. Two things were expected of her. As hiring manager for the Principal Product Manager requisition on the collections and recovery line, she had to name a finalist. As a director of product with eleven years behind her, she had to say whether she wanted the general manager's job on that same line, or whether she would go on being the person in the company who understood default behaviour better than anyone else.

When the requisition opened in August she had assumed these were separate questions. By November they were not: whichever profile she hired would decide what she herself was free to become, and she suspected both decisions were framed to suit everybody except her.

2. Jaanch Systems, and the decision of April 2022

Jaanch Systems was founded in Bengaluru in 2017 by Jyotika Barve and two engineers from a private bank's technology arm. It sells the software that sits between a loan application and a yes or a no: bureau pulls, bank-statement analysis, income inference and policy rules assembled into one automated verdict. In the year to 31 March 2026 it billed roughly ₹200 crore across four product lines and employed about 900 people, engineering split between Bengaluru and Pune.

One decision from April 2022 still shapes everything. Offered a third-party rules engine, Jaanch built its own; Jyotika argued that a lending-decision engine is not plumbing but the product itself. The second half of that decision mattered more and was barely discussed: the company resolved to hire only product managers with direct domain experience. Every one hired between 2022 and 2024 came from a lender, a bureau or a collections agency; none from consumer internet, marketplaces or developer tools.

The policy worked for what it was aimed at: Jaanch's underwriting product is the most configurable in the Indian market and survives regulatory change with less rework than its rivals'. But it left a product organisation of twenty-two people in which, by Jairaj Menon's count, not one had ever shipped something a customer could buy without a signature. Jaanch has never run a self-serve motion.

3. The industry

Indian lending infrastructure in 2026 is crowded and heavily governed. The Reserve Bank of India's digital lending framework, its rules on first-loss default guarantees and its expectations on recovery conduct all bear on what a product like Jaanch's may automate, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act turned consent, retention and grievance handling into requirements with named owners. The Account Aggregator framework made consented financial data routine, removing one of Jaanch's early advantages. TransUnion CIBIL, CRIF High Mark and Experian remain the spine of any decision; Perfios, Lentra and Signzy compete for the same bank budgets.

The economics also shifted: lenders that spent freely on acquisition between 2021 and 2024 found their unsecured portfolios souring by 2025, and budget moved from the front of the funnel to the back. Collections became the fastest-growing line item.

Jaanch's exposure is not only Indian. Its second-largest new contract of 2026 came from a Nairobi lender, signed in June after a four-month evaluation and sold on the recovery module. Its principal data scientist sits in Warsaw, its design lead in Stockholm, its Asia-Pacific success lead in Manila and its sales head in Melbourne (Figure A). Recovery is its first multi-market product, and the only one whose buyers include institutions that will never meet a Jaanch salesperson.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Jagruti joined Jaanch in 2019 from a housing finance company, where she had spent four years on credit policy before moving into product. She owned fraud and identity, then underwriting, and from 2024 the small recovery initiative Jyotika treated as an experiment. She built it with two engineers and an analyst. It billed ₹12 crore in its first full year; the FY27 plan asks ₹36 crore.

Three beliefs guided that plan, and each has weakened. The first was that recovery would sell to underwriting's buyers through the same committees; in practice the Nairobi contract and two Indian NBFC deals came in through a different door, a collections head rather than a chief risk officer, with a smaller budget and less patience. The second was that the line needed deeper domain knowledge than Jaanch already had. The third was that Jagruti would go on running it herself.

The third broke in September. Jyotika told Jagruti that recovery would become a line with its own profit and loss from April 2027, and that the general manager's role was hers if she wanted it. A general manager at Jaanch carries revenue, pricing and a quota. It is, as Jagruti wrote in her notes, "a job that will not use the only thing I am unusually good at."

The requisition opened on Monday 3 August 2026 and the slate closed on Friday 6 November, ninety-five days later. On Jagruti's instruction Jairaj Menon's team worked two tracks in parallel, because she could not decide which she wanted: candidates with deep collections experience, and generalist platform product managers who had built self-serve products elsewhere. Exhibit 1 is the funnel that resulted.

The shape of Exhibit 1 is the first thing the executives disagree about. The specialist pool was small, 180 records against 420, and concentrated: more than half came from four employers, three of them lenders Jaanch sells to. It also converted better at every stage. Jaideep Rane reads that as the market naming what is scarce and therefore valuable. Jairaj reads the same table as a warning that the pool is nearly exhausted and that replacing such a hire would be far harder than replacing a generalist.

Compensation sharpened the disagreement. Exhibit 2 sets out what each finalist is asking, against the band the compensation committee approved in April.

Jaswant's ask of ₹110 lakh sits ₹13 lakh above the approved ceiling of ₹97 lakh, about 13 per cent above it. It is also, to the rupee, what Jagruti earns. Juhi's ask of ₹89 lakh is ₹8 lakh inside the ceiling. The difference between the finalists is ₹21 lakh a year. Set against the ₹12 crore recovery billed in FY26 that is 1.75 per cent of the line's revenue; set against the ₹36 crore the FY27 plan asks of it, 0.58 per cent. Jigar Vora, the chief financial officer, holds that the gap is trivial against revenue and serious against precedent: break the band once for scarcity and it stops being a band.

Exhibit 3 places the line inside the company.

Exhibit 4 is the evidence everyone cites and nobody agrees about. It covers the ten product managers Jaanch has hired since April 2024, sorted by the profile they were hired as.

Jaideep reads the median column and sees twelve weeks: the specialist shipped in seven, the generalist took nineteen, and twelve weeks of a loaded squad is a cost he can price. Jyotika reads the same two figures the other way. A specialist ships in seven weeks, she argues, because a specialist ships what the domain already knows how to build; the generalist spends a quarter discovering something nobody had asked for, which is what a new line needs, and the promotion column is where that shows. Both are reading rows of six and four people. Figure B sets out how the decision arrived.

5. The people

Jagruti Phadnis, 37, director of product, Bengaluru. Seven of her eleven years have been inside credit risk, and few people in India can argue about roll rates and recovery conduct rules in the same sentence. Her stated position is that the line needs depth before breadth. Her incentive is unclear even to her: the GM role pays ₹140 lakh against her present ₹110 lakh, but she has told two friends she does not want to spend her forties on a quota. What she is not saying is that she holds the outside offer in Exhibit 2, a generalist head of product role at a consumer lending app, expiring on 30 November.

Jyotika Barve, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. She wants Juhi. Her position is that the next ₹100 crore will come not from bank RFPs but from smaller lenders buying recovery without a procurement committee, which nobody in product has built. Her incentive is the Series D conversation she expects to open in 2027, where self-serve revenue carries a multiple enterprise renewals do not. What she is not saying is that two investors have asked why a company of 900 people has no product-led motion, and that the ₹40 crore self-serve figure in her board deck was her answer.

Jaideep Rane, vice-president of engineering, Pune. He wants Jaswant. His position is that recovery is a regulated workflow product where a wrong default assumption produces a compliance incident rather than a bad quarter, and that his squad cannot educate a product manager while shipping to the Nairobi contract. His incentive is a roadmap he has committed to. What he is not saying is that the two staff engineers he put forward for the recovery architecture role both failed the domain round, and that a generalist would make that gap visible rather than absorb it.

Jigar Vora, chief financial officer, Bengaluru. Indifferent between the candidates, hostile to the exception: Jaanch granted four out-of-band offers in FY25 and spent the following year levelling people up to match. His incentive is the FY27 cost plan. What he is not saying is that his note disputing the self-serve figure has never reached the board.

Jairaj Menon, head of talent, Bengaluru. He wants the requisition closed, and says unprompted that Jaswant is the last candidate of his type Jaanch will see this year. His incentive includes a time-to-fill target this requisition has already missed. What he is not saying is that he has never told Jigar the ask breaks the band, hoping to settle it with Jyotika first.

Jaswant Thube, 40, the specialist finalist. Twelve years all in collections: four at a bank's recovery unit, five at an agency, three at an NBFC building in-house tooling. His debrief is the strongest Jaanch has recorded on domain judgement and the weakest on discovery; one interviewer wrote that he answered every question about users by describing a process. His competing offer expires on Tuesday 17 November. He would rather join Jaanch, and has not moved on money.

Juhi Kanitkar, 34, the generalist finalist. Nine years across four domains: a travel marketplace, a developer-tools company, a quick-commerce app, and for two years a payments company's merchant platform, where she launched self-serve onboarding. She has never worked on lending. Her debrief praises her discovery work and her pricing instinct, and notes that she could not explain what a bucket is. She has twice asked who she would report to in two years.

Jolanta Zawadzka, principal data scientist, Warsaw. She built the line's propensity models and is the only person who has seen both take-home exercises. Her position is that the domain can be taught in six months to someone who reads, and that what cannot be taught is willingness to kill a model that does not pay for itself. What she is not saying is that she applied for the role herself in August and withdrew after one conversation with Jagruti.

6. Voices

"We are not hiring a product manager. We are hiring the only person who can tell me whether a sixty-day bucket behaves differently in Coimbatore and in Kochi, and whether that difference is a feature or a bug. Juhi is excellent at something we do not need yet."

Jaideep Rane, debrief call, 9 November

"Every time this company has faced depth against reach it has chosen depth, and four times out of five it was right. The fifth time is now. Look at who signed Nairobi: a collections head with a budget she did not have to ask anyone for. There are two thousand lenders like her and we cannot send a salesperson to one of them."

Jyotika Barve, product review, 11 November

"Both take-homes were fine. His was correct and boring. Hers was wrong in two places and asked a question about write-off timing that I have not been able to stop thinking about. I do not know how to score that."

Jolanta Zawadzka, written feedback, 6 November

"My clients in Manila and Nairobi do not buy a product. They buy whoever shows up on the call at eight in the morning and knows the regulation in their market. That person is Jagruti. If Jagruti becomes a GM, who is that person?"

Jomar Salcedo to Jessica Thorne, 13 November

"Stop asking which of them is better. Ask what you want to be doing in 2031. If the answer is running a line, hire the one who makes you replaceable. If it is being the person Jomar just described, hire the one who makes you necessary. You have been trying to have both since 2024."

Johanna Lindholm, voice note to Jagruti, 14 November

7. The options as Jagruti frames them

Option A. Hire Jaswant, break the band, sign the nomination. The line gets depth immediately, Jaideep's roadmap holds, and Jagruti moves into a commercial role knowing her successor understands the subject. The costs are an exception Jigar will fight, a Principal PM earning exactly what his manager earns, and a fifth consecutive year of hiring specialists. It also turns her away from the craft she is best at, at the moment she is most valuable in it.

Option B. Hire Juhi, stay a director, let the nomination go. Jaanch acquires its first product manager who has shipped a self-serve product, and Jagruti remains the depth the Nairobi and Manila accounts rely on. The costs are nineteen weeks, if Exhibit 4 means anything, before Juhi ships; an engineering team that must teach her; and another year in which Jagruti's specialisation deepens with no evidence she wants it to. Johanna's phrase for this option, "the one who makes you necessary", was not meant kindly.

Option C. Hire neither, re-open in January, take the outside offer. The head of product role pays ₹130 lakh, is explicitly generalist, and would test within eighteen months the question Jagruti has avoided for four years: whether her strength is credit risk, or product judgement that happens to have been applied to credit risk. The costs are plain: the requisition lapses on 30 November, the line enters its first P&L year with neither a GM nor a Principal PM, and the Nairobi contract requires a named product owner by 1 January 2027.

There are reasons to doubt the frame. It assumes the two decisions must be taken together, when the board asks only that each be answered. It assumes the line needs one Principal PM, when ₹21 lakh is roughly the difference between a senior hire and a contracted domain adviser alongside a cheaper generalist. Most of all it assumes the axis is depth against breadth, when what Exhibit 3 disputes is whether Jaanch is a self-serve company at all — which neither finalist, and arguably neither executive, has settled.

8. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board talent review is at ten on Monday 16 November. Jaswant's competing offer expires on Tuesday 17 November, and Jairaj believes a one-week extension is possible but not two. Jigar will not approve an out-of-band offer without a written exception signed by the chief executive, and Jyotika has not been asked. The requisition's budget lapses on 30 November; re-opening in January needs fresh approval in the FY28 planning cycle, which Jigar chairs. Jagruti's notice period as a director is ninety days, so an outside move accepted on 30 November would not begin before 1 March 2027. Juhi's notice is sixty days. And the Nairobi contract names 1 January 2027 as the date by which a product owner must be designated for consent and grievance handling, a clause legal added without consulting product.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 establish about the market for each profile, and what does the uncorrected base of 180 specialist records do to that reading?
  2. Jaideep and Jyotika draw opposite conclusions from the same two figures in Exhibit 4. What evidence would settle it, and could Jaanch have collected it?
  3. Jagruti's seven years in credit risk are both her strength and her constraint. Which parts of that experience are genuinely domain-specific, and which would travel to Option C?
  4. Does the ₹22 crore disagreement in Exhibit 3 change which candidate Jaanch should hire, or is it a separate argument attached to this one?
  5. If a specialisation is a bet on a market lasting, what would have to be true of Indian lending in 2031 for Jagruti's bet to pay off, and what would falsify it earliest?
  6. What should Jagruti do when she walks into the room on Monday morning, and what exactly should she say to the board about her own nomination?

10. Sunday, late

At a quarter past eleven she squared the three papers into one pile. Jolanta's feedback was on top, with its line about the question she had not been able to stop thinking about. Jagruti had spent seven years becoming the person who already knew the answer to questions like that, and could not work out whether to hire someone who would also already know, or someone who would keep asking.

The nomination form was still unsigned. She turned off the balcony lights, which nobody had switched on all week, and left the pile where it was.
exp20v2-craft.specialise:
Choosing a PM Specialisation

Which lane fits my strengths, and which lane does the market pay for?

1. The offer with a deadline

On Thursday, 1 October 2026, Charvi Menon, a senior product manager at Bhavishya Commerce Works in Bengaluru, opened two messages within an hour of each other. Five years into product work, she earned a cost-to-company (CTC, the total annual pay package) of ₹42 lakh. Her head of product, Dinesh Kulkarni, offered her the lead role on growth, the team that raises the number of customers who sign up, return and buy. The role paid ₹46 lakh. A recruiter at Eklavya Capital Services, the Hyderabad global capability centre (GCC, an India-based unit that does product and engineering work for an overseas parent firm) of a foreign bank, offered a platform product manager role at ₹52 lakh, valid until Friday, 16 October.

The gap in pay is easy to state. Against her current ₹42 lakh, the platform offer is ₹10 lakh higher, about 23.8 per cent, and the growth role is ₹4 lakh higher, about 9.5 per cent. (One lakh is 100,000; one crore is 100 lakh.) The harder part was that each offer was also a statement about who she would be known as at the next job change. A third course remained: decline both and stay a generalist, able to run any kind of product team.

Eshwar Rao, a former director who had mentored her, asked one question. "Which of these can you still reverse in two years, and which narrows who will interview you?" Charvi had no answer.

2. The idea

A PM specialisation is a deliberate concentration of a product manager's experience in one lane, where a lane is a recognisable kind of product problem with its own metrics, its own counterparts and its own hiring market. The common lanes are growth (acquiring, activating and retaining users), platform (building internal or developer-facing capabilities that other teams build on), data and machine learning (ML), consumer (products bought by individuals), B2B or enterprise (products sold to businesses through long sales cycles) and infrastructure (the systems underneath everything else). The opposite is the generalist, who rotates among problems and is valued for judgement rather than depth.

The idea is older than the title. Through the 1990s and 2000s one product manager typically ran a whole product. As firms grew past a few hundred engineers, the work split, and by the 2010s large technology companies advertised "growth PM" and "platform PM" roles. The Indian market followed as Flipkart, Swiggy and PhonePe scaled and GCCs multiplied. Specialisation solved a hiring problem: no employer can test a generalist's judgement in a forty-minute interview, but all can test whether a candidate has moved a retention curve.

The usable picture is a T. The vertical bar is the lane where you can be believed without proof. The horizontal bar is the working knowledge that lets you collaborate with other lanes. Specialisation lengthens the bar and decides which employers see you; it does not delete the top.

"A lane is a bet on where problems will be hard and well paid in three years, and I am making it with a reversal plan."

3. How it actually works

Four steps; the third is rarely said aloud.

Step one: your evidence accumulates. Each shipped outcome becomes a line on your record: "raised seven-day retention", "cut partner onboarding time", "launched an application programming interface (API), a defined way for one piece of software to be used by another". After two or three years the lines cluster, and a cluster is what a recruiter reads. Charvi's record shows checkout, referral and notification work, which looks like growth without her having chosen the label.

Step two: the market reads the cluster through job descriptions. A job description (JD) is the employer's list of required experience, and recruiters filter on its keywords before a human reads anything. "Experimentation" and "funnel" clear growth JDs; they rarely clear a JD asking for "schema design".

Step three: the screen is asymmetric. This is the implicit step. Hiring managers fear a wrong hire more than they value a right one, so they seek the safest evidence of fit. Depth multiplies your chance inside one lane and reduces it elsewhere. That is what the model below measures.

Step four: the band follows the scarcity. Bands, the pay ranges attached to each level, differ by lane because supply differs. Roughly, in Bengaluru and Hyderabad: associate PM (APM), ₹18 lakh to ₹28 lakh; PM, ₹30 lakh to ₹48 lakh; senior PM, ₹40 lakh to ₹70 lakh; director, ₹1.2 crore to ₹2 crore (120 lakh to 200 lakh). These are illustrative ranges, not survey data, and they vary by company.

4. A worked example

Charvi asked Eshwar to help her build a simple model. For each lane he used four inputs. Openings are the product roles at her level advertised each quarter across Bengaluru, Hyderabad and the National Capital Region. Clearing share is the proportion of those openings whose JD she would pass today. Offer rate is the proportion of cleared roles that end in an offer. The offer-value index is expected offers multiplied by the lane's senior-PM band midpoint in lakh. The figures are Eshwar's illustrative estimates.

LaneOpenings per quarterClearing shareRoles clearedOffer rateExpected offersBand (₹ lakh)Offer-value index (₹ lakh)
Generalist12025%3010%3.042126.0
Growth6070%4210%4.246193.2
Platform4030%1220%2.452124.8
Data / ML3010%320%0.65834.8
Total250–87–10.2–478.8

Table 1. Today. Roles cleared = openings × clearing share; expected offers = roles cleared × offer rate; index = expected offers × band.

Growth gives the highest index, 4.2 expected offers at ₹46 lakh, or 193.2. Platform pays more per offer but she clears few platform JDs, so it yields 2.4 offers and 124.8. The generalist has the widest pool, 120 openings, but only a quarter fit, giving 3.0 offers and 126.0. Today, on these numbers, growth fits her best.

Now change one input. Suppose she takes the platform job and, after eighteen months, her platform clearing share rises from 30 per cent to 80 per cent, with everything else held fixed. Platform roles cleared become 40 × 0.80 = 32; expected offers become 32 × 0.20 = 6.4; the index becomes 6.4 × 52 = 332.8. The totals become 107 roles cleared, 14.2 expected offers and an index of 686.8, which is 43.4 per cent above 478.8.

That second pass is flattering, so Eshwar made her pay for it. Eighteen months away from growth would plausibly erode her growth evidence: if the growth clearing share fell from 70 per cent to 40 per cent, growth would give 24 roles cleared, 2.4 expected offers and an index of 110.4. Applied on top of the second pass, with the platform clearing share still at 80 per cent, the total would be 12.4 expected offers (14.2 less 4.2 plus 2.4) and an index of 604.0 (686.8 less 193.2 plus 110.4). Finally, if platform openings halved from 40 to 20 while her clearing share stayed at 80 per cent, platform would give 16 roles cleared, 3.2 offers and an index of 166.4, still above the generalist's 126.0. The lane survived the shock, but the margin is thin.

5. The nuances

Lane versus archetype

A PM archetype is a style of working, such as the technical PM or the operator. A lane is a problem domain. A technical PM can sit in growth. Blurring the two leads people to ask "am I a growth person?" when the question is "do I want these problems?"

Depth is judged by outcomes, not tenure

Three years near a lane do not make you a specialist. "Supported the growth team" does not count against "raised week-four retention from 18 to 22 per cent".

Lanes shrink and swell

Hiring moves with funding cycles and technology waves. A lane that is hot at the decision date may not be hot at the exit date, so the model's openings are a snapshot.

Employer type shapes the lane

A platform PM at a GCC often serves internal engineering customers, with decision rights split between Hyderabad and the overseas head office. The same title at an Indian product company such as Razorpay usually carries ownership of an external developer product. Read the scope in the JD, not the title.

What the model cannot tell you

It cannot tell you whether you will enjoy the work, whether your manager will back you, or whether the estimates are right. Every input in Table 1 is a guess from a small sample of recruiters.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Whose data produced the openings? Is the offer rate measured or remembered? Would the clearing share change if I rewrote my résumé? If one input swings the result, what evidence would settle it?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace, early and large

The lane labels carry different content depending on the kind of product. A marketplace, a product matching buyers with sellers (the way Swiggy matches diners with restaurants), has two customer sides, so "growth" means balancing supply and demand rather than only acquiring users.

LaneConsumerB2B / enterpriseMarketplace
GrowthFunnel, retention, referral; experiments weeklyPipeline and product-led trials; sales partnership mattersSupply-demand balance; cold-start in each city
PlatformShared checkout, identity, notificationsAPIs, integrations, admin controlsPricing, matching and payments services
Data / MLRecommendations, personalisationForecasting, anomaly detectionRanking, fraud, delivery-time estimates

Table 2. The same lane carries a different job in each product type.

Company stage matters just as much. At a ten-person start-up nobody can afford a lane: the PM does growth, platform and support in one week, and the market rewards range. In a firm with several hundred engineers, each team demands someone who has done its specific job. A lane is therefore worth more in a large organisation than a small one, and a specialist moving to a start-up often finds the depth underused.

7. Common mistakes

MistakeSymptom from outsideMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Choosing the lane by pay aloneCandidate moves for the larger CTC and is unhappy within a yearTreating the band as the whole value of the laneAsk which of this lane's problems you would work on unpaid
Labelling without outcomesRésumé says "growth PM" but lists activitiesBelieving the title is the evidenceWrite one outcome line with a number for each claimed lane
Locking in too earlyEarly-career PM refuses roles outside one laneMistaking a preference for a callingList three adjacent lanes you could not yet answer a technical question in
Never choosingSix years of varied roles, few interviews at senior levelsAssuming breadth signals ability on its ownCount how many JDs in your target band you clear today

Table 3. Four mistakes, their symptoms and the quickest test of each.

The first is the commonest: the pay gap is visible and the fit is not. The fourth is the quietest, since nothing goes wrong in any single year. Both are caught by writing down the inputs before a deadline creates pressure.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version begins with the model above, every input marked as measured or guessed. She would spend two evenings testing the weakest inputs: asking three recruiters whether a platform clearing share of 30 per cent is plausible, and three platform managers what the first year looks like. She would ask Dinesh Kulkarni for a written scope and a decision date for the growth role, since the platform offer expired on 16 October and the growth offer had none, and ask Eklavya how decisions are split between Hyderabad and the parent office.

She would also fix a reversal plan before accepting: a named project that keeps her growth evidence fresh. A good decision is one whose reasoning a sceptical mentor could follow, including what would have changed her mind.

9. The decision, and what comes next

Charvi took the platform role, on the condition that Eklavya's hiring manager confirm in writing that she would own an externally facing payments interface rather than only internal tooling. She declined the growth lead role with Dinesh's blessing, and kept the generalist option alive by agreeing with Eshwar to maintain one growth experiment on the side. Her reasoning followed the model. On its numbers, growth was the best lane today. The platform lane, however, offered the higher band (₹52 lakh against ₹46 lakh), the larger improvement in expected offers (10.2 to 14.2) and a market she judged to be growing as banks and insurers in India build GCCs. She accepted a real risk, that her growth evidence would decay, in return for a larger long-run return.

To go further, read about PM archetypes, then about reading a PM job description, which turns the keyword filter of step two into a skill. After that, look at which PM paths are more and less exposed to automation, since a lane's future demand is the hardest input in any model of this kind.

Two questions to sit with. First, which input in Table 1 would change your own answer most, and what could you do this month to replace a guess with evidence? Second, if your chosen lane lost half its openings within two years, as in the halved-platform test, what part of your record would still make you hireable?
exp40v2-craft.specialise:
Choosing a PM Specialisation

How a lane accumulates, how fast it decays, and what it costs to change one.

1. Two decisions, a week apart

On Monday, 21 September 2026, Rukmini Sathaye read an offer letter twice before seeing what was wrong with it. A group product manager at Saptak Commerce Collective, a Bengaluru marketplace company, nine years in, she was on ₹68 lakh. Ritambhara Capital Group, the Hyderabad capability centre of a European bank, offered her Director, Payments Platform, at ₹1.05 crore — ₹105 lakh, since a crore is 100 lakh. That is a rise of ₹37 lakh, or 54.4 per cent, valid eighteen days, to Friday, 9 October.

What was wrong was that she could not say why they wanted her. Her nine years broke into four blocks: three on consumer growth, two on payments platform, two on seller tools, two on marketplace ranking; three plus two plus two plus two is nine. The platform work had ended four years earlier. Sudhanshu Rele, Saptak's vice-president of product, had meanwhile offered her the internal ranking lead at ₹79 lakh, a rise of ₹11 lakh, or 16.2 per cent.

A week later, on Monday, 28 September, Satyen Rasal faced the mirror image in Pune. Six unbroken years at Rooprekha Systems had made him an enterprise product manager and nothing else: procurement workflows, access control, an audit trail satisfying four Indian banks. On ₹58 lakh, he held an offer from Saaransh Labs, a forty-person AI-native company in Bengaluru: Head of Product at ₹52 lakh plus equity, due Wednesday, 14 October — a cash cut of ₹6 lakh, or 10.3 per cent. Rukmini had no lane to sell; Satyen had one and wanted to leave it.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Define a lane precisely: a class of product problem with its own success metric, its own primary counterpart function, and its own hiring market in which employers screen for prior work on that class. All three must hold. Growth qualifies on all three. “Mobile” fails the third test in 2026. Specialisation concentrates demonstrable outcomes inside one lane; generalism refuses to.

The construct solved an employer's problem, not a candidate's. One product manager once owned a product end to end; as organisations passed a few hundred engineers the work fractured, and by the mid-2010s the large platforms posted lane titles for lane-shaped vacancies. India imported both at once, as Flipkart, Swiggy, PhonePe and Razorpay scaled into lane-shaped org charts and the GCCs of banks and insurers multiplied beside them. A hiring manager cannot test general judgement in a four-hour loop but can test whether a candidate moved a curve: lanes are a cheap instrument for reducing hiring variance.

That origin shapes the disagreement. The scarcity-rent school holds that pay follows supply, supply is thinnest in the newest lanes, and the job is to hold inventory in the scarce one. It will sign “the median data and AI role in Bengaluru pays more than the median core product role at the same level”; not “depth in a lane makes you a better product manager.” The judgement school holds that lanes are a hiring artefact and what transfers is the ability to frame the right problem. It will sign “the leaders you can name have changed problem class twice”; not “a generalist and a specialist face the same screen.” The stack school holds that what transfers is the substrate operated — a payments rail, a recommender — and denies that “growth” names anything portable.

3. Mechanics: what the market is actually doing

Start with supply. Rozgaar Search Partners logs product roles at senior product manager level and above across Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and the National Capital Region — an illustrative book, not a census.

Less obviously, core product roles also grew, from 268 to 414, a ratio of 1.54, while their share fell from 41.9 to 28.0 per cent. Read shares alone and generalism looks dying; read counts alone and nothing changed.

Now demand. Roshni Sabharwal, Ritambhara's director of platform, posted the directorship on Tuesday, 11 August 2026 and closed applications on Tuesday, 22 September — 42 days, six weeks.

Three mechanisms are visible; only one is usually discussed. First, aggregate odds are terrible in every lane: two offers from 1,240 applications is 0.16 per cent. Second, the lane filter does nearly all its work at the first gate. Of 744 applicants stating an in-lane outcome, 172 cleared the recruiter screen, a pass rate of 23.1 per cent; of 496 without one, 14 cleared, a rate of 2.8 per cent — the specialist's odds are 8.19 times the generalist's. Past that gate the lane stops discriminating, the share of survivors with in-lane evidence moving only from 92.5 to 100 per cent.

Third, and least discussed: the panel is staffed by lane peers. Roshni's five held four platform people and one generalist, and on three of six finalists their ratings differed by two points or more on her five-point scale. A lane decides not only which interviews you get but who judges you.

The formal treatment is a stock-and-decay model, the part competent practitioners skip. Treat lane credibility as a stock in evidence-years: a year of outcomes in a lane adds 1.0, and every lane not worked is multiplied by 0.75, a decay of 25 per cent. Assume a director-level lane role needs at least 3.0.

Her largest stock, 2.000, is below the 3.0 threshold, and her platform stock is 0.633. Ritambhara is not buying platform depth, and she does not know what it is buying.

4. When specialising is the right move, and when it is not

Claim one: the lane must clear a minimum annual role count at your level. Take a specialist's cold application-to-offer rate as 0.2688 per cent, which is 2 divided by 744, Table 2's two offers over its 744 in-lane applicants.

No lane yields two expected offers from cold applications, so a lane's function is not better cold-search odds but findability. Satyen passes on count for AI, at 385 roles; a sub-lane with seven roles a year fails outright.

Claim two: specialising pays only where the employer cannot test judgement cheaply. Ritambhara, with 1,240 applications and no instrument for judgement, buys the proxy. Saaransh Labs has forty people and a founder who will spend nine hours with Satyen, so the label buys him almost nothing there. It matters for his next move — the right reason to take the job, and not the reason usually given.

Claim three: the reversal window must exceed your time to a first credible outcome in the new lane — section 11 computes Satyen's. Claim four: a lane is yours only if its evidence survives being stated as a number. Rukmini's ranking work does: add-to-cart rate on recommended items rose from 4.8 to 6.3 per cent, 1.5 points, a relative rise of 31.25 per cent. Her platform block does not, and here the idea turns actively misleading: years adjacent to a lane feel like stock, and the first gate disagrees.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

The multi-product company. Saptak runs four product lines across 61 surfaces with 38 product managers, of whom 9 hold a lane title, 23.7 per cent; the other 29 are generalists attached to a line. Its careers page says lane-based organisation; its headcount says otherwise.

The GCC seam. At Ritambhara, of 22 items on the payments platform roadmap, 14 are owned in Hyderabad and 8 in Amsterdam, so 63.6 per cent of decision rights sit in India. The title says Director, Platform; the scope is two-thirds of one. The Hyderabad band also sits below the Indian product-company band: ₹105 lakh against a platform-director midpoint of ₹148 lakh, or 70.9 per cent of it. The lane is real; the title is discounted.

Regulated products. At Rinmukti Lending Services, under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending framework, 5 of 14 roadmap items last quarter were regulatory, 35.7 per cent. A lending manager's lane therefore contains compliance work no job description names and no interview tests. Candidates from unregulated consumer products clear the screen, then find a third of the job is a lane they have never worked.

Hardware plus software, and AI-native. At Sanchika Devices Industries firmware ships twice a year and the companion app fortnightly, 26 times a year — a cadence ratio of 13 to 1. A manager owning both is two half-specialists, the hardware half decaying slowest and paying least. At Saaransh Labs, 6 of 11 product decisions last quarter were evaluation design, or 54.5 per cent. It had no column in Table 1's 2023 figures, which is why it is scarce and unstable.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A lane is a problem class, not a product area. The tell is “I specialise in payments”: payments is a domain, and platform, growth and risk are three lanes inside it. The obvious reading is wrong because domain knowledge is the easiest thing to supply.

Depth is counted in outcomes, and it decays. The tell is a lane claim resting on years that ended more than two years ago, as Rukmini's does at 0.633 evidence-years. Experts ask when, not how long: experience is inventory with a shelf life.

The premium is paid at the level, not in the step. Table 5 shows senior-to-director multiples of 2.38 to 2.46 times across five lanes: the lane changes where you start, not how fast you climb. The tell is choosing a lane for promotion velocity, which the firm's growth sets.

Narrowing happens one level below where people look. Nobody over-specialises into “growth”, but into supply-side growth for freight marketplaces: 7 roles a year against 222, or 3.2 per cent of the lane. The tell is work describable only with a compound noun carrying three modifiers.

Share and count move independently. The tell is an argument about a lane's health quoting only one. Core product lost a third of its share and still grew 1.54 times; leaving on share alone meant leaving a growing market.

The decay rate belongs to the lane, not to you. Lanes whose tooling turns over fastest decay fastest: an AI manager's 2023 evidence has aged more than a B2B manager's. The tell is one reversal window applied to every lane, and the obvious reading — newer lanes are better — ignores that scarcity and decay are one phenomenon seen twice.

Internal and external filters are opposed. Promotion committees reward breadth; external screens reward depth. The tell is a strong internal candidate who cannot get an external first round, and a career planned against one filter stalls at the other.

“Generalist” is not a lane, but some generalisms are. “I take over product lines that have missed two consecutive quarters” passes all three tests in section 2. The tell is a numbered list of instances, which most self-described generalists cannot produce.

7. How the picture changes by product type and company stage

The lane premium itself is modest and uneven. Below are illustrative midpoints for Bengaluru and Hyderabad, in ₹ lakh throughout.

LaneSenior PM midpoint (₹ lakh)Premium over coreDirector midpoint (₹ lakh)Director ÷ senior ratio
Core / generalist product52—1282.46×
Growth567.7%1362.43×
Platform / infrastructure6117.3%1482.43×
Data, ML and AI6830.8%1622.38×
Enterprise / B2B543.8%1322.44×
Mean across the five lanes58.2—141.22.43×

Table 5. Premium is the midpoint less 52, over 52. The last row is a mean, not a total: 291 over 5 is 58.2, 706 over 5 is 141.2.

The widest senior-level premium is 30.8 per cent, for data and AI; the narrowest is 3.8 per cent, for enterprise. The widest is real money, ₹16 lakh a year, but far smaller than the 2.43-times step from senior to director, which barely varies by lane. Anyone choosing a lane to maximise pay is optimising the smaller term.

The differences across product types are genuine in some places and imagined in others. In consumer products lanes are sharpest, because the metrics are public: a retention curve means the same at two companies. In enterprise and B2B they blur, being bound to an account and a sales cycle — which is why Table 5 shows enterprise at the smallest premium. In platform and marketplace work the lane splits along a seam the titles hide: a marketplace “growth” role is two lanes. In AI products the lane is forming while being hired for, so premium and decay are both high.

Stage changes the arithmetic more than product type does. Saptak's 38 product managers cover 61 surfaces, 1.61 each; Saaransh Labs' 3 cover 9 surfaces, 3.00 each, 1.87 times as many. Nobody at Saaransh can afford a lane and nobody at Saptak can avoid one, so the usual order is to earn range early, convert it into a lane in the middle, and spend the lane on scope later.

8. Three worked examples

The lane that compounded. Sohini Raikwar joined Qalam Learning Exchange in 2019 on ₹24 lakh and stayed in data and machine learning products for seven years. By 2026 she was director of data science products on ₹1.52 crore, or ₹152 lakh — ₹10 lakh below her lane's ₹162 lakh midpoint in Table 5. That is 6.33 times her 2019 package over seven years, a compound annual rate of 30.2 per cent. The mechanism was not the band: in FY2025–26 she received 11 inbound approaches, 9 of them data and ML roles, 81.8 per cent. She never ran a cold search.

The sub-lane that nearly closed. Sharvari Rode spent three years on supply-side growth at Rajpath Freight Network, raising monthly active truck supply from 18,400 to 29,900 vehicles, a gain of 11,500 or 62.5 per cent. The outcome was excellent, the lane tiny: Rozgaar counted 7 senior supply-side growth roles a year in freight marketplaces against 222 growth roles in all, 3.2 per cent of the lane. Twelve months of taking demand-side experiments too widened the descriptions she cleared from 7 to 31, a factor of 4.43. She did not abandon the lane; she climbed a level up its abstraction.

The lane that failed. Rishab Sohoni was product manager for connected metering devices at Sanchika Devices Industries for five years, on ₹54 lakh, when in January 2026 Sanchika exited the line. His market was nine Indian firms building such hardware, of which four hired managers at his level, generating roughly six roles a year. From Monday, 19 January to Monday, 27 April 2026 — 98 days, fourteen weeks — he applied to 31 roles: 6 in lane, 25 outside. He reached interview in 5 of the 6 in-lane roles, 83.3 per cent, and in 2 of the 25 others, 8.0 per cent. The one offer was for a role then frozen. His lane worked perfectly and had nowhere to send him.

The recovery was a reframing, not a retraining: he restated his five years as regulated-hardware compliance platform work — device certification, release governance, audit evidence. From Monday, 4 May to Monday, 20 July 2026 — 77 days, eleven weeks — he applied to 18 enterprise and platform roles, reached interview in 7, or 38.9 per cent, and took one of two offers at ₹46 lakh. Against ₹54 lakh that is a cut of ₹8 lakh, 14.8 per cent. He concluded not that specialising was a mistake, but that he had specialised in a product line rather than a problem class — and a product line can be cancelled.

9. Failure modes, their early signs, and the cost of lateness

Failure modeEarliest warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
A product line, not a problem classThe claim names your employer's productWhich four other Indian firms run this?Rishab's: 14 weeks, then a 14.8% cut
Sub-lane narrowingThe title needs three modifiersHow many roles a year match my description?A 12-month widening while peers advance
Stale lane, confidently claimedBest in-lane outcome is over 24 months oldWhat did I ship in this lane since last year?Clearing screens, failing peer-staffed panels
Rotating indefinitelyNo lane stock above 2.0 after eight yearsWhich lane could I defend for 45 minutes?Rukmini's position: a 52.3% stock shortfall
Buying the title, not the mandateBand below the lane's midpointWhat share of the roadmap is decided here?A director title with 63.6% of the scope
Treating the premium as the prizeYou know the band gap, not the daily workWhich problems here would I work on unpaid?A switch at the trough, paid for twice

Table 6. Costs are figures computed elsewhere on this page.

The first and fourth are the expensive ones, and opposites: one commits to something too specific to survive, the other to nothing. Both are invisible year by year and obvious in aggregate, which is why every diagnostic above counts something.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The scarcity-rent position rests on Tables 1 and 5. Data and AI roles grew 6.02 times in three years while the lane's senior midpoint sits 30.8 per cent above core product, and its evaluation work — 54.5 per cent of decisions at Saaransh — cannot be learned from a course, so supply will not catch demand soon. The position fails if premia compress as supply arrives; its holders argue the rent is collected first.

The judgement position rests on Table 5's other column. The senior-to-director multiple is 2.38 to 2.46 times in every lane, so the lane explains almost none of the step in pay, which is won on scope and scope on judgement. It also rests on Rukmini's offer: Ritambhara wanted her with a platform stock of 0.633. The position fails if the first gate is impassable without lane evidence, and Table 2 shows it nearly is, at 2.8 per cent. Its holders answer that referral and inbound paths bypass the gate.

The stack position rests on Rishab's two searches. Nothing about his lane label changed between January and July 2026; the substrate he named did. Reframed as regulated-hardware compliance, his interview rate moved from 8.0 to 38.9 per cent on identical experience. The position fails if substrate claims do not transfer across industries, and its weakness is the 14.8 per cent cut: the transfer worked, at a discount, which is some evidence the market priced the lane after all.

11. What mastery looks like

Satyen holds 6.000 evidence-years of enterprise and nothing else. At 25 per cent decay his enterprise stock runs 4.500, 3.375, 2.531, 1.898 and 1.424 over five years while his AI stock runs 1.000 to 5.000. Combined, that is 5.500, 5.375, 5.531, 5.898 and 6.424 — a trough in year two and a return above 6.000 in year five, the lines crossing in year three. His enterprise stock stays above 3.0 through year two and falls below it in year three, so his reversal window is two years, not the five he assumed.

Decay rateYear enterprise stock first falls below 3.0Year AI stock first exceeds enterprise stockReversal window
15%544 years
25%332 years
35%231 year

Table 7. Sensitivity of the reversal window, from 6.000 enterprise and 0.000 AI evidence-years.

Someone who has merely studied this picks a lane and defends the choice. Someone who has internalised it names the decay rate assumed and what would change it; knows the reversal window in years and holds a dated plan for keeping it open; separates the lane from the product line and the stack; and treats the first gate as the only place the lane matters.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Rukmini declined Ritambhara. Her reasoning was not the band discount but that she would join a lane with a stock of 0.633 and a mandate covering 63.6 per cent of a platform, at a firm whose panel she could not have cleared without her referral. She took the internal ranking role at ₹79 lakh with one written condition: a numerically stated outcome within two quarters. Two more years in data lifts that stock from 2.000 to 4.000, past the threshold, at the price of letting her other three fall to 0.300, 0.356 and 0.633.

Satyen accepted Saaransh Labs and the ₹6 lakh cut, having reset his window from five years to two. He asked one commitment: that within twelve months he own an evaluation-design decision he could state publicly with a number, because a switch producing no citable outcome inside the window turns a trough into a loss. He kept a Rooprekha advisory seat, which the model treats as slowing his enterprise decay — in Table 7, the difference between a one-year and a four-year window.

Three questions. First, Ritambhara offered Rukmini a lane she does not hold; was declining right, or does the offer show the screen is looser than Table 2 implies? Second, which figure here is your own decision most sensitive to, and what would replacing that guess with data cost? Third, if the step from senior to director is 2.43 times and the widest lane premium is 30.8 per cent, is choosing a lane a first-order career decision, or a second-order one dressed as a first?

13. Going deeper

PM archetypes supplies the vocabulary: the archetype is the style, the lane is the problem. Reading a PM job description turns Table 2's first gate into a skill, since it runs on keywords. Which PM paths are more and less exposed supplies the decay rates taken as given here. PM interviews explains what the lane-peer panel examines; Building a PM portfolio and narrative is how a stock becomes legible, as Rishab's recovery shows. From PM to founder is the limiting case, where every lane is yours and none priced. A PM's operating system and Continuous learning as a PM slow the decay. Transitioning into product management is the prior question, since the first lane is chosen for you, and Your first 90 days in a PM role is where a chosen lane produces its first stated outcome or does not.
case20v1-craft.specialise:
Charulata Kulshreshtha and the Two Offers

Choosing a PM specialisation: a decision case set in India

1. Opening

On the evening of Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Charulata Kulshreshtha sat at her dining table in Pune with two offer letters and a legal pad. One came from Chinar Payments Systems, a Mumbai merchant-payments company that wanted her as a senior product manager for its UPI and card acceptance products. The other came from Chamak Consumer Works, a Gurugram beauty and personal-care marketplace that wanted her as a senior product manager across its whole shopper app. Chinar's letter expired on Wednesday, 14 October. Chamak's expired two days later.

Charulata was thirty-one, with seven years in product, and she had spent the past eight weeks searching. The compensation figures were close enough that money alone would not settle anything. What troubled her was the longer question: was she about to become a payments specialist, and would that narrow her options or sharpen them? She had to decide by the fourteenth which letter, if either, she would sign.

2. Company background

Charulata's current employer is Charkha Retail Network, a Pune-based marketplace connecting about 1,20,000 small apparel and home-textile sellers with shoppers in smaller towns. Modelled loosely on firms such as Meesho and Flipkart's value segments, it competes for the same price-sensitive shopper, and its growth depends on cheap acquisition, cash-on-delivery conversion and repeat purchase. For three years she owned the checkout funnel, and for the last eighteen months she has led a small squad that built Charkha's UPI intent flow and its prepaid nudges.

Chinar Payments Systems sells acceptance to merchants, from QR codes and soundboxes to a payment gateway, and competes with Razorpay, PhonePe for Business and Paytm. It operates inside the rules of NPCI and the RBI, and a large share of its product roadmap is shaped by their circulars. Chamak Consumer Works sells to shoppers directly and competes with Nykaa and the beauty categories of Flipkart and Reliance Retail. It is growing quickly, and its product organisation is explicitly generalist: product managers rotate across discovery, checkout, loyalty and seller tools every eighteen to twenty-four months.

3. The situation

Charulata began the search in a mood she later called indiscriminate. Between 3 August and 28 September, a span of eight weeks, she catalogued sixty postings that matched her level. Twenty-four, or 40 per cent, were in payments and fintech. The other thirty-six were for generalist consumer roles. She applied to twelve of the first group and eighteen of the second, so thirty applications in all. Exhibit 1 follows each group through the process.

The funnel surprised her. Both tracks converted half of her applications into screens, so the market did not seem to penalise either profile at the first look. Payments recruiters, however, advanced her to a full loop in half of her screens, against one in three for the generalist roles, and she thought she knew why. At the payments companies her checkout and UPI intent work was read as depth. At the consumer companies it was read as one strong funnel among many, and interviewers pressed her on discovery, content and marketplace supply, where she had thinner stories.

Compensation, laid out in Exhibit 2, favoured Chinar but only modestly. All figures are annual, in ₹ lakh, with employee stock options annualised over a four-year vest at the grant value each company quoted.

The people around her saw it differently, depending on where they sat. Her former manager, now in Amsterdam, told her bluntly that payments was a regulated, slow-moving field in which expertise compounded. Her friend Carmen Ortega in Mexico City, who had moved from product into a chief-of-staff role, warned that specialists got typecast and that the best leaders she had met had worked in four or five domains.

4. The people

Chirag Salvi, vice president of product at Chinar in Mumbai, wants an owner for merchant acceptance who will not need a year to learn the vocabulary of settlements, chargebacks and UPI dispute rules. He has told Charulata plainly that her UPI intent work is what separated her from other candidates, and that he sees her as a future head of a payments line.

Chaitali Bose, group product manager at Chamak in Gurugram, wants a versatile senior hire for the rotation model. She has promised Charulata ownership of checkout and loyalty in her first two years, and a likely move to discovery or seller tools after that.

Cornelis de Wit, Charulata's former manager in Amsterdam, leads product at a European payments scheme operator. He favours the specialist route and believes the next decade of Indian commerce will be decided as much by payment rails and regulation as by interfaces.

Exhibit 3 shows the compressed window. One more constraint belonged to Charulata herself. Charkha required a sixty-day notice period. If she resigned on 15 October, her last day would be 14 December, after Diwali on 8 November, and Chinar's start date of 15 December fitted that exactly. Chamak wanted her by 1 December, which meant negotiating a buyout from Charkha.

Her last piece of evidence was long-run pay, which she obtained from two recruiters. Exhibit 4 shows what they quoted for total annual compensation at the middle of each band.

The premium widened with seniority, from ₹6 lakh at Senior PM to ₹20 lakh at Director. Yet the recruiters added a caveat: generalist director roles were fewer, and when they existed they were often general-manager posts with larger scope.

5. The options

Option 1: Sign with Chinar and commit to payments. The upside is the highest compensation, a mentor in Chirag, and a profile that Exhibit 1 suggests the market already values. The cost is concentration. A single regulatory change, such as a cap on any one app's share of UPI volume, could reshape the field, and a payments title can make consumer recruiters see her as narrow.

Option 2: Sign with Chamak and stay a generalist. The upside is breadth: four product areas in four years, and the option to specialise later with better evidence of what she enjoys. The cost is ₹6 lakh a year today, a thinner stock grant, and a funnel in which her depth counted for less.

Option 3: Stay at Charkha and negotiate. Her current employer has hinted at a platform-product role, and a counter-offer would be possible. The upside is no notice period and no ramp-up. The cost is a ₹48 lakh package that trails both offers and a role that does not test whether specialising suits her.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What do Exhibits 1 and 2 tell Charulata about how the market values each profile, and what do they leave unsaid?
  2. Which of her strengths are genuinely domain-specific, and which would travel to any product area?
  3. How reversible is each option? What would it cost her, in time and compensation, to switch tracks after three years?
  4. Given Exhibit 4, how should she weigh a premium that grows with seniority against the risk that the field narrows?

7. A note for the learner

Choosing a specialisation is choosing an archetype, and the question is rarely "breadth or depth" in the abstract. It is three tests applied together. First, strength: does the evidence say you are good at this domain's problems? Second, market: do employers pay for it, and are there enough of them? Third, reversibility: if the bet fails, how cheaply can you step out?

Apply them here. On strength, Charulata has eighteen months of UPI work and the interview data show payments employers reading it as depth. On market, the specialist track offers a premium of ₹6 lakh at Senior PM that widens to ₹20 lakh at Director, and the funnel shows no penalty at the screening stage. On reversibility, the evidence is softer: Carmen's warning about typecasting is plausible but untested, and Chaitali's rotation model suggests consumer companies still hire senior people who have been deep somewhere.

One defensible path is Option 1, with conditions. She should sign with Chinar, because two of the three tests favour it and the third can be managed. She can manage reversibility by negotiating written scope that includes merchant onboarding and growth, which keeps her connected to general product problems, and by agreeing with Chirag that she will present to the wider product organisation each quarter.

Reasonable people could choose Option 2. If Charulata could not name a single payments problem she would happily work on for five years, strength would fail, and breadth would be the wiser choice. What would be hard to defend is deciding on the ₹6 lakh alone. At Senior PM, that is about 11 per cent, and it is the smallest of the gaps in Exhibit 4.
case40v1-craft.interview.ai.fluency:
Anwesha Rath and the Sealed Notebook

A candidate decides what evidence of AI fluency she is able to show — and who it belongs to

1. Sunday night, Bengaluru

At twenty past eleven on Sunday, 11 October 2026, Anwesha Rath sat on the floor of her Indiranagar flat in Bengaluru with three documents open: an invitation she had to accept or decline by nine the next morning, a take-home brief from a Gurugram company due Friday, and a slide she had rewritten six times, titled Shelf Intelligence: discovery to launch in fourteen weeks.

She was thirty-two, a Senior Product Manager at Tulya Retail Systems, and had three live paths at once. Each would ask her, differently, to prove she was fluent with AI tools. She was reasonably sure she was. She was no longer sure she could show it.

The invitation was for Thursday, 22 October: ninety minutes in Mumbai, the final craft round at Vikalp Credit Network, labelled AI Workflow Assessment (Trayi) + live exercise. Eleven days away. Declining it meant the highest-paying opportunity she had been shown would close, and that she would learn in January whether Tulya had funded the promotion her manager called all but certain.

What kept her on the floor was not the choice of employer. It was a sentence Marisol Quintero had said on a video call eleven days earlier.

2. Tulya Retail Systems

Tulya was founded in Bengaluru in 2015 by two former sellers of point-of-sale terminals to grocery distributors. In the year ended March 2026 it reported revenue of ₹780 crore, employed about 1,900 people, and had its ordering and shelf-analytics software in roughly 2.4 lakh outlets across eleven states. Besides Bengaluru and Pune it had customer success in Jakarta, a two-person enterprise pilot in Chicago, and one employee in Dublin keeping a European pilot inside both the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the European rules.

One earlier decision shaped everything Anwesha could now say about herself. In March 2024, under pressure to show enterprise revenue before a funding round, Tulya signed a three-year confidentiality agreement with its largest distributor client, effective 1 April 2024 and running to 31 March 2027. It covered not the client's data alone but the category: no employee, during the term or for two years after, could describe the client's workflows, the research run in its outlets, or the methods used. Legal flagged the breadth; the revenue was ₹96 crore a year and the clause stayed in. Anwesha's best work — the shelf-intelligence programme of 6 April to 13 July 2026, fourteen weeks and 126 merchant interviews — sat entirely inside that client's outlets.

3. The industry

Indian retail software in 2026 was squeezed from both ends. Reliance Retail and Avenue Supermarts were building their own supply-chain stacks and buying little. The quick-commerce platforms — Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart — were pulling the better kirana stores into dark-store partnerships, which changed what those stores needed from software. GST e-invoicing and UPI acceptance meant even a small shop now generated structured data, and ONDC had made catalogue interoperability a board topic.

The consequence for product managers was specific. Discovery that took five months was expected to take two, and by mid-2026 almost every senior product opening at a serious Indian firm carried a round on running that compressed cycle with AI assistance. Almost every candidate claimed to be good at it.

Vikalp Credit Network lent to small merchants through regulated partners under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending framework: Tulya's merchant base, a far bigger balance sheet. Udyam Commerce Labs built seller tools for marketplaces and had last raised at a 2024 valuation.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

On Tuesday, 15 September 2026, Reshma Chandiramani called about a Director of Product role at Vikalp, credit products, reporting to Lalit Sardana. She had not been looking, and took the call because the fixed component alone exceeded her whole package.

Two rounds passed easily. On Wednesday, 30 September — eleven days before the Sunday on the floor — she cleared the product-craft round with the strongest written feedback Reshma had seen that quarter. That evening the coordinator described the round to come: a licensed instrument from Trayi Assessment Group called the AI Workflow Index, then a live exercise in which the candidate is handed an unfamiliar brief and a model, and watched.

Anwesha believed three things: that she could pass a walkthrough of her own work, because it was real and she remembered it; that the instrument was a formality; and that the clause could be managed by changing names. All three turned out wrong, in order.

The clause went first. On Thursday, 1 October, Tulya's counsel, asked a careful hypothetical, replied that the research method was itself covered, having been co-designed with the client's category team. Anonymising would not help: Anwesha could say she had run a fourteen-week programme, but not what she learned, how, or from whom. She did not tell Reshma, fearing it would read as excuses made before the round.

The instrument went second. On 4 October Soumitra Ghoshal, a former colleague now at Udyam, sent her Exhibit 6, which he should not have sent: how Vikalp's own hires had scored on the Trayi index against their six-month manager ratings. The relationship ran the wrong way.

The third went on the call of 30 September. Anwesha had asked Marisol Quintero, the data scientist in Chicago who supported the programme, to review the slide. Marisol read it twice and said the part Anwesha was proudest of — discarding fourteen of the twenty-four model-generated theme syntheses, because they kept collapsing a minority of high-volume outlets into the average — had been her own call in a Tuesday data review, and that Anwesha had argued against it for two weeks before agreeing. Anwesha's notebook, reconstructed in the week of 7 September, recorded the decision without an author.

Neither of them was lying. That was the difficulty.

Figure 1. Twenty-six days separate Reshma's first call from Sunday night, and eleven days Sunday night from the Vikalp round. The Tulya slate locks nineteen days after Sunday night, a day after the board hears the shelf-intelligence results.

5. The people

Siddhartha Mahadevan, Vice-President of Product at Tulya and her manager, says she should stay: the promotion is on the slate and the board hears her story on 29 October. Losing her now would leave two of four product lines ownerless in the festive quarter. He is not saying that the Group PM position has been slated twice without being funded, and that finance wants flat headcount.

Reshma Chandiramani, partner at Vastu Talent Partners, says Anwesha is the strongest candidate on the shortlist and should walk in and be herself. Her fee is one-third of the fixed component, on joining. She is not saying that Vikalp rejected her last two shortlists at this same round, and that she now suspects the instrument rather than the candidates.

Lalit Sardana, Director of Product, Credit, at Vikalp, is the hiring manager. He says he wants judgement rather than tool familiarity, and that the live exercise, not the index, is what he reads. His roadmap is two quarters late and he must hire senior. He is not saying that the Trayi licence was bought at his own recommendation for ₹41 lakh over three years, which makes arguing with its scores awkward.

Marisol Quintero, Senior Data Scientist, Chicago, ten and a half hours behind Bengaluru in October. Her position is factual: discarding the syntheses was her decision. Her staff-level promotion case closes in December and the programme is her strongest item. She is not saying that she is unsure too; the Tuesday reviews were unrecorded, and she remembers the argument more vividly than the conclusion.

Soumitra Ghoshal, Group Product Manager at Udyam Commerce Labs, Gurugram, says she should come to Udyam, where the assessment is a take-home then a walkthrough of past work, and where he can tell her what the reviewers reward. He earns a referral bonus and an ally in a function where he is isolated. He is not saying that Udyam's last two external Group PM hires left inside nine months.

Dewi Kusumawardani, Customer Success Lead, Jakarta, an hour and a half ahead of Bengaluru, is the only person who sat through the Tuesday reviews with both. She says the authorship question is meaningless: they argued everything into shape together. She reports to neither and wants to keep both.

Aparajita Bose, Anwesha's former manager, now a principal at a Mumbai venture firm who interviews candidates for her portfolio companies, says Anwesha is preparing for the wrong thing: a sealed notebook is a reason to build new, publishable evidence, not to rehearse the old. She is not saying that both roles she has in mind pay less.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the only reliable picture of what Anwesha is walking into.

Describe the fourteen weeks as workflow rather than content: the five steps in Exhibit 2, the disposition counts, the reasoning behind the synthesis rejections, nothing about the client. The legal position is probably defensible. The risk is that a workflow without its subject matter sounds like the rehearsed performance Lalit says he spots in ten minutes, and that the story's strongest moment is one she may not be able to claim.

Accept Vikalp and go in on the live exercise. Treat the index as noise, since Exhibit 6 suggests it is, and bet on the unfamiliar brief, where the work is produced in front of the panel and authorship cannot be questioned. The risk is that the index gates the room before the room happens, and that Lalit's claim not to read it sits oddly beside the licence he recommended.

Pivot to Udyam. A take-home in five days and a walkthrough for which Soumitra will brief her. Vikalp needs a reply by nine on Monday, 12 October; the round is ten days later. The board product committee meets Thursday, 29 October, with Siddhartha owning the deck; the slate locks Friday, 30 October, any promotion effective 1 January 2027. Diwali is Sunday, 8 November, and both external processes mean to close first.

The confidentiality agreement runs to 31 March 2027 with a further two-year restriction on method, and counsel has given an opinion, not a waiver. Her notice period is three months, reducible to two. Vikalp's offer is contingent on the 22 October round, with no exceptions. Marisol's case closes in December. Nothing about the authorship is written down by anyone but Anwesha.
