In the version she had rehearsed, she had made the hard call on the syntheses and the fourteen weeks proved a method she owned. In Marisol's, she had argued two weeks against the best decision in the programme and then written it down as her own. In Dewi's there was no decision to own, only an argument that resolved itself. All three were available on Thursday, and the room could not tell them apart. She closed the laptop without replying.
exp20v2-craft.interview.ai.fluency:
Showing AI Fluency in a PM Interview

How a candidate shows a workflow and the judgement kept human, instead of reciting a tool list.

1. The Sunday before the round

On Sunday 11 October 2026, Pooja Kelkar, a product manager at a Pune payments firm, sat with a laptop and a note that read "AI round, Tuesday". On Tuesday 13 October she would meet Mukund Iyengar, head of product at Pinaka Lending Systems, a Bengaluru company that makes small-ticket working-capital loans for kirana owners. The role was Senior Product Manager, with fixed pay of ₹45 lakh. Eleven candidates had reached the final stage; Pinaka would hire one. Iyengar had told the recruiter that the last round would include forty minutes on "how you work with AI".

Kelkar's first draft of her answer ran: "I use ChatGPT for PRDs, Claude for research, Notion AI for notes and Perplexity for competitor scans." She read it aloud and heard what Iyengar would hear: four product names and no decision. A friend who had interviewed at two Indian fintechs called it the commonest and least remembered answer. Scored as a tool user, she would be indistinguishable from ten others. Shown as someone with a workflow and a reasoned boundary around it, she would be the candidate Iyengar could picture on his team. Her task was to turn a tool list into one workflow, narrated in ninety seconds and defended for ten minutes.

2. The idea

AI fluency, in an interview, means the ability to describe a specific piece of product work in which a model does some steps, you keep others, and you can say why the line sits where it does and how you know. A large language model (LLM) is software trained on vast text collections to predict plausible continuations of a prompt, and a prompt is the instruction and material you give it. Because an LLM produces fluent text whether or not it is true, its output is cheap to produce and costly to trust; the interview round probes that asymmetry.

Interviewers added this round after 2023, borrowing from older tools. The structured behavioural interview, which asks for a past situation rather than an opinion, dates from industrial psychology in the mid-twentieth century. The verification half borrows from acceptance sampling, worked out by Harold Dodge and Harry Romig at Bell Labs in the 1920s and 1930s: inspect a sample of a batch, estimate the defect rate, and decide whether to accept the batch.

The sentence Kelkar could repeat without sounding glib was this: "Here is the step the model does, here is the step I keep, and here is how I know the line is in the right place." Each clause maps to a row of the rubric in section 4.

3. How it works

The mechanics are a loop with five steps, shown below. Two are routinely left unsaid, and interviewers listen for them.

Step 1, framing, is the first implicit step. Kelkar decides what question the work answers (why do shopkeepers abandon the loan application?) and what an acceptable output looks like, before any model is touched. Step 2 is the model's turn: given transcripts of forty customer calls, it tags themes and drafts a summary, and she instructs it to attach a verbatim quote to every claim so each can be traced. Step 3, the second implicit step and the most important: she checks a sample of the claims against the transcripts. Step 4 has three exits: accept, tighten the prompt and rerun (the dashed loop), or abandon the model for this task. Step 5 records the measured error rate so next time she starts from evidence.

Anyone can say "I use AI for research". The candidate who says where framing, auditing and deciding sit shows she treats the model as a fast, unreliable colleague whose work needs inspecting, which is the mental model the round screens for.

4. A worked example

Kelkar had real numbers from a project in September. She had forty customer-call transcripts and, she estimated, ten distinct claims in each for the model to summarise: 40 × 10 = 400 claims. Doing it by hand took about 60 minutes per call: 40 × 60 = 2,400 minutes, or 40 hours.

With the workflow, she audited 12 transcripts, which is 12 × 10 = 120 claims, at about 20 minutes each, then spent 90 minutes on synthesis. That is 240 minutes plus 90, or 330 minutes: 5.5 hours. The saving was 40 − 5.5 = 34.5 hours, or 86.25 per cent of the manual effort (about 86 per cent). The audit result matters more.

The second pass changes one input: the instruction to attach a quote to every claim. Wrong claims fall from 18 to 12, the expected wrong claims in the unaudited 280 fall from 42 to 28, and each transcript audits faster because the quote tells the checker where to look. Kelkar can now say: "I measured 15 per cent wrong, changed one instruction, and measured 10." She must also say what the data cannot show. With 120 claims, the 95 per cent range around 15 per cent is roughly 9 to 21 per cent, since 1.96 × √(0.15 × 0.85 ÷ 120) is about 6.4 points. Around 10 per cent it is roughly 5 to 15. 5. Nuances a learner must know

Fluency is not volume

Using AI for many tasks is not fluency, and a candidate who claims it everywhere raises suspicion. An interviewer such as Iyengar wants to hear at least one task where the candidate decided not to use the model, and why.

"I check everything" is not credible

Auditing all 40 transcripts would take 40 × 20 = 800 minutes, plus 90 for synthesis, or 890 minutes (about 14.8 hours against 40 by hand), a saving of about 25.2 hours or 63 per cent. Still a saving, but the extra 28 transcripts cost 560 minutes, about 9.3 hours, to inspect 280 more claims. A boundary is an economic claim: verify in proportion to the cost of being wrong. Her 12-of-40 sample was a deliberate trade, and she should say so.

A sample gives a rate, not a location

Acceptance sampling tells you roughly how bad the batch is, not which items are bad. If a single claim will drive a lending-policy change, audit that claim by itself, whatever the sample says.

Errors are not equal

A distorted claim that "customers dislike the form" costs little; an invented claim that "customers distrust the interest rate" can redirect a quarter. Good answers weight errors by consequence.

Data governance is part of the workflow

Customer transcripts contain personal data. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending norms constrain what a lender may send to an outside service. Kelkar anonymised names and phone numbers first, and skipping this signals a gap at a regulated lender.

The measurement expires

The 15 per cent figure describes one model version, one prompt and one set of transcripts. Providers update models, so a workflow needs re-auditing when anything changes. "I measured once" is weaker than "I re-measure when the model changes."

The model answers the question it is given

No audit tells you whether abandonment was the right question. Framing stays human because only a person knows what the business needs to decide. A thoughtful newcomer should ask of any AI-assisted result: what would make me abandon this method?

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; early-stage and large

In a consumer product, feedback volume is high and any one wrong claim is cheap, so wide sampling suits; the risk is mistaking loud themes for representative ones. In B2B, as at Pinaka, a handful of enterprise or lender conversations carry large revenue, so a wrong summary of one account can be expensive, and the audit should cover every claim from the biggest accounts. In a marketplace, there are two sides, and a candidate should show that the model's summary of one side (say, sellers) has been checked against the other (buyers), since a fix for one may hurt the other.

Scale changes the answer too. An early-stage company has few people and little process, so the interviewer wants to see speed with a safety habit: a one-page audit note is enough. A large company such as a bank or a big e-commerce firm wants documented controls, data-handling rules and a view on who approves model use. In the startup, lead with the time saved and the check; in the large firm, lead with the control and the record.

7. Common mistakes

The tool inventory

Symptom: the answer names four products and no decision. Misunderstanding: the interviewer is assessing exposure. Diagnostic: delete every product name from your answer; if nothing is left, you have no workflow.

Universal verification

Symptom: "I always check everything." Misunderstanding: that care means checking everything. Diagnostic: ask yourself what fraction you checked and how long it took; if you cannot give both numbers, the claim is rhetoric.

Only the success story

Symptom: every example ends well. Misunderstanding: that failure signals weakness. Diagnostic: find one case where the model was wrong, what it cost and what you changed. Kelkar's 7 invented claims in pass 1 were her best material.

Numbers without meaning

Symptom: "it saves 86 per cent of my time" and nothing more. Misunderstanding: that speed is the point. Diagnostic: ask what the quality was at that speed; if you cannot answer, add the audit result.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled Kelkar answer is about two minutes long. She names the task (forty calls, one question), states which step the model owns, and says what she kept: the question, the sample audit and the ship-or-redo decision. She gives the figures: 15 per cent wrong at first, 10 per cent after requiring quotes, the ranges overlapping so she would re-measure on the next batch. She mentions anonymising the data and one task kept manual, the final recommendation to the credit team. She names the edge of what she knows.

9. Closing: what Kelkar decides

On Monday night Kelkar deleted the tool list. She decided to lead with the forty-call workflow, to show Figure 1 on paper if Iyengar permitted, and to put the audit table at the centre. Her reasoning: a specific, measured story is hard to fake and easy to probe. She also chose to admit that the improvement from 15 to 10 per cent was not proven, because an interviewer who can see a candidate's limits is more likely to believe the rest.

To learn next, study how teams build evals, the repeatable tests that score model output against a standard, because they turn her one-off audit into a standing practice. Then read about taste and editorial judgement, the scarcer skill the audit protects.

Two questions to sit with. First, in your own last piece of AI-assisted work, what fraction did you check, and what error rate would have made you stop? Second, which step of your workflow would you refuse to hand to a model however good it became, and is that refusal reasoned or merely habit?
exp40v2-craft.interview.ai.fluency:
The AI-Fluency Round: What It Measures and How It Is Won

What looks like talk about tools is, in good hands, about measurement, cost and where a human belongs.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On Monday 12 October 2026 in Chennai, Jaskaran Bedi, vice-president of product at Nauka Freight Exchange, a two-sided marketplace matching shippers with fleet owners, read a hiring summary he disliked. Since January 2025, twenty-one months, Nauka had hired fourteen product managers; 9 of the 14, 64.3 per cent, were rated effective or better at six months. The five who were not were, he thought, hired on fluency of speech.

Between January and September 2026 Nauka received 1,480 applications, ran 185 phone screens, 12.5 per cent of applicants, advanced 52 candidates to the final loop and made 11 offers, of which 8 were accepted. All 52 faced the forty-minute round Bedi introduced in February, titled "AI fluency", and only 9 of the 52, 17.3 per cent, scored above its midpoint. A round that fails five in six is either screening something rare or measuring nothing.

Three days later, on Thursday 15 October, Nandita Phansalkar arrived at a Hyderabad tower for the final loop at Jigyasa Learning Systems, which sold an adaptive practice app, Jigyasa Abhyaas, to 60,000 paying students at ₹499 a month, monthly revenue of ₹2.994 crore. Its core was a model that generated mathematics hints. Phansalkar was a senior product manager at Nishtha Insurance Services in Pune, owning the motor-claims intake queue. Two interviewers waited: Hitesh Lokhande, head of product, and Nilanjana Baruah, who led applied science with Jigyasa's machine-learning lead in Kraków, Jolanta Michalak.

Phansalkar's problem mirrored Bedi's: real work with models, and no idea how to make forty minutes of it legible. Her first draft named four assistants and no decision; the third named a number: 42.

2. What the round is actually for

AI fluency, assessed in an interview, is the demonstrated ability to reason about a product built on a probabilistic component: how the model fails, how the failure is caught before a customer meets it, what you measure and why that measure maps to money, where a human stays in the loop, and what the thing costs to serve at the latency the product needs. It is not tool familiarity.

The round is new; its parts are old. The work-sample test has been among the better-validated predictors since the 1998 meta-analysis of Frank Schmidt and John Hunter, which put its validity near 0.5. The measurement vocabulary comes from signal detection theory, developed by Wilson Tanner and John Swets on radar operators in the early 1950s: a detector has no single accuracy but an adjustable operating point trading misses against false alarms. The rubric quarrel belongs to Paul Meehl, whose 1954 monograph showed mechanical combination of evidence beating expert clinical judgement.

Four schools contend over what the round should test. The craft school holds that fluency is a property of a workflow: it signs "a candidate who cannot name the step she kept for herself is not fluent", and refuses that it can be inferred from a take-home a model may have written. The evaluation school holds that fluency is the ability to specify a measurement: it signs "no eval, no product" and refuses "a narrative is evidence". The economics school asks first whether gross margin survives the inference bill at tolerable latency, and refuses "an eval score settles it". The judgement school holds that models commoditise production, so what stays scarce is knowing what good looks like: it signs "you cannot write a useful eval for a product you have no taste in".

3. Mechanics: the six things a fluent answer contains

Phansalkar's 42 came from a model Nishtha put into motor-claims intake in June 2026. Roughly 1,20,000 claim emails arrive a year, and the model predicted for each whether it needed a human adjuster. She drew a golden set, a hand-labelled sample treated as ground truth, of 600 emails from the 10,000 that arrived in June. In 210 of the 600, 35.0 per cent, a human was genuinely required. The third is capacity, where models meet payroll. The fifth element, cost and latency, belongs to the product being interviewed for. Jigyasa's hint generator takes about 2,400 input tokens and returns about 300; a token is the unit a model bills by, roughly three-quarters of a word.

Routing's p95 latency of 8.1 seconds is also worse than the large model's 7.4, because an escalated request pays both calls and, at 22 per cent escalation, the slowest five per cent of traffic sits inside the escalated group.

The sixth is human review. Nishtha is human-in-the-loop: an adjuster sees every escalated claim first. Jigyasa is human-on-the-loop: hints ship instantly and a teaching team samples 300 a week. The choice is set by reversibility, not caution. A wrongly auto-processed claim is slow and costly to undo; a bad hint is seen for ten seconds and regenerated.

4. When the frame applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as claims and tested against both protagonists. First, output varies for identical input: true at Jigyasa, where the hint generator is the product, and at Nauka, where a classifier reads load descriptions; false in a payments ledger, where determinism is the requirement. Second, errors are asymmetric in cost: overwhelmingly true at Nishtha, ₹9,000 against ₹100; weak at Jigyasa, where a bad hint and a cautious one cost about the same. Third, volume is high enough for a sample to estimate a rate: true at 1,20,000 claims a year; false for Nauka's forty largest shipper accounts, where the method is to inspect all forty. Fourth, inference cost is material: true for Jigyasa at 4.87 per cent of revenue, while Nauka's bill is a rounding error.

The frame misleads in three situations. Where the base rate is tiny, fraud at one in ten thousand, a 600-item sample holds no positives. Where the output has no single right answer, as in brand copy, a pass-or-fail eval entrenches one reviewer's taste. And where the binding constraint is regulatory permission, measurement is beside the point.

5. Hard edges

In a multi-product company the seam is the golden set: each product wants its own labels and each team under-invests. The tell is a candidate who can say who re-labels the set when the taxonomy changes.

In a two-sided market the seam is whose error you counted. Nauka's classifier tags lane, tonnage and vehicle type from a fleet owner's free text, and measured against shipper satisfaction it looks excellent: a mis-tagged tonnage costs the truck owner a wasted trip and the shipper nothing. Bedi's best question was which side a candidate's metric was computed on, since the right answer, two confusion matrices, is rarely reached unprompted.

In regulated settings the seam is lawful basis. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs what Nishtha may do with claimant data, and the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India expects demonstrable control over automated decisions affecting policyholders. Experts separate where data is processed, what a vendor may retain, and whether a human can explain an adverse decision.

In hardware-plus-software the seams are memory and update cadence: a model small enough for a warehouse scanner cannot be swapped weekly, so the eval must anticipate a year of drift. In AI-native products the eval set is the roadmap. Mature companies say they have one eval practice; most have three, one per founding team.

6. Eight things an expert notices

The denominator is missing. A candidate says the model is "about 90 per cent accurate". Of what, measured on how many, labelled by whom? The obvious reading, exaggeration, is usually wrong: more often someone else ran the eval.

Accuracy was the wrong objective. The August change cut accuracy by 5.5 points and earned ₹3.63 crore. The tell is one quality number offered for an asymmetric decision; most candidates know the definitions but have never attached rupees to each cell.

The golden set came from the easy month. Her 600 emails were all from June, and motor claims are seasonal. The tell is an eval set with no sampling frame. An expert asks what would make the result wrong, and re-samples across quarters.

Review capacity, not model quality, binds. The ₹3.63 crore needed two adjusters Nishtha lacked. The tell is a proposal that raises escalation volume without saying who absorbs it; candidates read this as operations, but the operating point is the product decision.

The improvement was never re-measured. On 1 September the provider updated the model, and three weeks later the same 600 emails gave recall of 82.4 per cent against August's 90.0, precision flat. The tell is "we measured it" with no cadence; nobody budgeted the re-run.

The failure mode was named generically. "Hallucination", fluent output unsupported by any source, is one failure among several. A candidate who knows only that word cannot reason about distribution shift, where live inputs stop resembling the eval set, prompt injection, where content inside the data instructs the model, sycophancy, or silent version drift.

Human review was a safeguard, not a design. "A human checks it" is not a design; the design is which human, seeing what fraction, with what authority to overrule. The tell is the absence of a fraction. Phansalkar's 23 rework cases were a more useful commitment than checking everything.

The candidate never declined to use a model. The strongest signal across Bedi's fourteen hires was naming a task deliberately kept manual. Nauka's rate-negotiation guidance stayed human because an error there is invisible until a fleet owner leaves. The tell is universal enthusiasm.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products volume is high and any single error cheap, so the question becomes aggregate quality and cost per interaction, Jigyasa's shape. In B2B and enterprise, a few accounts carry the revenue and sampling is often the wrong instrument; census inspection of the top accounts belongs in the answer. In platform and marketplace products, Nauka's shape, the requirement is per-side measurement. In hardware, the constraints are memory, power and the impossibility of a Friday rollback. For AI products, where the model is what is sold, the eval set doubles as the specification. Where the difference is overstated: the underlying reasoning is identical throughout.

Stage matters more than type. At seed stage the fluent answer is a one-page measurement note and a bias to shipping; demanding a maintained golden set of a six-person company is a misread. At Jigyasa's scale the answer adds ownership and cadence; in a large insurer it adds lawful basis, model-risk sign-off and an auditable measurement.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

The answer that worked. Phansalkar opened with the decision, not the model: Nishtha was missing 8,400 claims a year that needed a human, at a measured ₹9,000 each. She showed both matrices, named the trade she had bought, attached ₹3.63 crore to it, then said the awkward part, that it needed a ninth and tenth adjuster. Pressed on the sample, she gave the interval, 74.6 to 85.4 per cent around the July recall, and volunteered that the June-only frame was the weakest link.

The recovery from drift. Lokhande asked twice about 22 September. At the post-update point the annual cost of being wrong was ₹728.80 lakh against August's ₹445.80 lakh: ₹283.00 lakh of the ₹363.00 lakh gain erased by a change nobody at Nishtha made, leaving ₹80.00 lakh. The recovery was a monthly re-run of the same 600 emails, a threshold Nishtha could move itself, and notice of version changes. The asset was the labelled set, not the prompt.

The answer that failed. On 4 June 2026 Jasleen Oberoi interviewed with Harsha Nimkar, head of product at Haazir Workforce Services in Noida, and presented a support assistant that had "deflected 38 per cent of tickets": 86,000 tickets a quarter, of which it closed 32,680, 38.0 per cent, saving ₹62 of agent time each, so ₹20,26,160 a quarter. A deflection meant the assistant closing the conversation. Nimkar asked what share of those customers returned within a week; Oberoi did not know. Checked afterwards it was 11,438 of the 32,680, or 35.0 per cent, making true deflection 21,242, which is 24.7 per cent of 86,000 rather than 38.0, and the saving ₹13,17,004, an overstatement of ₹7,09,156 a quarter. She was rejected. Eleven weeks later, on 20 August, she presented the same project elsewhere, leading with the seven-day repeat-contact definition; an offer followed. The recovery was a definition, not a technology.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The tool inventory is commonest. Warning sign: product names and no decision. Diagnostic: "what would you have done differently if the tool had not existed?" Late, it costs a hire who cannot be trusted with a model-backed feature.

The metric that counts actions is Oberoi's failure and the costliest. Warning sign: a success metric that is an event the system itself produces. Diagnostic: "what would the customer say happened?" Late, it funds a year of work against ₹7.09 lakh a quarter of imaginary saving.

The unpriced inference bill is particular to 2026. Warning sign: a model choice justified by quality alone. Diagnostic: "at what volume does this move gross margin by a point?" At scale it eats contribution margin quietly, the bill growing with success.

The frozen measurement is subtlest. Warning sign: "we validated that", with one date. Diagnostic: "when did you last re-run it?" Late, it looks like Nishtha's September: ₹2.83 crore of annual value gone with no deployment and no alert.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should this be a separate round at all? Integrationists argue that every question here is a product-sense question with a probabilistic component, and that Bedi's distribution, 29 of the 52 in the bottom band, suggests a round measuring familiarity with a genre. Separatists argue that generic questions never force a candidate to name an operating point, and that the skill is new enough to be absent in otherwise strong people; for them to be wrong, strong hires would have to be identifiable without the round. Nauka's data cannot settle it: of the six hires above the midpoint, 5 of the 6 were later rated effective; of the eight below, 4 of the 8. A 33.3-point gap on fourteen people is indistinguishable from noise.

Should candidates use a model during the interview? The permissive position is that the job allows it, and watching someone prompt and reject output is the most direct work sample available. The restrictive position is that the round must measure the candidate's judgement rather than the tool's output. What would move the restrictive camp is a format where the candidate critiques output they did not ask for.

Rubric or holistic judgement? Meehl favours the rubric. The counter-argument, held sincerely by good interviewers, is that a weighted score flattens the one disqualifying answer: a candidate who would send claimant data to an unvetted service should not be rescued by scoring well on cost.

Durable skill or artefact of 2026? Sceptics say it is yesterday's "can you write SQL", a transient scarcity tooling will erase, while the enduring skills already have names. The opposing view is that reasoning about a non-deterministic component is a new addition to product craft. The sceptics are wrong if, five years on, candidates still differ sharply on where human review belongs.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this leads with the decision and the money, introducing the model as an implementation detail. She volunteers the limits of her own evidence first, because the sampling frame is the part she is least sure of. She moves between registers, rupees for the general manager, confusion matrix for the scientist, latency percentile for the engineer. And she has one task deliberately kept human, defended economically rather than morally. Someone who has merely studied the topic defines precision and recall faster, and cannot say which one Nishtha should have optimised.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Bedi kept the round and rebuilt its scoring. The February version scored narration; the October version weights five dimensions, each marked 0 to 4.

Nauka AI-fluency rubric, October 2026WeightTool-list

Weights sum to 25 + 25 + 20 + 15 + 15 = 100. The weighted score sums weight × score and divides by 100. Tool-list: 25 + 25 + 0 + 30 + 15 = 95, so 0.95. Project without measurement: 75 + 50 + 20 + 30 + 45 = 220, so 2.20. Phansalkar-type: 75 + 100 + 80 + 45 + 60 = 360, so 3.60.

He added a named veto for any answer that would put customer data where Nauka could not account for it, and a commitment to record every AI-round score against the six-month rating, so that the round's predictive value can one day rest on more than fourteen people.

Phansalkar was offered the Jigyasa role and took it. Her account of why it worked was not that ₹3.63 crore at an insurer is impressive, but that every figure came from a set she had built, so every follow-up had an answer. The part she had hesitated to include, the September drift that erased ₹2.83 crore, was what both interviewers remembered.

Discussion questions.

1. The August operating point was worth ₹3.63 crore a year and needed two adjusters Nishtha did not have. If only one could be hired, what operating point should she choose?

2. Nauka's round puts 43 of the 52 candidates at or below its midpoint, 82.7 per cent, and Bedi cannot show it predicts performance. Keep it, soften it, or fold it into the product-sense round?

3. The routed configuration costs 1.72 per cent of revenue and fails 15 per cent of its eval; the large model costs 4.87 per cent and fails 11 per cent. What evidence would settle the choice?

13. Going deeper

AI tools in the PM workflow supplies the raw material: without a real workflow there is nothing to narrate. Taste and editorial judgement as the scarce skill explains why a candidate with no view of good output cannot compose a useful eval set. A PM's operating system holds the cadence of re-measurement. Continuous learning as a PM unlocks answering the drift question honestly. PM interviews gives the structure of the loop this round sits in, and building a PM portfolio and narrative is where the worked example gets written down, numbers preserved. Transitioning into product management matters because candidates from engineering, data and operations each arrive with a different half of the answer. And your first 90 days in a PM role is where the claims get tested: the joiner who re-runs the eval set and reports what moved has made the answer true.
case20v1-craft.interview.ai.fluency:
The Round That Asks What You Overruled

Designing and reading the AI-fluency interview at Jivika Exchange

1. Opening

At 8:40 on Monday, 5 October 2026, Meenakshi Iyer sat in a glass-walled meeting room at the Koramangala headquarters of Jivika Exchange in Bengaluru, with a laptop open to a blank scorecard. She was Director of Product, and she had four product manager openings to fill, each budgeted at ₹38 lakh annual cost to company, a combined annual commitment of ₹1.52 crore. Nandini Rao, the head of talent acquisition, needed the format of the new "AI-fluency round" by Friday, 9 October, so that invitations to thirty shortlisted candidates could go out on Monday, 12 October. The round itself would run from Monday, 19 October to Friday, 23 October, and offers had to land by Friday, 30 October, ahead of Diwali on 8 November, when the best candidates would already be weighing other offers.

Every candidate now said they were AI-fluent, and Meenakshi could no longer tell who was. She had to decide what the round should reward.

2. Company background

Jivika Exchange, founded in 2016, sells working-capital credit and UPI acceptance tools to small merchants, chiefly kirana stores, pharmacies and neighbourhood wholesalers. It serves about 9 lakh merchants across 14 states, employs about 1,100 people and reported revenue of ₹640 crore in the last financial year. Its credit products operate under the RBI's digital lending guidelines through regulated lending partners, and its payments flows ride on UPI rails run by NPCI.

PhonePe for Business and Paytm sit in the same merchant's shop on the same counter, Razorpay courts the larger merchants, and ONDC has begun to pull small sellers towards open-network commerce. Jivika competes on credit decisions made faster and explained better, which is why its product managers are expected to work with machine-learning teams daily and to use AI tools in their own work. The company also holds sensitive merchant data, so the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 shapes what product managers may paste into any external tool.

3. The situation

In April 2026 Jivika had piloted a take-home exercise for sixty candidates across three open roles. Candidates, told AI tools were allowed, produced a one-page product brief for a merchant-credit feature. Reviewers scored the briefs on a five-point scale. The briefs were, almost uniformly, polished.

Ishaan Verma, a data scientist in Sydney who sat on the pilot panel, proposed a simple follow-up. In a twenty-minute call, he asked each candidate one question: which part of your draft did you change after the tool wrote it, and why? Exhibit 1 shows what he found. Of the sixty candidates, only twenty-four could name a specific change and give a reason for it, and the share who could do so was no higher among those with the best briefs.

Exhibit 1. April 2026 take-home pilot (AI permitted), by output score
Output score bandCandidatesNamed a specific change and reasonShare who did

Middle (3)20840.0%

Total / overall share602440.0%

Source: Jivika Exchange talent team, April 2026. Share is the third column divided by the second. The follow-up question was asked of all sixty candidates in the same words.

The lesson Meenakshi drew was uncomfortable. The take-home had measured the output, and the output was now cheap. What she wanted to see was the workflow behind it: where a candidate used a tool, where they refused its answer, and how they knew. She remembered two candidates from that cycle. One had listed five assistants and could not say what any had got wrong. The other, Tanay Bhatt, then a final-year student at ISB Hyderabad, had described how he drafted a customer-interview guide with a model, discovered that it kept proposing leading questions, rewrote six of them by hand, and stopped using it for synthesis because it flattened a minority view that he considered the most important.

4. The people

Harpreet Sodhi, head of engineering in Pune, wants product managers who can prototype and write specifications with AI quickly. He distrusts rubrics and prefers the original take-home, with an added tool question, because it is fast and shows what a candidate can ship.

Nandini Rao, in Hyderabad, owns the process. She wants a format that is consistent across interviewers, can be defended if a rejected candidate complains, and respects candidates' time. She will accept more interviewer hours only if she can show what they buy.

Ishaan Verma, in Sydney, wants the follow-up question built into the format. Sydney is five and a half hours ahead of Bengaluru, so a 4:00 pm India panel falls at 9:30 pm for him, and the rubric must work for a tired, remote panelist.

Meenakshi Iyer, in Bengaluru, owns the outcome and the hires. She has to choose a format she can explain to the CEO and to the candidates.

5. Exhibits

Nandini supplied the cost of each candidate format, priced at a loaded ₹3,000 per interviewer-hour (Exhibit 2). The take-home needs one reviewer for an hour and a half, the walkthrough needs two interviewers for an hour each, and a closed-book in-person case needs three. For thirty candidates the differences are real but small: the walkthrough costs ₹45,000 more than the take-home, and the in-person case costs ₹1.35 lakh more.

The second question was what a walkthrough would score. Meenakshi drafted the rubric in Exhibit 3, weighting judgement above everything else and giving tool breadth the least.

6. The options

Option A: keep the take-home and add a tool question. This is Harpreet's preference. It is the cheapest at ₹1.35 lakh for thirty candidates and needs no new training. The cost is the finding in Exhibit 1: the score rewards output that any candidate can now produce, and a tool question invites exactly the tool list Meenakshi wants to avoid.

Option B: a forty-five-minute workflow walkthrough. The candidate brings one real piece of past work and walks two interviewers through it, scored on Exhibit 3. It tests the thing she cares about and is only ₹45,000 more than option A for thirty candidates. The costs are interviewer calibration, anonymising confidential past work, and the risk that a fluent talker performs a workflow they did not follow.

Option C: a closed-book in-person case with no AI. Nandini finds it easy to defend, because it looks like a conventional interview and removes any question of who produced the answer. It costs ₹2.70 lakh, the most of the three. It also tests a condition that will not exist in the job, and it says nothing about how a candidate would use the tools that every Jivika product manager now uses.

7. Questions for discussion

1. What did the April pilot measure, and what did it fail to measure? Use Exhibit 1 to explain why a high output score is weak evidence of AI fluency.

2. Using Exhibit 2, what does the extra spend of option B over option A buy, and how does it compare with the ₹1.52 crore annual cost of the four roles being filled?

3. Examine the weights in Exhibit 3. Would you change them? How would a rubric treat Tanay Bhatt's account of the interview guide against a candidate who listed five tools?

4. Which option should Meenakshi take to the panel on Friday, and what single safeguard would you add against a candidate who performs a workflow they did not follow?

8. A note for the learner

This case frames an interview as a measurement problem. The question a hiring manager should ask is what evidence of the scarce skill, judgement over output, the format can produce. In a world where a model can draft a brief, a candidate's artefact is cheap to make, so the artefact is weak evidence. The strong evidence is the trail behind it: the steps, the moments of refusal and the checks. This is also what a candidate should rehearse. A concrete workflow with the places where human judgement was kept is stronger than any list of tools.

One defensible path is option B, with two additions. First, every candidate receives a short AI-drafted paragraph containing a planted factual error and has ten minutes to review it aloud, so that the panel sees verification happen live rather than hear it described. Second, the two interviewers score independently before comparing, and Ishaan's remote panels use the same written anchors as everyone else.

The reasoning is as follows. Exhibit 1 shows that output scores do not separate candidates who can explain their judgement from those who cannot, so option A repeats the problem. Option C removes the tools instead of testing how they are used. Option B costs ₹1.80 lakh against ₹1.35 lakh, an extra ₹45,000, which is about 0.3 per cent of the ₹1.52 crore annual cost of the roles. That is cheap insurance against a wrong hire. Its main risk is a rehearsed story, and the live review is designed to expose it. Nandini's need for defensibility is met because every score is anchored to written evidence.
exp20v2-craft.interview.behavioural:
Behavioural Rounds Without PM Experience

1. The scene

On Saturday 3 October 2026, Farhan Banerjee sat with a coach and a printed calendar. Banerjee was an operations manager at Bhoomi Freight Exchange, a Pune-based marketplace that matches manufacturers with truck owners. He had spent six years there and had never held a product title. In ten days, on Tuesday 13 October, he would sit the behavioural round of a five-round interview loop for an associate product manager role at Falgun Retail Labs, an e-commerce company in Bengaluru.

A behavioural round is an interview in which the candidate is asked to describe things that actually happened, not to speculate about what they would do. The premise, worked out by industrial psychologists such as Tom Janz in the 1980s, is that past conduct predicts future conduct better than stated intentions. The commonest prompt in a product loop is some version of: tell me about a time you got a result from people who did not report to you.

The funnel was unforgiving, as Table 1 shows. Falgun had received 1,200 applications and invited 60 to a phone screen, which is 5 per cent. Fifteen of those 60 reached the full loop, a rate of 25 per cent, and the company intended to make 3 offers, which is 20 per cent of 15. Of 1,200 applicants, 3 would be hired: 0.25 per cent. Because each of the five rounds delivers one vote to the hiring committee, the behavioural round carried 1 of 5 votes, or 20 per cent of the signal.

Table 1. Falgun Retail Labs hiring funnel, associate PM role
StageCandidatesConversion from previous stage
Applications1,200n/a
Phone screen605%
Full loop1525%
Offers320%

His coach, Bhavna Fernandes, a former product lead at a payments company, asked a blunt question: which stories will you tell? Banerjee answered that he did not have any, since he had never run a product. Fernandes said he was treating the round as a test of titles, when it was a test of evidence, and he was assuming the evidence had to come from product work.

2. The idea

Influence without authority means changing what another person or team does when you cannot instruct them, reward them or discipline them. Product managers live in that condition. Engineers, designers, sales heads and legal counsel do not report to them, yet the product ships only if all of them move in one direction. Interviewers therefore ask for stories about it, since the behaviour is the job in miniature.

A story, in this sense, is a compact account of one episode with a fixed shape. Many coaches teach the acronym STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result), which grew out of the structured-interview tradition. STAR lets a candidate spend most of the time on situation and outcome, which a title explains; the five-part variant below puts the weight on the middle.

The sentence Banerjee could repeat to Fernandes, or to any interviewer, without sounding glib was this: a story is evidence that I moved people who did not have to move, and the evidence is the decision I changed, not the title I held.

3. How it works

The five parts are Stakes, Divergence, Move, Result and Residue. Stakes states what was at risk and for whom, in numbers. Divergence names the specific people whose interests differed and why each had a reasonable position. Move is the thing the candidate did, in the first person, which was not an order. Result is the changed decision or metric. Residue is what remained afterwards: what the candidate would do differently and what the relationship looked like a quarter later. Residue is the part practitioners most often leave implicit, and it is the part that persuades interviewers the story is real.

Figure 1 shows why the budget is lopsided. An interviewer is silently asking one question: what did this person do that I could not have predicted from their job description? Only the Move answers it. A candidate who spends 100 of 260 seconds there gives roughly 38 per cent of the answer to the evidence that matters; a candidate who compresses it into twenty seconds has told a story about an outcome.

Before any of this comes mining. Banerjee had no stories on his list because he searched for the wrong thing. He searched for product episodes. The correct search is for any occasion on which his formal power ran out. In consulting these are recommendations a client was free to ignore. In engineering they are design disputes with a peer. In operations they are rules owned by another department, and in sales they are commitments that depend on delivery staff you do not manage. Fernandes asked him to list every episode in six years where he needed something from someone who owed him nothing. He produced eleven in an hour and kept five.

4. A worked example

Having five candidate stories, Banerjee needed a way to choose among them. Fernandes proposed four criteria, each scored 0 to 5: Stakes (was something material at risk), No authority (how completely did he lack the power to order the outcome), Own action (can he say precisely what he did, apart from the team), and Measurable result. The total is the simple sum of four scores, a maximum of 20. Table 2 gives his first pass.

Table 2. Banerjee's five stories, first-pass scores (0 to 5 each)
StoryStakesNo authorityOwn actionResultTotal (of 20)
A. Rerouting dispute across three hub managers454417
B. Carrier penalty terms, with the sales head533516
C. Dispatch dashboard adopted by the dispatch team344314
D. Night-shift incident fixed under pressure415414
E. Internal hackathon prototype22318

Story A led. In it, three hub managers each believed that rerouting trucks would hurt their own detention figures. Banerjee had no authority over any of them. He ran a two-week trial on one corridor and showed each manager their own numbers. Weekly delayed dispatches, across about 4,000 trips, fell from 18 per cent to 11 per cent. That is 720 delayed trips falling to 440, a reduction of 280, or about 39 per cent in relative terms (280 divided by 720).

Story B scored 16 and looked weaker only because Banerjee had described it as a joint effort. Quarterly carrier penalty claims fell from ₹42 lakh to ₹27 lakh, a saving of ₹15 lakh, which is about 36 per cent of ₹42 lakh. When Fernandes pressed him, he recalled that he had drafted the clause, argued it to the carriers' regional managers, and persuaded the sales head to concede a rate review. The sales head had only signed. Rescored for what he did, Own action rose from 3 to 5. Table 3 shows the second pass.

Table 3. Second pass: one input changed (Story B, Own action 3 to 5)
