One honest re-description reversed the ranking: 16 plus 2 is 18, which now exceeds 17. The scores are not precise; the ranking was simply most sensitive to the criterion where candidates habitually under-claim.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Authority is about the lever, not the title

A senior director can still lack authority over another director's roadmap, and a junior analyst may hold real authority over a spreadsheet's design. The test is whether the person could have been instructed. If yes, the story is about management, however impressive.

"We" hides the evidence

The remedy is not boasting but partition: say what the team did, then say what you alone did, and why the team could not have done it without you.

It is not persuasion, charisma or stakeholder management

Stakeholder management usually means keeping people informed. Influence, as tested here, means changing a decision.

Fabrication fails at the third follow-up

Interviewers ask what the other person said next and how the relationship stood afterwards. An invented episode runs out of detail by the third question. A real one gets richer.

The round cannot tell you product judgement

A flawless influence story shows that a candidate can move people. It does not show they know what to build. Other rounds test that, and strength in this one does not rescue weakness in them.

Questions to ask before relying on a story

Would I be comfortable if the other person were in the room? Can I state the opposing view so that its owner would agree with my summary? Is the result attributable to me, or would it have happened anyway? A story that fails any of these should be dropped, however good the number.

6. How it differs by context

The same story is read differently depending on the company's shape. Table 4 summarises what an interviewer is typically listening for.

Table 4. What the interviewer listens for
ContextPreferred evidenceTypical gap in an ops, consulting or sales story
Consumer productChanging a peer's mind with behavioural data about usersStories about internal clients, with no end-user in sight
B2B productAligning a customer, sales and engineering around one commitmentSales stories that end at a signed deal, not a delivered one
MarketplaceBalancing two sides whose interests conflictStories that favour one side without naming the other's cost
Early-stage companyBreadth, speed and visible ownershipProcess-heavy stories from large employers
Large companyAlignment across layers and tolerance for slow decisionsHeroic solo stories that ignore the organisation

Banerjee's marketplace background was an unusual asset here. Both Stories A and B involved two sides, hubs against dispatch and carriers against the sales team, with real costs on each. At a start-up he would lead with B for its speed; at a large employer, with A.

7. Common mistakes

The résumé recital

Symptom: the candidate narrates responsibilities ("I managed twelve hubs") and never reaches an episode. Misunderstanding: that the round reviews the CV. Diagnostic: ask whether the opening sentence contains a date and a named person other than the candidate. If not, it is a summary, not a story.

The hero without opposition

Symptom: no one in the story ever disagrees. Misunderstanding: that conflict reflects badly on the teller. Diagnostic: write one sentence for each opponent beginning "reasonably, he thought that...". If you cannot, the Divergence is missing.

The unattributed number

Symptom: a large result with no mechanism. Misunderstanding: that size impresses. Diagnostic: ask "what would the number have been without me?" If the answer is "the same", pick another story.

One story, five questions

Symptom: the same episode appears for conflict, failure and leadership prompts. Misunderstanding: that stories are fixed to prompts. Diagnostic: tabulate each story against the prompt types; any story used more than twice is carrying too much.

8. What good looks like

Banerjee, on 13 October, was asked to describe a time he persuaded someone with no obligation to listen. He opened with a date and a figure: in March, 18 per cent of weekly dispatches across 4,000 trips were late. He named the two hub managers who objected and gave each a reasonable position. He then spent his longest passage on the Move, the corridor trial and the decision to show each manager only their own data. He gave the 18 and 11 per cent figures, said plainly that this was a seven-point absolute drop, and ended with the residue: one manager still distrusted the dashboard, and he had since changed his sequencing so that sceptics saw data before the presentation. Table 5 shows how the answer divided its time.

Table 5. Time actually used in Banerjee's answer
PartSeconds
Stakes35
Divergence45
Move105
Result35
Residue40
Total260

The Move occupied 105 of 260 seconds, about 40 per cent.

9. The decision, and what next

Banerjee chose Story B to lead, and kept A in reserve, since the rescored table made B the stronger evidence of his own action and A the stronger evidence of patience with several owners. He rehearsed the Move for each, not a script, because that is where follow-up questions land.

To go further, study the neighbouring topic of influence without authority itself, since the mechanics of the Move (aligning incentives, sequencing conversations, using the other side's data) are taught there in depth. Then practise with a person who will interrupt you.

Two questions to sit with. First, which episode in your own last three years would collapse by the third follow-up question, and what does that tell you about why you are drawn to it? Second, in the story you are proudest of, who disagreed with you, and could you state their position well enough that they would sign your summary?
exp40v2-craft.interview.behavioural:
Behavioural Rounds Without PM Experience

How candidates with no product title build, score and defend influence-without-authority stories.

1. Two candidates, two live decisions

On Monday 21 September 2026, Yamini Kharbanda sat in a borrowed meeting room in Gurugram with a problem she could not name. Kharbanda, thirty-one, an engagement manager at Kautilya Advisory Collective, had in six years of supply-chain and pricing work never held a product title. In twenty-four days, on Thursday 15 October, she would sit the full loop for a product manager role at Kalrav Audio Network, a Hyderabad company whose podcast and regional-music app reported 41 lakh monthly listeners. Her recruiter had mentioned a round called leadership and collaboration, carrying a quarter of the decision. She planned to prepare for it last.

Two days later, on Wednesday 23 September, Kunal Yardi faced the same round from the opposite direction. Yardi, thirty-five, was a staff firmware engineer at Yantrika Instrument Works in Coimbatore, which makes industrial flow meters — hardware with a heavy embedded-software layer, sold to cement, chemicals and water utilities. He had nineteen days before his loop at Kshetra Factory Systems, a Pune firm selling manufacturing-execution software into the very plants his meters sat inside. He had a decade of episodes in which he had changed what others built, could not tell which counted, and said "we decided" too often.

Exhibit 1. Hiring funnels for the two roles, as disclosed by the recruiters (June–October 2026)
StageKalrav Audio NetworkRateKshetra Factory SystemsRate
Applications received3,600—940—
Recruiter screen2166.0%9410.0%
Hiring-manager screen7233.3%3840.4%
Full loop2433.3%1231.6%
Offers416.7%216.7%

Each rate is conversion from the row above. End to end, Kalrav hired 4 of 3,600 applicants, or 0.11 per cent; Kshetra hired 2 of 940, or 0.21 per cent — not comparable as difficulty, since Kalrav's pool was open and Kshetra's largely referral-sourced.

What mattered, though, was the weighting inside the loop: for a candidate without a product title, the behavioural round is at once the one they discount most and the one where a point is cheapest to buy.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A behavioural round is an interview in which the candidate recounts episodes that actually occurred and is scored on the conduct the account reveals, not on a hypothesis about the future. In a product loop it tests influence without authority: the capacity to change what another team does when one cannot instruct, pay, promote or dismiss them. That is the product manager's standing condition, and the round is a cheap simulation of it.

The technique has a traceable history. John Flanagan's critical incident technique, published in 1954 for aircrew selection, showed that specific recalled incidents yield more reliable judgements than global impressions. David McClelland's 1973 argument that competence be tested directly rather than inferred from aptitude produced the behavioural event interview. Tom Janz's behaviour description interviewing, formalised in the early 1980s, supplied the premise still quoted in recruiter training: past behaviour predicts future behaviour better than stated intention. Latham and Saari's situational interview, from 1980, offered the rival move of anchored hypotheticals. Product loops today are unacknowledged hybrids.

The evidence base is contested. Meta-analytic estimates from the 1990s put the predictive validity of structured interviews near 0.5, unstructured conversation far below. Re-analyses in the 2020s, correcting for range restriction in the original corrections, lowered both — structured nearer 0.4, unstructured nearer 0.2. The ordering survived; the confidence did not.

Four schools can be told apart by what each will and will not sign. The competency school, descended from McClelland, signs that a structured interview with a published rubric beats unstructured conversation by a margin worth its cost; it will not sign that the domain of the past behaviour is irrelevant. The transfer sceptics sign that conduct is situation-specific — a consultant's success in moving a client's plant heads says little about moving an engineer who outranks her and knows she cannot read the code; they will not sign that non-product evidence is worthless, only that it is discounted. The narrative-performance school signs the deflationary claim that what is measured is the ability to construct a causal account under pressure, a job-relevant skill but not the conduct described; it will not sign that a well-told story is evidence of the event. The work-sample school signs that two hours on a real artefact dominates recollection; it will not sign abolition where the job's difficulty is relational.

Kharbanda's and Yardi's panels, then, would not agree on what the round measures. That is a design constraint, not a grievance: the expert response is material that scores well under all four readings at once.

3. Mechanics: the four claims and the lever arithmetic

Expert candidates do not prepare stories; they prepare evidence that survives interrogation. An influence story is four claims, probed in order. The authority claim: you could not have ordered this outcome. The agency claim: you did the thing that moved it, distinct from what the team did. The counterfactual claim: it would not have happened anyway, on that timetable, without you. The durability claim: the change held, and the relationship survived. Most candidates establish the first and fourth and collapse on the second and third, which is why the follow-ups carry the score.

The formal treatment experts use is a weighted rubric, and reconstructing it is a planning advantage. Exhibit 2 pairs Kalrav's weights with Kharbanda's mock-loop scores of 26 September.

Exhibit 2. Kalrav loop weights and Kharbanda's mock scores (each round scored 1.0 to 4.0)
RoundWeightMock scoreWeight × score
Product sense253.075.0
Execution and analytics202.550.0
Leadership and collaboration252.050.0
Technical collaboration153.045.0
Hiring manager153.045.0
Total100—265.0

Weighted average = 265.0 ÷ 100 = 2.65. Kalrav's documented hiring bar was 3.00.

The lever arithmetic follows. Kharbanda was 0.35 below the bar. Lifting the behavioural round from 2.0 to 3.5 adds 1.5 × 25 = 37.5 points, giving 302.5 and an average of 3.03 — over the bar. Lifting product sense from 3.0 to 3.5, far slower work, adds 0.5 × 25 = 12.5 points, giving 277.5 and an average of 2.78 — still short. It was the only single-round improvement that cleared the bar by itself.

The step usually left implicit comes first: mining. Candidates without a title search for product episodes, find none, and conclude they have nothing. The correct search term is every occasion on which formal power ran out and something moved anyway.

Exhibit 3. Story mining, run as a filter chain (September 2026)
FilterKharbandaPass rateYardiPass rate
Episodes recalled in one sitting34—27—
Survives the authority claim1955.9%1244.4%
Result statable as a number1157.9%866.7%
Rehearsed to Level 4 depth654.5%562.5%
Taken into the loop350.0%360.0%

Each pass rate is against the row above. Overall, 3 of Kharbanda's 34 episodes reached the loop, 8.8 per cent; 3 of Yardi's 27 did, 11.1 per cent.

The second-order effect is what coaches watch for: the chain does not merely select stories, it changes what the candidate believes about their career. Kharbanda called eleven of her thirty-four episodes, unprompted, "not really mine"; nine of those eleven survived the authority filter. Its real work is correcting a systematic under-claim.

4. When the approach applies, and when it misleads

The case for influence stories built from non-product work rests on three testable claims, each able to fail.

That the behaviour generalises across domains. Test whether the mechanism was domain-specific. Kharbanda's strongest episode turned on showing three plant heads their own cost data before any meeting: sequencing and self-interest, which transfer. Yardi's turned on reading a calibration log only a firmware engineer could read — partly expertise-authority, which transfers less well, since at Kshetra he would influence people whose domain he does not command.

That counterparty distance in the story matches the distance in the job. Persuading one's own partner, in one's own firm, sharing a bonus pool, is a weaker analogue than persuading a client's operations head who could simply decline. Consulting is rich here, as even the sceptics concede; Yardi's internal episodes sit closer, and he must choose accordingly.

That the result is attributable. This fails most often. Test it plainly: what would the number have been had I been on leave that month? Where the honest answer is "about the same", the episode is discarded however large the figure.

The approach actively misleads in three situations. Where the role is zero-to-one and the panel is testing appetite for ambiguity, influence stories answer a question nobody asked. Where the loop is work-sample based and the behavioural round vestigial at five or ten points, effort should follow the weights, not the folklore. And where the real deficit is product judgement, a polished narrative buys a point while leaving the gap untouched — Yardi's risk exactly, his mock product-sense score being 2.5.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Standard advice assumes one product, one counterparty and a clean metric. Real loops ask about situations with none of those.

Two-sided businesses. A marketplace interviewer listens for whether the candidate can state the cost borne by the side that lost. Take the illustration Kharbanda was given, from Kadamb Produce Exchange, an agri marketplace. It raised its take rate from 12 per cent to 14 per cent on annual gross merchandise value of ₹340 crore, lifting revenue from ₹40.80 crore. Four per cent of its 18,000 sellers left — 720 sellers, smaller than average at ₹1.1 lakh of annual GMV each against a platform average of ₹1.89 lakh — so ₹7.92 crore of GMV departed. Remaining GMV of ₹332.08 crore at 14 per cent yields ₹46.49 crore, a net gain of ₹5.69 crore. A candidate who says "I raised revenue by ₹5.69 crore" tells a weaker story than one who names the 720 departures.

Hardware plus software. Yardi's world. A software decision reverses in a sprint; a tooling decision does not for eighteen months. Influence exercised late in a hardware programme is objection, and the tell is a date.

Regulated products. In lending, insurance and health the counterparty with veto power is compliance, and "I convinced risk to let us ship" reads badly to anyone who has worked there. The expert version reframes the influence as finding a design that satisfied the constraint, naming the regulation.

AI-native products. The counterparty is partly a model nobody fully controls, and influence turns on winning acceptance for an evaluation protocol rather than a feature. Candidates who narrate AI disputes as feature disputes sound dated.

What mature companies actually do. Guidance says every interviewer uses a rubric and submits written evidence before debrief. In practice write-ups appear after the debrief has begun, and one anecdote carries disproportionate weight because it is what everyone remembers. The expert response is design, not cynicism — one episode, one number, one named opponent, repeatable by whoever heard it once.

6. Eight distinctions between the expert and the competent

Authority is a lever, not a rank. The competent candidate maps authority onto seniority and assumes juniority guarantees influence stories. The expert knows a vice-president has no authority over a peer's roadmap, and a junior analyst may hold complete authority over a report everyone depends on. The tell is "I was only an analyst", offered as though it settled matters; the question is whether this outcome could have been instructed, and by whom.

The agency partition serves the listener; it is not a boast. Told to stop saying "we", competent candidates overcorrect into an unpleasant first person. The expert partitions: here is what the team did, here is the thing I did that they could not have, here is why. The tell is the praise for the counterparty, which makes the partition credible rather than self-serving.

The opposing position must be stated at its strongest. The competent describe an opponent who was wrong; the expert one who was reasonable given what that person was measured on, and only then explains what changed. The tell is the sentence "and he was right about that part": invented opponents are never partly right.

Residue is scored even when it is not asked for. Where the relationship stood a quarter later is the durability claim, and a panel's fastest discriminator. The tell is that the expert volunteers it unvarnished: one plant head never trusted the model, and she says so. Candidates fear this reads as failure; interviewers read it as the signature of someone who was there.

Numbers are chosen for defensibility, not size. The competent reach for the largest figure available; the expert for the one whose derivation they can reconstruct under questioning. The tell is naming the system a number came from and the period it covers. A ₹40 lakh result you can derive beats a ₹6 crore result you cannot.

Portfolio coverage is planned, not improvised. Kalrav's loop carried behavioural prompts in three of its five rounds, about two each, so roughly six prompts. Kharbanda's six rehearsed episodes, used at most twice, give twelve slots against six prompts — a coverage ratio of two to one. The expert computes this, and checks no episode serves conflict, failure and leadership at once.

Failure stories need a decision, not a misfortune. The competent answer the failure prompt with something that happened to them — a cancelled programme, a departed sponsor. The expert names a wrong choice, the information they had at the time, and how it differed from what they wish they had had. The tell is a date on which a different decision was available.

Over-preparation has a signature. Beyond roughly four rehearsals a story acquires the cadence of a recital, and attention moves from content to performance. The expert rehearses the middle — actions and follow-up answers — and leaves the opening loose. The tell is that three tellings differ in their first line and agree exactly on the numbers.

7. How this changes by product type and company stage

Exhibit 4. What the behavioural round is listening for, by context
ContextPreferred evidenceCharacteristic weakness of a non-product story
ConsumerChanging a peer's mind with evidence about usersInternal-client episodes with no end user
B2B softwareOne commitment held across customer, sales and engineeringSales episodes ending at signature, not delivery
EnterprisePatience across layers; a two-quarter decisionHeroic speed implying the organisation was bypassed
Platform and marketplaceNaming the cost to the side that lostOne-sided results framed as unambiguous wins
Hardware and physical goodsIntervention dated before the point of no returnObjections raised after tooling is committed
AI productsAgreement won on an evaluation or escalation protocolFeature-shaped disputes where the issue is reliability

By stage the difference is sharper than most advice admits, but in one direction only. Early-stage companies discount process-heavy episodes and reward breadth and speed; late-stage companies discount solo heroics and reward alignment. Where advice overstates matters is the competence beneath: both test the same four claims, and a candidate who tries to sound like a different person at a start-up only sounds uncertain.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Kharbanda's SKU master. At a packaged-foods client with nine plants she inherited 40,000 SKU records of which 23 per cent were duplicates — 9,200 records — leaving 30,800 distinct items. Three plant heads resisted, each reasonably, since the duplicate codes encoded local packaging variants their teams relied on, and she had authority over none of them. She built a single-plant pilot, showed each head only their own stock-out data, and let them propose the merge rules. Over two quarters the stock-out rate fell from 7.4 per cent to 5.1 per cent, an absolute fall of 2.3 points and a relative fall of 31 per cent, and the client released ₹6.2 crore of working capital. The episode survives all four claims; its weakness, which she names unprompted, is that the ₹6.2 crore was the client's estimate while the stock-out figures are hers.

Yardi's calibration drift. Yantrika shipped 18,000 meters in FY2025, of which 612 returned for calibration drift — 3.4 per cent — at an average service and logistics cost of ₹9,400 each, or ₹57.53 lakh. Yardi believed the cause was a firmware rounding behaviour, not the sensor the mechanical team blamed, and could instruct neither that team nor the quality head. He instrumented forty field units on his own initiative, waited eleven weeks for data, and showed the quality head privately before any group meeting. The fix shipped. In FY2026, 21,500 meters shipped and 258 returned, a rate of 1.2 per cent. Because volumes differ the saving must be normalised: at the FY2025 rate, 21,500 units would have produced 731 returns, so 731 less 258 is 473 avoided, worth 473 × ₹9,400 = ₹44.46 lakh. The relative improvement is 2.2 points on 3.4, or 65 per cent. His instinct was to open with the rate; his coach moved him to the eleven weeks of waiting.

Where it failed. Yash Kotwal, an enterprise salesman at Kundan Trade Exchange, interviewed for a product role at Kanak Lending Network and was rejected on Wednesday 11 February 2026. His behavioural answer described closing a ₹4.8 crore annual contract. Asked who had disagreed with him internally, he said nobody; asked what he would do differently, he said close faster. Kanak weighted its five rounds 25 product sense, 25 analytical, 30 behavioural, 10 domain, 10 hiring manager. He scored 3.0, 3.5, 1.5, 4.0 and 3.0, giving 75.0 + 87.5 + 45.0 + 40.0 + 30.0 = 277.5, a weighted average of 2.78 against a bar of 3.00. Had the behavioural round scored 3.5, the total would have been 277.5 + (2.0 × 30) = 337.5, an average of 3.38 — comfortably clear. The failure was not a shortage of material. Kotwal had spent four years persuading implementation teams that did not report to him to honour commitments he had made, and never counted it as achievement, because the bonus plan counted bookings. He re-mined his history against the authority filter, found eleven qualifying episodes, rehearsed four to Level 4 depth, and sat a different loop a little over seven months later, on Tuesday 15 September 2026, where the behavioural round became his strongest. His deficit, uncomfortably, was manufactured by his employer's measurement system.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Exhibit 5. Five failure modes, with the sign that appears first
Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Responsibility recitalOpening sentence has no date, no second personWho else is in the first thirty seconds?One round lost; usually fatal
Unopposed heroNobody in the account disagreesCan I write "reasonably, she thought…" per opponent?Episode is read as invented
Orphan numberA large result, no stated mechanismWhat would the figure be had I been on leave?Credibility lost in later rounds
Single-episode overloadOne story answers conflict, failure, ambiguityHow many prompts does each episode cover?Visible thinness by round three
Weight blindnessPreparation spread evenlyWhich single-round gain clears the bar?Effort where the point is dearest

Each is detectable in a first draft and nearly undetectable after four rehearsals — the argument for a hostile reading early. Kharbanda's coach made her tell each episode once, unprepared, to someone instructed to interrupt; it caught the orphan number in her working-capital figure on 26 September, nineteen days before the loop.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does the round measure past conduct or present articulacy? The behaviour-description tradition rests on the predictive validity of structured interviewing and on the observation that probing degrades a fabricated account faster than a real one. The narrative-performance position rests on the correlation of scores with verbal fluency and on interviewers verifying nothing. For the first to be wrong, coaching would have to raise scores without raising on-the-job influence; the modest evidence suggests it does raise scores, which is uncomfortable for that camp without settling the matter.

Does non-product evidence transfer? The permissive camp notes that consulting, enterprise sales and staff engineering each depend structurally on influence without authority, so the base rate of relevant experience among non-PMs is high. The sceptics reply that the product manager's version is distinctive — sustained influence over people still there next quarter, with no engagement end-date — and that consultants practise a form of influence that ends when the deck is delivered. This would be wrong if former consultants performed no worse than internal transfers in year one; nobody has a clean dataset, because firms that track it do not publish it.

Should the round be replaced? The work-sample camp argues that two hours on a real artefact dominates forty minutes of recollection, and that the round survives because it is cheap and interviewers enjoy it. Defenders answer that no work sample yet tests conduct toward a colleague with different incentives, and that the weakness is implementation, not concept: most behavioural rounds are unstructured conversations in a rubric's clothing.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives with polished narratives and defends them. Someone who has internalised it differs in four ways. They choose the episode after hearing the question, holding an inventory rather than a script. They concede the weak part of their own evidence unpushed, which turns an interrogation into a joint assessment. They can state the opposing position well enough that its holder would sign the summary. And they are unembarrassed about the round's limits: asked whether a consulting episode predicts product conduct, they give the sceptics' argument accurately, then say what in their own record speaks to it. Panels remember that, because it is the behaviour of a colleague rather than an applicant.

12. The decisions

Kharbanda decided, on 2 October, to reallocate: of her thirteen remaining working days, three to product sense, one to execution and analytics, four to the behavioural round, the balance to logistics and rest. Her reasoning was the lever arithmetic of Exhibit 2 — the behavioural round was the only single improvement that cleared 3.00, and her execution score of 2.5 the second cheapest point. She led with the SKU master episode, stating the working-capital figure as the client's estimate, and held the pricing-test episode in reserve for the consumer-facing interviewer, it being the only one of her six with an end user in it.

Yardi decided the opposite way, defensibly. His behavioural material was strong once mined; his mock product-sense score of 2.5 was the real exposure, and Kshetra weighted that round at 20. He gave the behavioural round two evenings — enough to partition the agency claim in three episodes and rehearse the calibration follow-ups to Level 4 — and everything else to product judgement. Whether he was right turns on a question this case leaves open: whether a hardware engineer interviewing at a company selling into his former plants is judged mainly on relational skill or on product thinking.

Discussion questions. First, the two faced similar bars and chose opposite allocations; which would you defend, and what would have to be true of the panels for your answer to reverse? Second, Kotwal's deficit came from his employer's measurement system rather than his conduct — what obligation does that place on the interviewing company? Third, if the narrative-performance school is substantially right, should a candidate who knows it behave differently in the room, and would you want them to?

13. Going deeper

PM interviews gives the loop's shape, without which the weighting arithmetic has no inputs. Influence without authority is the competence this round samples, taught as practice rather than narration. A PM's operating system supplies the habits that generate future episodes. Continuous learning as a PM covers keeping an episode inventory current rather than reconstructing six years under deadline. Building a PM portfolio and narrative is this round's written counterpart; the two must agree. Transitioning into product management places the round in the longer path from a non-product role. Your first 90 days in a PM role matters because this conduct is what the first quarter tests. Confidence, doubt and judgement is the hardest neighbour: where conceding one's own weak evidence becomes a disposition.
case40v1-craft.interview.behavioural:
The Behavioural Bar at Rivaaj Retail Systems

Bengaluru, Sunday 4 October 2026 — a hiring manager, three finalists, and no product titles between them

1. Sunday night

Three interview packets lay fanned out on the floor of Urvashi Dandekar's flat in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, and a fourth document lay face down beside them: the loop debriefs for the three finalists for a Senior Product Manager position in Rivaaj Retail Systems' store-payments pod, and a calibration memo that had arrived unasked five days earlier and that she had read four times since, each time with less comfort.

At nine the next morning, Monday 5 October 2026, she had to tell Ritvika Gokhale, Rivaaj's Head of Talent, which name to put on an offer letter. The requisition had been open eighty-three days. One finalist held a competing offer expiring on Wednesday; another was on the Rivaaj payroll and had told colleagues she was being promoted; the third was the only one both engineering and revenue could tolerate, and nobody's first choice.

None of the three had ever held a product manager's title. That was not an accident of the market but the consequence of a decision taken nineteen months earlier, and it meant the hire would turn on the behavioural round: forty-five minutes describing episodes of moving people one does not manage.

2. The company, and the decision that constrains it

Rivaaj Retail Systems was founded in Bengaluru in 2017 by Uday Paranjape and two colleagues from a till-systems vendor, and sells store-operations software — billing, stock, returns, rostering, card-present payments — to Indian apparel and footwear retailers. By the close of FY26 it ran in about 42,000 store locations for 310 brands, employed 1,180 people and recorded recurring revenue of ₹214 crore, with nineteen product managers across seven pods.

In January 2024 Rivaaj hired Rutvij Palkar as a Group Product Manager. He arrived from a strategy practice with the best product-sense scores the loop had recorded, wrote an admired three-year plan for the payments pod, and left in November 2024 having shipped one module. The post-mortem of February 2025 was unsparing: the loop tested whether a candidate could think about products, never whether he could move an engineering manager in Pune, a designer in Amsterdam or a sales head in Austin without a reporting line.

In March 2025 Uday approved two changes together, and they constrain everything that follows. The first was the Behavioural Bar: a forty-five-minute round, two interviewers, four competencies, influence without authority weighted at two-fifths of the score, and no interviewer scoring a candidate in more than one round, so that no single opinion travelled through the loop. The second was a commitment to the board that over two years at least two-fifths of product-manager hires would come from people who had never held the title. Ushma Search Partners, on an exclusive mandate, was briefed accordingly: bring us people who have carried outcomes without a product title.

3. The industry

Organised retail in India was expanding and consolidating at once. Reliance Retail, Trent's Westside and Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail were adding stores while quick commerce drew footfall from the mall, and Myntra, Nykaa Fashion and Meesho had taught brands to expect inventory visible across channels. ONDC pressed store systems to publish catalogues; GST e-invoicing made the till a compliance instrument; the Reserve Bank of India's card-present tokenisation rules landed in Rivaaj's payments pod; and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governed both the records at the till and, as counsel noted in August, the interview recordings in Ritvika Gokhale's drive. For product talent it competed with Zoho, Freshworks and the product arms of Flipkart and Razorpay. Its exposure outside India ran through the Gulf: ₹31 crore of recurring revenue, the largest contract being Ruwad Retail Group of Riyadh at ₹7.4 crore — 7.4 of Rivaaj's 214 crore, or 3.46 per cent, the account whose renewal clause set this hire's timetable.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The requisition opened on Tuesday 14 July 2026 for a Senior Product Manager to own store payments and Gulf localisation. Ushma delivered six names thirty-eight days later, on 21 August; three cleared the screen, and the loop ran from 7 to 25 September.

Upasana Rege, thirty-three, a principal at Rachana Advisory Group in Mumbai, had run a markdown programme across a client's 900 stores; her influence stories were about executives who could have dismissed her at any time. Rohan Mudholkar, thirty-six, an embedded-systems tech lead at Unmesh Precision Industries in Pune, had spent eight years shipping payment terminals and twice stopped a release he did not own, once against his director's wish. Rukhsar Inamdar, twenty-nine, had been at Rivaaj three years, latterly implementation lead for the Gulf accounts, in Kochi; before that, eleven stores for Raunak Stores Group. She took the Ruwad rollout from pilot to 140 stores, and most of the engineers she would influence she had already influenced.

The behavioural rounds fell on three dates with three different pairs of interviewers: Upasana on Friday 11 September with Ravindra Pashilkar and Ruhi Mestry; Rohan five days later, on 16 September, with Urvashi and Udayan Saraf; Rukhsar on 23 September, twelve days after Upasana, with Umesh Chiplunkar and Reema Dhavle. Everyone believed the scores comparable: the rubric was identical and the guide four pages long.

Four things have since come to light. The scores are not comparable: Saraf's memo of 29 September (Exhibit 3) showed the interviewers' averages differ by a full point and the candidates drew panels of very different severity. The rubric's record is unencouraging: of eleven product managers hired since the Bar, the highest-scoring band has not produced the strongest performers (Exhibit 4). On 9 September — two days before Upasana's round, fourteen before Rukhsar's — Ritvika ran a two-hour workshop on telling influence stories from non-product work, which Rukhsar attended and the externals could not have. And in August, before any candidate was seen, Ravindra told his engineering managers Gulf localisation would run as an engineering programme, the new product manager owning store payments only. Nobody told Urvashi, or the candidates, all interviewed against the wider role.

5. The people

Urvashi Dandekar, Vice-President, Product, Bengaluru. Owns the requisition. Says the behavioural round is the only part of the loop that predicted Rutvij Palkar's failure. Her incentive is a pod that ships the tokenisation work without her writing the specifications, as she has for five months. Not saying: she scored Rohan's round.

Ravindra Pashilkar, Vice-President, Engineering, Pune. Wants an external hire with shipping scars; rates Rohan highest on substance. His incentive is a counterpart who will not renegotiate the roadmap. Not saying: Rukhsar's promotion costs him his implementation lead for nine weeks, and he has already removed Gulf localisation from this role.

Umesh Chiplunkar, Chief Revenue Officer, Austin. Wants Rukhsar, loudly; says she is the only candidate Ruwad's chief operating officer will take a call from. Not saying: he is the most generous scorer in the company, he knows it, and he sat on her panel.

Ruhi Mestry, Design Director, Amsterdam. Scored Upasana's round; found her the most articulate candidate in two years, and says the rubric rewards articulacy because the job does. Not saying: she found the stories unfalsifiable, every client anonymous.

Udayan Saraf, Lead Data Scientist, Nairobi. Wrote the calibration memo unasked after sitting on Rohan's panel; says the raw scores cannot be compared. Not saying: his adjustment is crude and additive, rests on as few as seven interviews, and assumes leniency is stable.

Reema Dhavle, Director, Customer Success, Melbourne. Scored Rukhsar's behavioural round and marked her written exercise. Says Rukhsar's were the only stories naming the person moved and what they gave up. Not saying: she has worked with Rukhsar on Ruwad for two years.

Ritvika Gokhale, Head of Talent, Bengaluru. Must send the offer on Monday or lose the mandate terms. Says the process must be followed as written, or every hire becomes an argument. Not saying: she designed and ran the 9 September workshop only the internal candidate could attend.

6. Exhibits

Two candidates are exactly tied at 3.11, and not through rounding. Upasana leads on the competency carrying two-fifths of the weight and trails on learning from a miss; Rohan is the reverse; Rukhsar leads on ownership, where an insider with a live rollout has the easiest evidence (Exhibit 2).

Exhibit 3 inverts Exhibit 1. Adjusted for the panel each candidate drew, the order becomes Upasana at 3.29, Rohan at 3.19 and Rukhsar at 2.89 — last, and below the 2.90 floor the Bar sets. Ritvika holds that a committee cannot invent a statistic after seeing scores; Udayan, that nobody invented the leniency, they noticed it.

Exhibit 4 was meant to settle the argument and settles nothing. The middle band has the best mean rating and perfect retention, the top band the lowest retention. With nine ratings the pattern could be noise, as Ritvika's covering line concedes, and it is still the only evidence the Bar works.

The envelope is ₹65.00 lakh of first-year cash. Upasana at the top of the band fits with ₹2.07 lakh to spare; at her ask she breaks it by ₹2.27 lakh. Rukhsar's path looks cheap in the offer column and is not cheap in the row: the backfill makes it the second most expensive, and Umesh disputes that backfill.

Exhibits 1 and 6 rank the candidates in opposite orders, and the Bar gives no rule for combining them: the round is a gate, not a weight, and nobody below 2.90 can be offered. On raw scores nobody is; on Udayan's adjustment, one is.

7. Voices

“Her best story was a markdown programme at a client I may not name, with a saving I cannot check, agreed by an executive whose title she would not give me. I scored her 3.8 on influence because the story is very good. I have no idea whether it is true.”

Ravindra Pashilkar, debrief, 1 October 2026

“Rohan talked for nine minutes about a firmware recall before I realised he had not once said what he wanted the other team to do. He is the most honest candidate in the loop and the worst at describing himself. If the round tests describing, he fails; if behaviour, he alone passes.”

Udayan Saraf, note on his scorecard, 16 September 2026

“The workshop was for everyone on the internal mobility list, not about this requisition. I will not pretend that teaching people to describe their own work is cheating.”

Ritvika Gokhale, email to Urvashi Dandekar, 2 October 2026

“Flagging that I marked Rukhsar's written exercise as well as sitting on her behavioural panel. Nobody else was in the Gulf time zone that week.”

Reema Dhavle, chat message to Ritvika Gokhale, 24 September 2026

“I keep being asked for a story where I changed someone's mind. The ones I am proudest of are where I was wrong and someone changed mine. Those score badly.”

Rukhsar Inamdar, in her behavioural round, 23 September 2026

8. The options as Urvashi sees them

Option A: offer Upasana Rege at the top of the band. Strongest on the rest of the loop, on the heaviest competency, and once the panel adjustment is applied. The costs: a ₹62.93 lakh bill with no room to negotiate, an expiring rival offer, a learning-from-a-miss score of 2.4, the lowest in the loop, and Mestry's doubt that any story can be verified.

Option B: offer Rohan Mudholkar at ₹52.00 lakh. The cheapest path, the one Ravindra will support, the candidate two interviewers called the only one whose evidence was checkable. The costs: an influence score of 2.6 against a rubric weighting it at two-fifths, the lowest product-sense score, and Urvashi's own hand on his scorecard.

Option C: promote Rukhsar Inamdar at ₹34.00 lakh. Honours the board commitment, keeps the Ruwad relationship, rewards the one candidate whose stories name real engineers. The costs: the weakest rest-of-loop record by a wide margin, a nine-week hole in Gulf implementation, a panel of the two most generous scorers, a written exercise marked by one of them, and a workshop only she attended.

Urvashi had written these three on a page, then added a fourth line and struck it out twice: is the question which one, or what the round is for? The role she had interviewed three people for was not, after Ravindra's August conversation, the role that exists. The competency she weighted most heavily was the one all three had been coached to perform. And the Bar rests on a sample of one.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Upasana's competing offer from Ujala Commerce Group expires on Wednesday 7 October. Ushma's exclusive mandate, under which the fee is 8.5 per cent rather than the 12 per cent open-market rate, lapses on 15 October, after which either external hire costs more. The envelope is ₹65.00 lakh of first-year cash, and Uday Paranjape, who has already named Rukhsar to two investors as proof the pipeline works, will not reopen headcount before January. The Ruwad contract requires a named product owner for Gulf localisation by 30 November 2026, fifty-seven days away, as a condition of the renewal conversation opening on 15 January 2027.

Two further constraints bind quietly. Counsel has advised that recordings and scorecards are personal data under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, held for this requisition's purpose alone; re-running the round on a calibrated panel means asking three candidates to consent to a second assessment, and telling them why. And the board commitment is now arithmetic: four of the eleven hires since April 2025 came from internal non-product roles. A twelfth from outside puts it at four of twelve, 33.3 per cent, below the two-fifths reported; Rukhsar makes it five of twelve, 41.7 per cent.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What is the behavioural round measuring? Using Exhibits 1 and 3, separate the part of each score that reflects conduct from the part that reflects who interviewed her.
  2. Rukhsar Inamdar's stories name Rivaaj engineers; Upasana Rege's name nobody. Is verifiability evidence about the candidate or about her employer, and which should a hiring manager pay for?
  3. Ritvika Gokhale's workshop taught internal candidates to convert implementation work into influence narratives. Preparation, coaching, or contamination — and does your answer change if the externals paid a consultancy for the same thing?
  4. Exhibit 4 shows the top behavioural band performing no better than the middle one. What would convince you the Bar should be reweighted, and what should Rivaaj have collected from March 2025 to answer that today?
  5. Ravindra Pashilkar removed Gulf localisation from the role without telling the hiring manager or the candidates. What does that do to the loop's validity, and what does Urvashi owe the candidates?
  6. It is nine o'clock on Monday. Which name does Urvashi give Ritvika; what does she do about the ₹65.00 lakh envelope, the 30 November clause and the board ratio; and when Uday asks her in January how Rivaaj hires product managers who have never been product managers, what exactly does she say?

11. Still Sunday

At a quarter past eleven Urvashi turned the memo face up and read its closing line for the fifth time. Beside it lay a sheet on which she had copied the four competencies and their weights, and beneath them a line from the February 2025 post-mortem: we tested whether he could think, and never whether he could move anyone. Three people had spent forty-five minutes each telling her about moving people, and she could not say which account she believed, or whether she had measured the moving or the telling.

Her phone showed a message from Ritvika, sent at ten: Need the name by 9. Ushma will ask for a reason in writing. Below it, unanswered since Friday, a message from Rukhsar Inamdar asking whether to book a flight to Bengaluru next week.
case20v1-craft.interview.behavioural:
Ishita Hosangadi and the Behavioural Round

A decision about preparation for a candidate with no product title

1. Opening

On the evening of Monday, 5 October 2026, Ishita Hosangadi sat at her desk in the Pune office of Hamsa Freight Services with a calendar invitation open on one screen and a blank document on the other. The invitation, from a recruiter at Ikshu Merchant Exchange in Hyderabad, confirmed a five-round loop for a Product Manager role, with the final onsite on Monday, 19 October. Round three was a forty-five minute behavioural interview with the hiring manager, Hemant Ogale. The recruiter's note was brief: "Hemant will want specific stories where you moved people you did not manage. Please come ready."

Ishita was thirty-one, an operations manager with seven years in freight, and she had never held a product title. She had fourteen days and, by her own count, forty-four usable hours around her day job. Mock interviews were due to begin on Saturday, and they would only be as good as the stories she brought.

2. Company background

Ikshu Merchant Exchange was founded in 2019 in Hyderabad and sells a payments-and-credit dashboard to small merchants, mostly kirana owners, pharmacies and neighbourhood restaurants. It competes for the same shopkeeper's phone screen as PhonePe, Paytm and Razorpay's merchant products and served about 4.2 lakh active merchants. Its thirty-one-person product organisation sat across Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Chennai, with a design lead in Lisbon.

Hamsa Freight Services, Ishita's employer, was a mid-sized road-freight aggregator with about 1,400 trucks on its platform and annual revenue near ₹310 crore. It was far smaller than Delhivery and had no product team, only a six-person technology group in Hyderabad.

3. The situation

Ishita's problem was not ambition but vocabulary. Every story she told naturally began with "my team": the dock crew she managed, the shift she ran, the targets she owned. Ila Hariharan, a product manager in Sydney, had read her draft answers and been blunt. "These are good manager stories. Product interviewers are not hiring a manager. They are asking whether you can get an engineer, a salesperson or a finance head to change course when you cannot tell them to."

That test, influence without authority, was the very thing the Ikshu rubric named. Hemant Ogale had said in a public talk that the round scored four competencies: influence without authority, handling disagreement, ownership and learning from a miss. Influence carried 40 per cent of the score.

She listed four episodes from her career. Exhibit 1 sets them out with the annual saving each produced, computed from the figures in her own reports. Only one, the dock turnaround programme, involved people who reported to her. In the other three she had needed something from someone else's team: a driver slot-booking feature from the Hyderabad technology group, a discount freeze from the sales head in Kochi, and a shorter payment cycle from the finance head so that fourteen Kolkata transporters would sign on.

The largest figure, ₹86 lakh, sat in the one story that did not answer the question. The driver feature had taken three months, two escalations and an open disagreement with the head of technology about displacing a customer-facing feature. Ishita had won, but strained a relationship she still needed.

4. The people

Hemant Ogale, Director of Product at Ikshu in Hyderabad, would conduct the round. He wanted evidence of behaviour, not polish, and was known to interrupt a rehearsed answer with "what did the other person want?"

Ojas Ingle, a former Hamsa operations head now at a Pune start-up, was Ishita's mentor. He believed she should lead with her strongest numbers. "Nobody remembers ₹31 lakh," he said. "They remember ₹86 lakh and a team of forty."

Ila Hariharan, in Sydney, was her mock interviewer. She wanted Ishita to treat the round as a pattern-matching test and to prepare four to five stories mapped to the rubric. She was five and a half hours ahead of Pune and could meet only before Ishita's workday.

Indu Hosur, Ishita's manager at Hamsa in Pune, was supportive but cautious. She had offered a role in a newly formed product operations group at ₹34 lakh, against Ishita's current ₹32 lakh fixed pay. It was a quiet alternative to the whole adventure.

5. The numbers around the choice

Ikshu's offer band for the role was ₹38 lakh to ₹44 lakh. At the ₹40 lakh midpoint, the move would raise her pay by 25 per cent from ₹32 lakh; at the band's edges it would be 18.75 and 37.5 per cent. The internal role at ₹34 lakh was a rise of ₹2 lakh, and a failed round might mean a long wait for the next comparable opening.

Time was the binding constraint. Ten weekday evenings at two hours each and four weekend days at six hours each gave her 20 plus 24, or 44 hours before the onsite. Exhibit 2 shows how she could divide them under each option.

6. The options

Option A: lead with the strongest numbers. Ishita would build her round around the dock turnaround story and one supporting story, and spend most of her time rehearsing delivery. This was Ojas's advice. The upside was fluency and an impressive headline. The cost was a mismatch with the rubric: the story's central act was directing people, the opposite of the competency carrying 40 per cent.

Option B: build a small portfolio of influence stories. She would rebuild stories 2, 3 and 4 so that each opened with what the other person wanted, and keep story 1 only as supporting evidence of ownership. The upside was fit: three stories matched the heaviest competency. The cost was rawness: smaller rupee figures, an unresolved disagreement, and only fourteen mock hours.

Option C: manufacture product experience. She would spend thirty hours building a small slot-booking prototype for a Hamsa lane, or a case-style product teardown of Ikshu itself, so that she could say she had done product work. The upside was an artefact to show. The cost was that fourteen days is too short to convince Hemant, it left only six hours for mocks, and it implied her real experience did not count.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, which stories could be told without once saying "my team"? What does the 61.1 per cent share tell you about where her real evidence lies?

2. Hemant often asks "what did the other person want?" Take story 2 and write the first two sentences of her answer. What would the head of technology have said his priority was?

3. Using Exhibit 2, which option leaves the least preparation time for the competency carrying 40 per cent of the score? Is more rehearsal ever better than better material?

4. Which option would you choose, and what single piece of evidence would change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

A candidate without a product title is not short of material; she is short of translation. Product interviewers ask for influence-without-authority stories because the product manager's daily condition is needing engineering, design, sales and finance to move while owning none of them. Consulting, engineering, operations and sales all contain such episodes, usually hiding behind "my team".

A well-reasoned answer begins with the rubric, not the résumé. Ishita's evidence in Exhibit 1 already contains the answer: three of four stories, worth ₹134.8 lakh of the ₹220.8 lakh total, were told from the position of someone with no authority. The ₹86 lakh headline is attractive precisely because it would score least.

The defensible path is Option B, with two refinements. First, keep story 1 as a short, honest supporting example of ownership, rather than discarding it. Second, treat the unresolved disagreement in story 2 as an asset: the learning-from-a-miss competency rewards an account of what she would do differently, and an interviewer like Hemant is more likely to trust a story with friction than a tidy one. She should also call the Kochi sales head: a story that survives a counterpart's version survives interruption.

Option A fails on fit, and Option C fails on arithmetic: thirty of forty-four hours on a prototype leaves six for the practice that tests whether the stories land. The internal ₹34 lakh role remains a fair fallback, and the decision to pursue Ikshu does not close it. Ishita should say so to Indu Hosur now and keep the conversation open. Under a deadline, spend scarce hours on what the evaluator is scoring, and let polish follow.
exp40v2-craft.interview.execution:
Execution and prioritisation rounds

Trade-off questions, shipping under constraint, and what to cut when the date is fixed.

1. Two rooms, nine days apart

On Tuesday 10 November 2026, Osheen Zarapkar sat opposite Zarina Ovhal at Odhani Retail Collective, a Bengaluru apparel marketplace whose buyers shop on a phone, over UPI, in two bursts a year. Zarina, a director of product, opened with the exercise. "Our spring catalogue goes live on Friday 15 January 2027. The date is not mine to move; the media buy is committed against it. You get seven engineers for the nine weeks from Monday 16 November. Three teams want eight things. Tell me what ships."

The eight asks came to 345 person-days. Seven engineers for nine weeks is 315 person-days before a single holiday. It was a subtraction problem, and Zarina listened for whether Osheen would say so.

Nine days later Zubin Oka sat in a different room. Zanjeer Freight Systems sells transport-management software to Indian manufacturers: e-way bill reconciliation against the GST network, dispatch planning, dealer tracking. Onkar Zirpe, its product head, laid out five asks from accounts renewing 31 March 2027. Zubin had four engineers for the nine weeks from Monday 4 January to Friday 5 March 2027. "Recurring revenue across those five accounts is ₹2,400 lakh," Onkar said. "Tell me which of them I am prepared to lose."

The exercises look identical and are not. Osheen's tests whether a candidate can draw a defensible cut line; Zubin's whether a candidate will name the customer whose revenue they will risk. The arithmetic is similar; the social act is not.

2. The idea, and the quarrel inside it

An execution and prioritisation round is a work-sample exercise: an objective, a hard constraint, more work than it admits, and a demand to commit publicly to a subset. Panels use it because judgement becomes observable the moment someone names what will not be done.

Its formal ancestor is scheduling theory, not the value-versus-effort grid. In 1956 W. E. Smith showed that sequencing weighted jobs by the ratio of weight to processing time minimises total weighted completion time, which is why "highest value per unit of effort first" is not folklore: under Smith's assumptions it is provably optimal. The selection version — fixed budget, indivisible items — is the 0-1 knapsack problem, where the rule is only an approximation. Reinertsen carried cost of delay into product development in 2009; SAFe turned it into weighted shortest job first; RICE and its descendants are the same ratio with more columns. Each step from Smith's assumptions costs part of the guarantee, and experts know which step they stand on.

Three schools disagree substantively about what the round should reward. The scoring school holds that a written ranking is the honest artefact: it can be attacked, and it survives its author. It signs "a documented ratio beats an undocumented instinct", never "the score decides". The thesis school, after Marty Cagan's outcomes-over-output, holds that ranking someone else's list is the junior move and contesting it the senior one. It signs "the list is a hypothesis, not an input", never "therefore refuse to rank", which reads as evasion. The flow school, descended from Reinertsen, Goldratt and queueing theory, says both argue about the wrong variable: throughput is governed by work in progress. It signs "cutting items in flight raises delivered value more than improving the ranking", never "selection is irrelevant".

3. Mechanics in depth: the five moves, worked

Expert practice has five moves, two usually silent.

Move one: establish which constraint is load-bearing. Osheen asked what happens on 16 January if an item is missing, who had spent money against the date, and whether quality was negotiable. Nothing catastrophic; the media buy is placed; no. Date and quality fixed, scope was the only free variable.

Move two: convert the constraint into usable person-days — the step most often asserted, not computed.

Exhibit 1. Odhani: capacity build-down for the nine weeks. Deductions are the engineering manager's historical averages.
LinePerson-daysBasis
Gross capacity3157 × 9 × 5

On-call and production support182 × 9 weeks
Release hardening, final week357 × 5 days
Total deductions8128 + 18 + 35
Net usable capacity234315 − 81

The 81 days lost are 25.7 per cent of the 315 gross. A team that cannot state that ratio will slip by about that much and call it bad luck. Against 234 usable days, the asks overshoot by 111.

Move three: rank by value per person-day. Odhani's analysts had attached an expected contribution margin to each ask, over the fourteen weeks from the catalogue switch. Move four: walk the list, committing until an item will not fit, then keep walking. Move five: perturb one input.

Exhibit 2. Odhani: eight asks ranked by value per person-day against 234 usable days. Ties break on smallest effort first. The last row holds totals, the ratio blended across all eight.
RankAskEffort (person-days)Value (₹ lakh)Value per person-day (₹ lakh)Running effortDecision
