The committed five cost 40 + 55 + 30 + 70 + 20 = 215 person-days and carry 260 + 330 + 150 + 280 + 60 = ₹1,080 lakh. That is 1,080 of the 1,445 lakh on the table, or 74.7 per cent of the value, for 215 of the 345 days requested, 62.3 per cent of the effort. The committed set averages ₹5.02 lakh a day (1,080 ÷ 215) against ₹4.19 lakh across all eight; the three cuts, ₹365 lakh over 130 days, average ₹2.81 lakh. Nineteen days stay unallocated.

Figure 2 supplies the bound that separates an expert from a careful amateur. In the divisible version greedy is exactly optimal: you would take 19 of the image pipeline's 45 days, 42.2 per cent of it, for 0.422 × 135 = ₹57 lakh. The indivisible optimum cannot exceed 1,080 + 57 = ₹1,137 lakh, so Osheen's answer sits at most 5.0 per cent below that bound (57 ÷ 1,137). "Within five per cent of optimal, and here is why" is a different claim from "this feels right".

4. When the method applies, stated as testable claims

Exhibit 3. The five conditions the ratio rule rests on, applied to both.
ConditionOdhani (consumer marketplace)Zanjeer (enterprise software)
C1. The constraint binds: someone outside acts on the dateHolds; media spend is committedHolds harder; renewals sit in signed contracts
C2. Items are separable: no value depends on another shippingMostly holdsFails; one ask serves four accounts
C3. Value is additive and linear, with no thresholdHolds in rangeHolds; accounts are independent
C4. Effort estimates are unbiased both waysFails; estimates skew longFails; customer-IT work is right-tailed
C5. Capacity is fungible across itemsFails; only 2 of 7 write client codeHolds roughly; four generalists

C5 is the one Osheen volunteered before Zarina could raise it. Client-side capacity is roughly two-sevenths of 234, about 67 person-days. The committed set holds 40 days of mobile work in the size widget, 25 in the checkout and 12 in wishlist alerts: 77 against 67, so the plan starts ten client-days short.

The method is actively misleading in three situations. When value is a step function rather than a slope — a compliance deadline, an accuracy threshold — partial builds are worth nothing and their ratios meaningless. When the real scarcity is attention, as in a startup where the founder's calendar binds, person-days measure the wrong resource. And when the list is itself the problem, ranking it well buys a confidently wrong quarter.

5. Hard edge cases

In multi-product companies the binding constraint is rarely your own capacity but the platform queue: an item costing 30 engineer-days plus a four-week wait for an identity service is not a 30-day item. Mature organisations say they use a published capacity market; most resolve it by escalation.

In two-sided businesses value accrues to one side and cost to the other. Odhani's seller stock sync was cut on a buyer-margin ratio, yet sellers who oversell cause the cancellations that depress buyer margin. Ranking a marketplace backlog on a single-sided metric is the commonest quiet error.

In regulated work the top of the list is not negotiable. A payments company facing an RBI circular, or a broker a SEBI deadline, subtracts mandated work from capacity before ranking: the mandate is a deduction, not a ranked item.

Hardware plus software breaks the symmetry between items. Oshadhi Devices Industries, which makes glucose monitors in Ahmedabad, has a fourteen-week tooling lead time, so firmware scope freezes about ten weeks before app scope. A firmware item cut late cannot be re-added at any price; an app item can, so run two cut lines.

AI-native products add a third failure of separability: the model is a shared dependency gating everything built on it, the trap in section 8. At organisational seams the honest figure includes queue time you do not control, so experts carry calendar-days-to-ship beside person-days.

6. Eight nuances that separate the expert

Capacity is a distribution, not a number. The tell is "we have 234 days", no reserve and no source. The obvious reading, that precision is rigour, is wrong: a single-point figure is a forecast pretending to be a measurement.

Lumpiness, not ranking, is where the money hides. The tell is slack beside a cut item too large to fit. Nineteen idle days at Odhani is tolerable; forty-five beside a cut 120-day item, as at Zubaan, says the greedy rule has failed and the plan needs restructuring, not re-sorting.

Value estimates are not independent of what else ships. The tell is a table whose forecasts were each written by a different person for a different document. If four items depend on a fifth clearing a quality bar, they are conditional and nobody wrote that down.

Skill pools, not headcount, set the ceiling. The tell is a plan whose mobile, data or machine-learning demand was never totalled separately. Osheen's 77-against-67 client-day gap was invisible in a plan tracking 215 against 234.

The cut list is the artefact; the build list is the receipt. The tell is a product manager who arrives with the cuts already socialised with their requesters by name. Cuts look like residue and are what the organisation argues about for nine weeks. Cut work does not vanish: it returns as escalations that eat the reserve.

Estimates are right-tailed, so buffers must be asymmetric. The tell is "we added twenty per cent". An item cannot take less than zero days but can take triple. A symmetric buffer protects the mean and does nothing for the tail that misses the date; buffer the widest-range items instead.

Sequence inside the committed set is a second decision. Value accrues from ship date. Odhani's checkout item is worth ₹260 lakh over fourteen weeks, a peak rate of ₹18.6 lakh a week. Shipping it at the end of week two rather than week eight adds six pre-season weeks at roughly 40 per cent of peak: 6 × 18.6 × 0.40, about ₹44.6 lakh, close to the whole loyalty upgrade. Candidates rarely pull it.

Reversibility deserves a column the ratio lacks. A cheap irreversible item — a schema migration, an announced price change — can outrank an expensive reversible one on value per day and still be the wrong first move. The tell is asking what it costs to undo before asking what it is worth.

7. Across product types and company stages

Exhibit 4. Where the inputs change meaning, and how the ratio misleads.
ContextWhat value is denominated inHow the ratio misleads
ConsumerActivation, retention, margin per cohortSeasonality: peak-week ratios overstate off-peak items
B2B and enterpriseRevenue at risk from named accountsConcentration: one account dominates; loss is not linear
PlatformTeams unblocked, integrations enabledValue is second-order, realised elsewhere
MarketplaceBoth sides, and liquiditySingle-sided ratios cut the supply work demand needs
Hardware and physical goodsUnit economics, committed toolingIrreversibility: cut dates differ by component
AI productsContainment, deflection, acceptance rateThreshold: below a quality bar, dependents are worth nothing

Stage changes the argument more than product type does. At seed stage the constraint is the founder's attention and the runway, and learning value outranks expected value: a reversible experiment beats a committed build. At growth stage, where Odhani and Zanjeer sit, the method is most honest — person-days are real currency and the queue is visible. At enterprise scale the arithmetic survives but the game shifts to coordination, and leverage comes from owning the build-down and the cut list, not the ranking.

8. Three worked examples

8.1 Zanjeer: where the greedy rule is provably not optimal

Value here was revenue at risk: recurring revenue times the probability the account walks without the ask. Capacity was four engineers for nine weeks, 180 gross person-days less a 25 per cent reserve of 45, so 135.

Exhibit 5. Zanjeer: five renewal asks. Revenue at risk is ARR times churn risk: for cement, 480 × 0.40 = 192. The last row holds totals; churn and ratio are averages.
Account askARR (₹ lakh)Churn risk, per centRevenue at risk (₹ lakh)Effort (person-days)Risk removed per person-day (₹ lakh)
Cement maker: e-way bill reconciliation48040192603.20
Pharma: cold-chain audit trail30055165752.20
Two-wheeler: dealer ETA interface65020130403.25
Steel trader: GST invoice formats15070105502.10
FMCG major: route-plan export82015123304.10
Total2,40040 (avg)7152552.80 (blended)

Walking the ratio order against 135 days, the FMCG export (30), dealer interface (40) and cement (60) total 130 days and remove 123 + 130 + 192 = ₹445 lakh, 445 of the 715 lakh at stake, or 62.2 per cent. Five days idle, ₹270 lakh exposed.

Then Onkar disclosed what the table omitted: the steel formats are also required by three mid-market accounts worth ₹210 lakh of ARR at 0.30 churn risk, adding 210 × 0.30 = ₹63 lakh. Steel now removes 105 + 63 = ₹168 lakh over 50 days, a ratio of 3.36, second place. Re-running greedy gives the export (30), steel (50) and the dealer interface (40): 120 days removing 123 + 168 + 130 = ₹421 lakh, 15 days idle and nothing small enough to fill them. The original selection still removes ₹445 lakh. Greedy on corrected ratios is ₹24 lakh — 5.4 per cent — worse than greedy on wrong ones, and enumeration confirms 445 is optimal. With lumpy items the rule is a heuristic whose error must be checked, and checking takes two minutes.

8.2 Odhani: the capacity shock

Zarina's perturbation was blunt. "Security has mandated a second hardening week. You lose 35 more days." Usable capacity falls from 234 to 199, down 15.0 per cent. Osheen re-walked the same ranking: checkout (40), size widget (95), return-reason (125), try-at-home (195). Wishlist alerts would reach 215 and the loyalty upgrade 220; neither fits. Four items ship for 260 + 330 + 150 + 280 = ₹1,020 lakh. Value falls by ₹60 lakh, 5.6 per cent of the original 1,080, because the loss came from the shallow end of the staircase. That asymmetry is what a ranked plan buys: it says in advance what a capacity shock costs.

8.3 Zubaan Speech Labs: where the method failed

Zubaan Speech Labs in Chennai builds voice support agents for Indian-language call centres, with a model team in Pune and two engineers in Lisbon. For the quarter to 30 September 2026 it had six engineers over the ten weeks from 6 July to 11 September: 300 gross person-days less a 15 per cent reserve of 45, so 255 usable.

Exhibit 6. Zubaan's Q2 plan; forecasts from customer success. The last row holds totals and the blended ratio, 960 ÷ 330.
ItemEffort (person-days)Forecast value (₹ lakh)Value per person-day (₹ lakh)Shipped in Q2
Call-summary export401604.00Yes
Agent-handoff rules502004.00Yes
Marathi and Gujarati coverage902703.00Yes
Dashboard revamp30903.00Yes
Hindi acoustic retrain1202402.00No — cut
Total / average3309602.914 of 5

The four shipped cost 40 + 50 + 90 + 30 = 210 days against 255 available, forecasting ₹720 lakh and leaving 45 idle — the lumpiness tell, ignored. Realised value was ₹185 lakh: 185 of the 720 forecast, or 25.7 per cent. The cause was a threshold nobody had written down. Hindi was 62 per cent of call volume, and the un-retrained model held containment — calls resolved without a human — at 31 per cent against a contractual floor of 45. Summaries of calls escalated anyway, and rules for handoffs that never happened, are worth little. Every forecast was conditional on a bar the one cut item alone could clear.

The recovery, in the quarter to 31 December 2026, was restructuring, not better ranking: the retrain left the list and became a gate, a capacity deduction like a regulatory mandate, with the remaining days ranked after it. It took 120 of the 255 days. Containment rose from 31 to 52 per cent, 21 points and a relative gain of 67.7 per cent, clearing the floor. Its standalone forecast had been ₹240 lakh; realised value, once it released the four features already built, was ₹610 lakh. Across both quarters Zubaan realised 185 + 610 = ₹795 lakh against 720 + 240 = ₹960 lakh forecast, or 82.8 per cent — a quarter late, after two renewals were renegotiated downward.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Exhibit 7. Four failure modes; the cost assumes the error surfaces at period end.
Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Ranking without a capacity figureNo cut line; all items P1What do the asks cost, and how many days have you?A quarter of partial work
Hidden threshold in the value columnForecasts by different authorsWhich number assumes another item shipped?Zubaan: three-quarters of value lost
Cuts never socialised with ownersUnplanned work risingWho has been told their ask was cut?Escalations eat the reserve
No falsification triggerThe plan ends at the ship dateWhat in week two would prove this wrong?A wrong bet funded a second quarter

The flow school adds a fifth the others underrate: too many items in progress. Little's Law gives cycle time as work in progress divided by throughput. Five items at 1.2 a week gives 5 ÷ 1.2 = 4.2 weeks; cutting work in progress to three at the same throughput gives 3 ÷ 1.2 = 2.5 weeks. Nothing in the ranking changed and value arrives 1.7 weeks sooner.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Do explicit scores discipline judgement or launder it? The scoring school's strongest case is auditability: a written ratio can be attacked, an instinct cannot, and at scale the artefact is the only thing that travels. The opposing case is that the inputs are guesses with two significant figures attached, and the arithmetic lends credibility they never earned. For the scoring position to be wrong, teams using explicit scores would have to make worse calls than teams using argued judgement; the evidence is organisational, not experimental.

Rank the list, or contest it? The thesis school rests on a real observation: most backlogs are the union of stakeholder requests, and that union is rarely a strategy. For it to be wrong, list composition would have to be usually fine and sequencing the place value is lost. Some panels reward "I would not build five of these"; others score it as refusing the question. The defensible move is to do both: rank as given, then name which items you would challenge and on what evidence.

Does the exercise predict anything? The meta-analytic case for structured interviews and work samples is strong, but it concerns structure and job-relevance, not this ninety-minute format. The sceptical position — that these rounds reward fluency in a ritual and favour those who practised it over those who shipped — has not been refuted. For the sceptics to be wrong, round scores would have to correlate with on-the-job prioritisation quality, and almost no company measures that. It is the field's largest unsettled question about its own hiring.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this produces a ranked table. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They establish first which constraint is load-bearing and who outside the room acts on it. They build capacity down from gross to net in public, naming each deduction's owner, so the interviewer can revise one input and watch the answer move. They treat the ranking as a heuristic with a known error — a fractional bound, a swap test — not an answer. And they spend as long on the cut list as the build list, with the name of whoever asked for each cut item and a trigger that reopens it.

The tell is temporal. A competent practitioner answers the question. An expert answers it, then says what would make the answer wrong, in which week they would know, and what they would do. That last sentence is hard to fake: it needs having been wrong before.

12. What each of them decided

Osheen recommended four items, not five: checkout, size widget, return-reason capture and try-at-home slots, for 195 of the 234 usable days. She moved the wishlist alerts into reserve on the client-side arithmetic — 77 days of mobile work against roughly 67 — preferring to hold 39 days than find a specialist shortage in week seven. She named the seller stock sync the cut she least believed in, because its value sits on the supply side and Odhani's table measured only demand.

Zubin declined the question as framed. He committed to the FMCG export, the dealer interface and cement for 130 of 135 days, removing ₹445 lakh of the ₹715 lakh at risk, then said the pharma ask was not a product decision: at 0.55 churn risk on ₹300 lakh of ARR, the company was choosing to lose that account, and that choice belonged to Onkar and the chief revenue officer, not a product manager with four engineers. Onkar's note called this the moment the interview turned.

Three questions for discussion. First: Osheen held 39 of 234 days in reserve, one day in six. Is that prudence, or pre-paying for estimates she does not trust, and how would you tell from outside? Second: Zanjeer's greedy answer on corrected ratios was ₹24 lakh worse than its answer on wrong ones. What should a team conclude, and what should it not? Third: Zubaan's threshold was knowable in advance. What process, rather than what insight, would have surfaced it before the quarter began?

13. Going deeper

PM interviews places this round in the full loop and shows how a panel aggregates signal, which changes what to optimise in any one round. Value vs effort is the reasoning this round applies, with the scoring variants and their failure conditions. A PM's operating system turns the five moves into weekly practice, so build-downs exist before a crisis demands them. Continuous learning as a PM matters because Exhibit 4's denominators shift as your product does. Building a PM portfolio and narrative is where examples you can tell under pressure come from. Transitioning into product management addresses the disadvantage this round imposes on those who never owned a date. Your first 90 days in a PM role is where the capacity model and stakeholder map get built. Confidence, doubt and judgement is the hardest: holding a cut line while entertaining that it is wrong.
case40v1-craft.interview.execution:
Three Answers to the Same Question

Yugal Wedding Network and the execution round — Jaipur, September 2026

1. The night before

At twenty minutes to eleven on the night of Sunday, 20 September 2026, Yashodhan Zende was at the dining table of his flat in Bani Park, Jaipur, with three scorecards open on one screen and a half-written message to his chief executive on another. Zende was vice-president of product at Yugal Wedding Network, and at half past nine the next morning he was expected to name the person who would run the vendor-growth pod.

Three finalists had sat the same sixty-minute execution round and given three different answers to the same prioritisation problem. Two cleared the company's decision rule; the one with the highest average score did not. The pod had been without a product manager since Friday, 3 July — seventy-nine days, or eleven weeks and two days. The freeze that covers the wedding season began on Saturday, 31 October, and nothing would ship between then and Tuesday, 15 December, a span including Diwali on 8 November. The board would re-approve the second-half headcount plan on Thursday, 1 October, and one finalist held a written offer elsewhere expiring at six o'clock on Wednesday, 23 September.

What kept Zende at the table was not the money or the calendar but two messages from the previous thirty-six hours, each suggesting the round had measured something other than he thought.

2. The company, and a decision taken eighteen months ago

Yugal Wedding Network was founded in Jaipur in 2019 by Yagnesh Zorabian, whose family had run banquet halls in the city for two generations. A listings directory for wedding vendors became a marketplace in which families book and pay through the platform and vendors are settled against milestones. By the close of FY26 it carried about 41,000 active vendors across 34 cities, intermediated roughly 1.9 lakh bookings, and earned revenue of ₹186 crore on gross booking value of ₹2,240 crore, a take of a little over 8 per cent. Product and engineering numbered 112, nine in the platform pod.

Two earlier decisions shape this month. In March 2023 Zorabian refused a third-party escrow provider and had the settlement ledger built in-house. It gave Yugal a payout speed rivals took two years to match; it also left the ledger in two engineers' heads, and the company unable to roll a migration backwards once the season's money is moving.

The second, which governs tonight, was taken on 14 March 2025. Zorabian collapsed a five-round loop into three interviews, the last a sixty-minute execution round in which candidates are handed a real, unresolved slice of the roadmap, with real effort and value estimates, and asked what they would cut. Take-homes went the same week, after a review against the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 raised questions about sending live vendor data outside the company. An offer requires two of three interviewers to score at or above a weighted 3.60 out of 5 — a rule Zorabian liked because it stopped one enthusiast carrying a hire. Tonight that rule has produced the deadlock.

3. The industry

The Indian wedding economy is large, informal and seasonal. Discovery is contested by WedMeGood and by the matrimony businesses upstream of it, Shaadi.com and BharatMatrimony; apparel and beauty spend leaks to Myntra, Meesho and Nykaa; venue and travel spend to MakeMyTrip and groups such as IHCL. None is a direct competitor; all are substitutes for one household budget. Yugal's ground is the vendor: a decorator in Jodhpur with a six-person crew who wants bookings, a schedule and money on time.

Three regulatory currents matter. Payments ride on UPI and the NPCI rails, and the Reserve Bank of India's payment-aggregation rules govern how long Yugal may hold a family's money before settling it. GST e-invoicing has pulled small vendors into compliance they are not equipped for. The DPDP Act governs guest lists, photographs and phone numbers — which is why Yugal records interviews only with consent and sends no roadmap material home.

The foreign exposure is narrow but lucrative: Gulf destination weddings, researched abroad, consumed in India. On 22 July 2026 Yugal signed its first such contract with Zarreen Celebrations Group, a planner in Doha serving Indian families across the GCC, worth ₹1.85 crore a year and conditional on the destination-wedding package flow being live before 31 October 2026.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The vendor-growth pod lost its product manager on Friday, 3 July. On Tuesday, 14 July, Zarina Yardi, Yugal's director of talent, signed a ninety-day exclusive mandate with Yashasvi Search Partners at 8.33 per cent of first-year fixed pay, payable on joining; it expires on Monday, 12 October. Exhibit 1 shows what the funnel produced by the end of August.

The round given to all twenty-four candidates who reached it was built in August from the platform pod's own pre-freeze plan: six items, thirty-seven engineer-weeks, capacity of twenty-four. Exhibit 2 reproduces it as candidates saw it. The value column came from Yasmin Zacharias, Yugal's lead data scientist in Nairobi.

The final loops ran from Monday, 7 September to Friday, 18 September. Zehra Yagnik, twenty-nine, a product manager at Zarurat Retail Works in Mumbai, answered in eleven minutes: rank by value per engineer-week, fill capacity from the top, keep A, B and D for twenty-two of the twenty-four weeks, cut C, E and F. Yatin Zambre, thirty-three, of Zehen Payments Systems in Bengaluru, refused to touch A at all, since a ledger migration cannot be unwound in season, and built B, C, E and F instead. Yamini Zope, thirty-five, a senior product manager at Yugal on the payments pod, spent twenty minutes asking where the value column came from, then committed only to E and F, proposing to decide the rest on live data at the halfway mark.

Then two things arrived. On Saturday, 19 September, Zacharias wrote to say the value column was wrong: A and B had each been credited with the same recovered abandoned bookings, and D's figure had been extrapolated from a three-week GCC test to a full month. Her revised estimates are Exhibit 3, and they reorder the list. On Sunday, 20 September, Yardi found the scenario posted almost verbatim on a public interview-preparation forum, dated Saturday, 29 August — nine days before the loops began — with a model answer identical in structure to Yagnik's. Yagnik had declined recording, as the DPDP notice allows, so the only record of her round is interviewer notes.

5. The people

Yashodhan Zende, 41, vice-president of product, Jaipur. Position: the pod cannot go through the season unmanned. Incentive: his FY27 commitments assume a manager by mid-October. Not saying: he designed half the scorecard, and if the round measures the wrong thing that is partly his signature.

Yagnesh Zorabian, 52, founder and chief executive, Jaipur. Position: two of three above the bar, or no offer. Incentive: the redesign is publicly his. Not saying: he has told two investors the pod is filled.

Zarina Yardi, 38, director of talent, Jaipur. Position: close on Monday. Incentive: her half-year target is four product hires and she has made one. Not saying: she found the forum post on Saturday night, not Sunday as recorded, and sat on it a day.

Yogita Zirpe, 34, senior product manager, Pune, second interviewer. Position: Yagnik alone decided anything inside the hour. Incentive: Zirpe has been passed over for this role twice. Not saying: she scored Zope two on commitment knowing Zope's objection to the numbers was the one she herself raised in July.

Zubin Yeolekar, 46, engineering director, Bengaluru, third interviewer. Position: Zambre alone grasped that A is irreversible. Incentive: his two ledger engineers are the scarcest resource in the company. Not saying: he has already moved A behind F in his own sequencing sheet.

Yasmin Zacharias, 36, lead data scientist, Nairobi. Position: no decision should rest on the original value column. Incentive: her estimates were used without her authorisation. Not saying: her revised D figure is itself a single-test number, and she does not know the Doha contract exists.

Zaheer Yunus, 44, head of enterprise partnerships, Austin. Position: D ships whatever the ratios say, a signed contract not being a hypothesis. Incentive: the Doha deal is his. Not saying: the conditionality was his concession.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Product-manager search funnel, 14 July to 31 August 2026

7. Voices

“Eleven minutes. She ranked them, took the top three, told me what she was dropping and why. Forty candidates this year and nobody else has done that.”Yogita Zirpe, debrief, 18 September
“She dropped the GST item and the WhatsApp item to protect a nine-week ledger change. Nine engineer-weeks, two engineers who can do it: four and a half calendar weeks. Starting 28 September it lands on 28 October. The freeze is on the 31st. I want three weeks of stabilisation and she gave me three days.”Zubin Yeolekar, debrief note, 18 September
“Please do not take a hiring decision on my August numbers. That was a working sheet in a thread. A and B double-count the same ₹21 lakh. D is one three-week test grossed up to a month.”Yasmin Zacharias, from Nairobi, 19 September
“The post is dated 29 August, nine days before the loops opened. Structure, letters, the capacity number, the twenty per cent on-call haircut, all of it. I am not saying anyone read it. I am saying we cannot know who did.”Zarina Yardi, to Zende, 20 September
“Whatever the ratios say about D, Zarreen have a signed contract with a 31 October condition in it. ₹1.85 crore. Nobody asked me about the scenario. I would have told you D is not optional.”Zaheer Yunus, from Austin, 20 September

“Cutting the vernacular app is the cut nobody notices until February. My non-English vendors churn at twice the rate of the rest.”Yuvika Zutshi, Kuala Lumpur, 16 September

8. The options as Zende saw them at eleven o'clock

Offer Yagnik, tonight, at ₹48 lakh. She clears the rule on two of three scores, decided fast and defended the cut — the heaviest-weighted criterion — and is the cheapest in first-year cash at ₹52.00 lakh. She is also the only finalist whose answer matches a model answer published nine days before her round, the only one whose round was not recorded, and the one Yeolekar scored at 2.60 on a dimension that, on his arithmetic, means a ledger migration landing three days before a freeze.

Offer Zambre, and override the rule. He has the highest mean at 3.70 and the only score above 4 on sequencing, and his answer is the strongest under the corrected numbers of Exhibit 3: of the combinations that leave A alone, B, C, E and F is the best available, at ₹94 lakh a month against the ₹147 lakh on the table. But a ninety-day notice puts him in the seat on 21 December, after the season has gone, and overriding the rule means overriding the founder in the room where it was written.

Promote Zope. She clears the rule on two of three, sits inside band at ₹38 lakh, can move in a fortnight, and the objection that earned her a 2.33 proved correct on 19 September. Against that: she scored lowest on the criterion the company says it values most; the backfill puts her first-year cash at ₹66.17 lakh, only ₹66,580 below Zambre; and taking her off the payments pod opens a second hole in the same season.

Three options, three defensible cases. Zende had written them in that order without noticing what the ordering assumed: that the round measured the candidates, not their luck with a scenario whose value column was wrong, whose one contractual obligation was never shown to them, and whose predictive record, in Exhibit 5, is eleven people and a ten-point gap.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Money. The band is ₹38 lakh to ₹46 lakh fixed; two of the three asks breach it. The 8.33 per cent fee falls due on either external hire, not on Zope.

Dates. Yagnik's offer from Zakhira Commerce Works expires at six o'clock on Wednesday, 23 September; the mandate expires 12 October; the board re-approves headcount on 1 October; the freeze runs 31 October to 15 December. Zope would start in early October, Yagnik in late October, Zambre on 21 December.

People. Two engineers can touch the ledger, both reporting to Yeolekar; the pod has had no manager for eleven weeks.

Contract and regulation. The Zarreen contract of ₹1.85 crore a year carries a 31 October condition on item D, whose revised value is ₹12 lakh a month, or ₹144 lakh a year — less than the contract it secures. The DPDP consent regime means one finalist's round cannot be re-examined, and is why no take-home exists.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Work Exhibit 2 as the candidates were asked to. With 24 usable engineer-weeks, what does ranking by gain per engineer-week select, what does it cut, and how much of the ₹210 lakh goes?
  2. Re-rank on Exhibit 3. Which items change places, and what happens to each answer once the value column is corrected?
  3. Exhibit 4a satisfies the two-of-three rule for two candidates and denies it to the one with the highest mean. Is the rule doing Zorabian's job, or laundering a disagreement between Zirpe and Yeolekar?
  4. Zacharias says the numbers are wrong; Yunus says a contract makes D compulsory regardless. If both are right, what was the round testing, and could any candidate have passed it on the merits?
  5. Exhibit 5 is eleven people; Exhibit 6 is three offers differing by ₹14.83 lakh in first-year cash and eleven weeks in start date. Which should carry more weight on Monday, and what must you believe for that to hold?
  6. It is half past nine on Monday, 21 September, and Zorabian is waiting. What does Zende do — and what does he tell the board on 1 October about a round he helped design, a leak he cannot test, a value column he circulated and a contract no candidate was shown?

At ten past midnight Zende reopened the forum post and read the model answer twice. It was, line for line, what he would have said himself at twenty-nine, and it was the answer his own company had rewarded. He did not know whether that made it right, or merely cheap. The message to Zorabian was still unsent.
case20v1-craft.interview.execution:
Six Days Before the Execution Round

A case on preparing for the analytical interview

1. Opening

On the evening of Monday, 12 October 2026, Esha Rangnekar sat at a desk in her rented flat in Baner, Pune, with a calendar invitation open on her laptop. Falak Credit Works, a Hyderabad lender, had moved her to the final stage of its product-manager loop. Four rounds were done. The fifth, a forty-five-minute execution round, was set for Saturday, 17 October, at 11 a.m., by video, and would be run by a senior product manager she had never met.

The recruiter's note was brief: "Expect a prioritisation scenario with a fixed date. You will be asked what you would cut." Esha had five evenings and Saturday morning, which she estimated at 36 usable hours, and a decision to take before she opened a single book: how to spend them. A wrong choice would not show until she was sitting in the round with the clock running.

2. Company background

Falak Credit Works sells small-ticket credit lines through UPI. Its customers are salaried first-jobbers in tier-2 cities and neighbourhood shopkeepers who need ₹5,000 to ₹50,000 for a few weeks. The field is crowded: PhonePe and Paytm put credit on the same rails, Razorpay supplies lending infrastructure, and Bajaj Finance is the consumer-lending benchmark. Falak works within the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending guidelines.

The company has about 18 lakh active borrowers and a product organisation of roughly forty people. Diwali falls on 8 November 2026, when lending volumes climb and the release freeze bites. Falak's head of product, Farhan Siddiqui, had recently told colleagues that most of the candidates he met could describe a framework but could not say what they would drop on a Tuesday afternoon.

3. The situation

Esha was an associate product manager at a Pune software firm, three years in, earning ₹22 lakh a year. Falak's offer band was ₹30 lakh to ₹34 lakh. She had cleared four rounds. She had never made a real trade-off, because at her current firm her manager set the roadmap and she wrote specifications.

She asked around. Fenil Gor, a former colleague now working at a Bengaluru fintech, sent her a sample scenario that a previous candidate had shared with him. It came from Falak's own question bank, written with input from the lender's data lead, Emeka Obi, who works from Lagos on the underwriting models. Esha's notes on the sample are reproduced in Exhibit 1. The scenario fixes a capacity of 120 engineer-days before the Diwali freeze and lists five features that together need 135.

The five features need 135 engineer-days in total, so at least 15 days of work must go. The last column divides gain by effort: WhatsApp reminders return ₹6.00 lakh per engineer-day, AutoPay ₹5.00 lakh, the eligibility check about ₹4.67 lakh, and regional-language screens and referral rewards ₹2.40 lakh each.

Gain is the interviewer's stated estimate of extra monthly disbursals (A, C, D) or recoveries (B, E), treated as comparable, in ₹ lakh. Capacity is 120 engineer-days. Gain per engineer-day is gain divided by effort. The total row divides 558 by 135.

Sorting by that last column and filling the 120 days gives a tidy answer: build E, B and A (90 days, ₹450 lakh of monthly gain), then C (25 more days, 115 in all, ₹510 lakh), and drop D. The cut removes 20 days and ₹48 lakh, which is 8.6 per cent of the total gain. But Fenil warned that the interviewer, Jhanvi Ahuja, a senior product manager in Chennai, usually changes the facts partway through: a regulator's note, an engineer's resignation, a moved festival date. What she scores is the reaction.

Fenil had also obtained Falak's scorecard and the results of the last 24 execution rounds (Exhibit 2). Candidates did acceptably at clarifying the constraint and planning for risk, but badly at quantifying the trade-off and defending a cut, which together carry 60 per cent of the weight.

Falak's fixed date was her fixed date too. Exhibit 3 shows the timeline she drew that night.

Fenil can give two 3-hour feedback sessions, one on Wednesday 14 October and one on Friday 16 October, for 6 hours of expert feedback in total.

4. The people

Esha Rangnekar, 27, Pune, wants the Falak role and its ₹30 lakh to ₹34 lakh band, but wants more to be hired for a reason she can articulate. Farhan Siddiqui, head of product in Hyderabad, wants a hire who can decide under a fixed date without waiting for permission. Jhanvi Ahuja, senior product manager in Chennai, will run the round and wants a clear recommendation inside the first fifteen minutes, with numbers behind it. Fenil Gor, in Bengaluru, wants to help but has a full job. Emeka Obi, Falak's data lead in Lagos, is not in the loop, yet his estimates sit under the scenario.

5. The options

Esha sketched three ways to use her 36 hours. Exhibit 4 shows how each would split them. All three total 36 hours.

Option A: drill the question bank. Work through some forty practice prompts, name a framework for each, and rehearse the vocabulary of RICE and MoSCoW. The upside is coverage. The cost is that the scorecard does not reward a framework name; reciting RICE without committing to a cut scores low on a criterion worth 30 per cent.

Option B: build one worked spine, then test it. Take a launch she actually worked on, rebuild it with real effort and gain numbers, and write down what she would have cut and why. Then spend ten hours applying that same method to Falak-style scenarios and use Fenil's 6 hours of feedback. The upside is that her answers rest on a decision she has lived, and she practises the move the scorecard rewards. The cost is that one spine is narrow, and an unfamiliar scenario may expose gaps.

Option C: nearly all mock rounds. Spend 24 hours on timed mock rounds. Fenil's 6 hours of feedback is the cap on expert help, so the other 18 hours would be self-recorded and self-marked. The upside is realism under time pressure. The cost is that much of it would repeat her habits uncorrected.

Exhibit 4. How each option spends the 36 hours

OptionQuestion-bank drillRebuild own projectFalak-style scenariosMock roundsTotal hours
A. Drill the bank2624436
B. Worked spine61410636
C. Mock-heavy4262436

All figures are hours. Expert feedback from Fenil is capped at 6 hours across the six days, so mock hours beyond 6 would be self-assessed.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. In Exhibit 1, rank the five features by gain per engineer-day and fill the 120 days. What is lost by the cut, in ₹ lakh and as a percentage of the total, and what would change if feature B could only be built after feature A?
  2. According to Exhibit 2, which two criteria hold 60 per cent of the weight, and where did past candidates score lowest? What does that suggest about what the round is really measuring?
  3. Using Exhibit 4 and the constraint on expert feedback, what does each option leave Esha unable to do on Saturday?
  4. If Jhanvi changes the facts after twenty minutes, which option leaves Esha best placed to respond, and what would she say first?

7. A note for the learner

An execution round tests one thing: whether a candidate can hold a fixed date, a limited team and uneven value in one head and then commit to a cut. Trade-off questions apply the same value-versus-effort reasoning a prioritisation course teaches, but under a clock and with an audience. The framework is the small part; the hard part is showing judgement about trade-offs you may never have made for real.

One defensible path is Option B. The scorecard in Exhibit 2 shows that 60 per cent of the weight sits on quantifying and defending a cut, and the sample in Exhibit 1 shows why: the answer is not hidden. Gain per engineer-day orders the features, the capacity of 120 removes 20 days of work, and the interesting content is the defence. A candidate who has rebuilt one of her own launches with real numbers can say, "I would drop referral rewards: they cost 20 engineer-days, return the least per day at ₹2.40 lakh, and removing them costs 8.6 per cent of the gain." That sentence is quantified, committed and checkable.

Option A fails because naming RICE is not a cut. Option C fails because 18 of its 24 mock hours would carry no expert correction. Because B's spine is narrow, Esha should prepare two moves for when the facts change: restate the constraint, then re-run the ratios aloud. She should also say what she would tell the engineering lead about the dropped feature, which covers the remaining 20 per cent of the scorecard. Depth on one real decision beats breadth on forty imagined ones.
exp20v2-craft.interview.execution:
Execution and prioritisation rounds

Trade-off questions, shipping under constraint, and what to cut when the date is fixed.

1. The Friday round

On Friday 16 October 2026, Damini Deodhar sat down for the fourth of five interviews for an associate product manager role at Darpan Ride Network, a Hyderabad-based ride-hailing company. Of the 38 finalists in that hiring cycle, six would receive offers, a rate of 15.8 per cent. Damini had four years of experience in a bank's digital team, where she had written specifications and chased vendors, but she had never owned a launch date with her name on it. Her interviewer, Qasim Dalvi, a group product manager, opened with a scenario instead of a greeting.

"Darpan is launching scheduled airport rides on Monday 30 November. The date is fixed because it is tied to the wedding-season travel peak. You have five engineers for six weeks. Here are six candidate features. What do you ship?" He turned his laptop around and showed her the list reproduced below. The phrase that mattered was "fixed". Damini understood that Qasim was testing whether she would say aloud what she would refuse to build, and justify it with numbers.

Exhibit 1. The brief as Qasim read it out. Effort is in person-days (one engineer working one day). Value is the expected extra paid bookings in the first month, the team's own estimate.
FeatureEffort (person-days)Value (extra bookings)
Pre-booking flow4012,000
Flight-delay tracking307,500
Fixed-fare quote208,000
UPI refund to wallet254,000
Driver scheduling alerts356,300
Referral credits151,500
Total16539,300

Damini's first instinct was to rank the six by importance. She stopped, because the list held a trap: six features cost 165 person-days, and five engineers working six weeks do not have 165.

2. The idea

An execution and prioritisation round is an interview exercise in which the candidate is given a goal, a fixed constraint (a date, a team size, a budget) and more candidate work than the constraint allows. The candidate must decide what to build, what to defer, and how they would know the decision was wrong. It exists because hiring teams cannot observe judgement directly; a constructed trade-off with shared numbers lets them watch it in real time.

The underlying logic is older than product management. Operations researchers in the 1950s, George Dantzig among them, studied the knapsack problem: given items with weights and values and a bag that holds a limited weight, which items maximise value? Product managers inherited the structure. Value-versus-effort grids are its informal form, and scoring models such as RICE (reach, impact, confidence, effort), popularised by Intercom around 2016, its spreadsheet form.

The sentence Damini could repeat in any meeting without sounding glib is this: "Because the date is fixed, scope is the only thing that can move, so I will tell you what I am cutting before I tell you what I am building."

3. How it actually works

The first move is to clarify, and Damini spent a full five minutes there. She asked what Darpan was optimising: bookings, revenue per ride, or the reliability of airport pickups. Qasim said bookings in the first month. She asked whether quality was negotiable and was told that it was not, since a missed flight is the worst possible outcome for this product. That answer fixed two of the three levers a project has (date and quality), so scope was the lever left. Weak answers escape by cutting quality or moving the date.

The second move is capacity, and it is the one most often left implicit. Five engineers over six weeks of five working days gives 5 × 6 × 5 = 150 person-days. Not all of it can be spent on features. Code review, bug fixing, a release freeze and the odd sick day consume time, so Damini reserved 20 per cent, or 30 person-days, leaving 120 usable. She added that she would ask the engineering lead whether 20 per cent matched the team's history. The 165 days requested exceeded the 120 by 45, or 37.5 per cent.

The third move is to rank by value per person-day, which is simply each feature's expected bookings divided by its effort. The fourth is to walk down the ranked list, committing items until the next one no longer fits, then to name the items left out and what leaving them costs. The fifth is to change one input and observe whether the answer survives. The next section does all five with real arithmetic.

4. A worked example

Dividing each value by its effort gives the ranking in Exhibit 2. Fixed-fare quote earns 8,000 ÷ 20 = 400 bookings per person-day, the highest. Pre-booking earns 12,000 ÷ 40 = 300, delay tracking 7,500 ÷ 30 = 250, driver alerts 6,300 ÷ 35 = 180, the refund 4,000 ÷ 25 = 160, and referral credits 1,500 ÷ 15 = 100. The column called committed effort shows the running total of what Damini keeps, and the verdict explains each decision.

Exhibit 2. First pass: usable capacity of 120 person-days. The total row averages across all six features (39,300 ÷ 165 = 238.2).
RankFeatureEffortValueValue per dayCommitted effortVerdict
1Fixed-fare quote208,00040020Build
2Pre-booking flow4012,00030060Build
3Flight-delay tracking307,50025090Build
4Driver scheduling alerts356,30018090Cut: 90 + 35 = 125 exceeds 120
5UPI refund to wallet254,000160115Build: 90 + 25 = 115 fits
6Referral credits151,500100115Cut: 115 + 15 = 130 exceeds 120
Total / average16539,300238.2115Four built, two cut

Note the skip at rank 4. A purely sequential reading would stop at the first item that fails to fit, yet the refund, ranked fifth, still fits in the 30 days remaining. Damini then tested the nearest alternatives: swapping delay tracking for alerts (keeping the refund) totals 120 days and 30,300 bookings, and swapping the refund for referral credits gives 29,000. Neither beat her selection.

The chosen four cost 20 + 40 + 30 + 25 = 115 person-days and deliver 8,000 + 12,000 + 7,500 + 4,000 = 31,500 bookings. That is 69.7 per cent of the effort for 80.2 per cent of the value. The cuts forgo 6,300 + 1,500 = 7,800 bookings (39,300 minus 31,500), and 5 days stay as slack.

The second pass

Qasim then changed one input. "Two of your engineers are pulled onto a payments incident for ten days each. What now?" Usable capacity falls by 2 × 10 = 20, from 120 to 100. Damini re-walked the same ranking. Fare (20), pre-booking (60) and delay tracking (90) still fit. The refund would take the total to 115, which exceeds 100, and referral credits would reach 105, also over. Three features are built, for 8,000 + 12,000 + 7,500 = 27,500 bookings, and 10 days remain unallocated.

Exhibit 3. Second pass: capacity 100 person-days. Capacity fell by 16.7 per cent (20 ÷ 120); value fell by 12.7 per cent (4,000 ÷ 31,500).
ScenarioCapacityEffort committedBookings deliveredShare of 39,300
First pass12011531,50080.2%
Second pass1009027,50070.0%

The lesson is in the asymmetry. A 16.7 per cent loss of capacity cost only 12.7 per cent of value, because the cut came from the bottom of the ranking, where each day buys least. She would hold the 10 spare days as contingency.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Value is a forecast, not a fact

The 12,000 bookings attached to pre-booking is somebody's estimate. A strong answer asks who produced it, and treats similar ratios (250 against 180) as close calls.

Ratio ranking ignores dependencies

Suppose Qasim reveals that pre-booking cannot work without driver alerts, since drivers would miss scheduled rides. The pair costs 40 + 35 = 75 days and delivers 12,000 + 6,300 = 18,300 bookings, or 244 per day. With fare (20) and the refund (25) the total is exactly 120 days and 8,000 + 18,300 + 4,000 = 30,300 bookings, 1,200 below the earlier answer, and delay tracking is cut.

Capacity is not headcount times days

The 20 per cent reserve is an assumption, and the whole answer inherits it. Always show gross (150), deduction (30) and net (120), so the interviewer can adjust one number.

Which constraint is really fixed?

Date, scope and quality form a triangle in which one side must give. Adding engineers late rarely helps, since newcomers consume the time of existing staff; say so before the interviewer offers it.

What it is confused with

Prioritisation by framework is not roadmapping, and neither is strategy. A scoring model ranks candidates you have already listed. It cannot tell you whether the list is the right list, or whether the airport segment deserves six weeks at all.

What it cannot tell you

The method cannot see correlated risk, learning value or reversibility. A cheap, reversible feature with uncertain value may deserve a place above its ratio because shipping it teaches you something.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Who estimated effort, and have they built something similar? What is the cost of being wrong in each direction? Does any item share code with another, so that their costs are not additive?

6. How it differs by product and by company

The mechanics are the same everywhere, but the definition of value changes.

Exhibit 4. Where the value term and the constraint differ.
ContextWhat "value" usually meansWhat tightens the constraint
ConsumerActivation, retention, conversion; high volume makes small effects measurableStore review cycles and seasonal peaks
B2BRevenue at risk from named accounts; one customer can dominate the rankingContractual commitments and integration partners
MarketplaceEffects on both sides; a feature for riders may starve driversLiquidity: supply must exist before demand features pay off
Early-stage companyLearning speed; reversible bets count for moreCash and a team of five
Large companyPortfolio balance and dependency on other teamsCoordination cost and platform queues

Darpan is a marketplace, which is why Damini's tension over driver alerts was the right instinct. In a large company she would also check whether a shared platform team's queue would delay her estimates.

7. Common mistakes

Exhibit 5. Three failures, how they appear from outside, and a quick test.
MistakeSymptomMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Ranking without capacityA tidy priority list with no cut line; every item "P1"Believes prioritisation means orderingAsk "how many person-days does your list cost, and how many do you have?"
Treating estimates as givenNever asks who produced the numbersTakes the interviewer's table as truthAsk what range you would put around the largest value
Silence on the cutsDescribes the build in detail, mentions cut items in passingThinks the cuts are the embarrassing partCount the seconds spent on what is not shipping
No way to check afterwardsEnds the answer at launch daySees the decision as finished at shipmentAsk "what would you see in week two that proves you wrong?"

8. What good looks like

A strong forty-five minutes is paced, and the pacing is itself a signal. Exhibit 6 shows the allocation Damini aimed for.

Exhibit 6. A target allocation for a 45-minute round.
PhaseMinutes
Clarify goal and fixed constraints5
Size capacity8
Rank by value per day12
Draw and defend the cut line10
Pressure-test and monitor7
Summarise the decision3
Total45

The portrait is a candidate who states the constraint first, shows capacity arithmetic, ranks transparently, skips what does not fit, and volunteers the weakest assumption before the interviewer finds it. She ends by naming a trigger: if bookings per day in week one fall below the plan, she would reconsider the cut items.

9. What Damini decided

Damini closed by recommending the first-pass four, fare, pre-booking, delay tracking and the refund, for 115 of 120 days. She called driver alerts the main risk, and said that if the engineering lead confirmed the dependency she would swap delay tracking out and build the 75-day bundle instead. Her reasoning was visible, which is what the round was designed to extract.

To go further, study value versus effort, which underlies everything above, then the broader loop of PM interviews, of which this is one round.

Two questions to sit with. First, if every estimate on Exhibit 1 were wrong by a third in either direction, which of your cuts would survive? Second, what is the cheapest piece of information you could obtain in ten minutes that might change your answer most?
case40v1-craft.interview.analytical:
Dhanak Finance Works: What the Analytical Round Measured

A case on analytical and metrics interviews. The case does not resolve.

1. The night before

On the evening of Sunday 8 November 2026, Suchitra Vaze sat at her dining table in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with three interview transcripts and a scorecard grid. By nine the next morning she owed the Chief Product Officer one name for Principal Product Manager, Growth, at Dhanak Finance Works.

The role had been open 178 days, since Thursday 14 May, and the finalists had taken the analytical round between Monday 26 October and Thursday 29 October. The panel's preferred candidate had the highest average score and an answer whose premise Suchitra now believed was wrong. The candidate who had found what was wrong with the question had the panel's lowest structure score and an offer elsewhere lapsing on Wednesday 11 November. The third already worked at Dhanak, had known the answer before she walked in, and could not be paid inside the band.

What unsettled her was not the choice but the instrument: the round she had designed to be the most rigorous hour in the loop had sorted the three in an order she could no longer defend.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2024

Dhanak Finance Works was founded in Bengaluru in 2017 as a budgeting app for salaried customers in their twenties, adding a savings sweep in 2019 and, in 2021, a co-branded credit card issued with Ekanta Bank, a mid-sized private bank. In the year ended March 2026 it had 2.4 crore registered users, 68 lakh transacting monthly, revenue of ₹680 crore and 2,100 employees, 48 of them product managers. Cards contributed ₹142 crore, just under 21 per cent of revenue, across roughly 5.9 lakh activated cards at about ₹2,400 of net revenue per card per year.

In February 2024, pressed by Ekanta Bank's reconciliation team and its own statutory auditors, Dhanak made the decision that shapes this case: rather than measure card performance on its own in-app event stream, it agreed to define every card metric off the bank's nightly settlement file. The file was auditable, and it ended a year of arguments in which the two sides' numbers differed by four to six per cent every month. The cost was that Dhanak no longer owned the definitions. When the bank migrated to a new file format on 1 July 2026, the activation flag changed from "first transaction within 60 days of approval" to "within 30 days". The change was announced in a release note, implemented correctly, and absorbed into Dhanak's dashboards without comment.

3. The industry

Dhanak competed for the same customer as Cred, Jupiter, Fi, Groww and Zerodha, and against the distribution muscle of PhonePe and Paytm. The Reserve Bank of India's digital lending framework and its co-branded card rules constrained who could own the customer relationship; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governed consent for the bureau pulls Dhanak made at CIBIL before an application reached the bank. UPI, run by NPCI, had absorbed almost all small-ticket payments, and credit lines on UPI were reshaping what a card was for.

The exposure was not only Indian. An analytics pod sat in Hyderabad; senior data science sat in Dublin, hired for a European reporting product built for Ekanta Bank's correspondent partners; a growth marketer in Jakarta ran a savings pilot with an Indonesian partner. No hour suited all three at once, and the panel had never met in one room.

4. The situation in detail

When Suchitra took over growth hiring in 2025 she replaced the loop's generic puzzles with one live problem from the business: forty-five minutes, no preparation. Candidates saw the funnel in Exhibit 1, were told activation had fallen, and were asked which metric they would hold themselves to, what had caused the fall, and how large the opportunity was.

On Monday 3 August, reviewing the July dashboard, Suchitra saw activation fall from 41.0 per cent in June to 33.0 per cent in July and opened a diagnosis workstream. On Friday 18 September, Pranjal Kotak circulated a memo attributing the fall to install mix: paid installs had risen after a July campaign, and paid cohorts converted worse. That memo became the house view, and the Exhibit 1 handed to candidates carried April's 45.0 per cent as its baseline.

Eighteen days later, on Tuesday 6 October, Niamh Corrigan sent Pranjal and Suchitra a recomputation done for an unrelated model: reading the bank's release note, she had rebuilt all six months on a consistent 30-day window. On that basis, in Exhibit 2, activation had fallen from 39.0 per cent in April to 30.0 per cent in September — nine points, not fifteen, with six of the fifteen an artefact of 1 July. Pranjal disputed its relevance; Suchitra left it unopened. Then the round happened.

Tejal Munshi, Monday 26 October

Tejal, a senior product manager at Evam Insurance Services and before that a consultant, gave what two interviewers called the cleanest hour of the year. She chose activation within 30 days as her metric, observed that installs had risen from 12,00,000 in April to 16,00,000 in July, a rise of 33.3 per cent, while the approval rate fell from 40.0 to 35.0 per cent, and concluded that the firm had bought volume at the cost of intent. She sized the damage against April's 45.0 per cent baseline at ₹12.80 crore of annualised revenue foregone.

How the panel should read Tejal's ₹12.80 crore. Her arithmetic is exact: against a 45.0 per cent baseline the shortfall is 53,340 cards, and at ₹2,400 each that is ₹12.80 crore. But that baseline was measured on a 60-day window and the outcomes she compared with it on a 30-day window — correctly computed on a basis that cannot be compared. Exhibit 5 shows both bases.

Kabir Dholakia, Tuesday 27 October

Kabir, a group product manager at Dastak Retail Network, a quick-commerce firm, spent his first twenty minutes refusing to diagnose anything. He asked who owned the activation flag, whether the window had always been 30 days, and what had shipped on the first of a month in the middle of the series: a step change on a month boundary, he said, is almost never behaviour. Putri Hartono, dialling in from Jakarta at the end of her day, wrote that he had "interrogated the brief rather than answering it". He gave no sizing and no recommendation, and produced, without access to Niamh's memo, the observation that split the panel.

Arunima Ghoshal, Thursday 29 October

Arunima, already a senior product manager at Dhanak in Pune, had been in the room when the bank's release note was discussed in June. She used the window change immediately, worked through Exhibit 3, and sized the shortfall at ₹7.16 crore on a consistent basis. At the whiteboard she wrote 1,26,000 × 0.30 = 3,780 — her own slip of a factor of ten, caught forty seconds later and corrected to 37,800 mid-sentence. Suchitra scored her highest of the three on judgement, and could not tell which part was reasoning and which recall.

On Monday 2 November, when the transcripts circulated, Niamh replied with her 6 October memo attached: "He found it in twenty minutes. We had it for four weeks."

Figure 1. The sequence the panel did not have on 29 October.

5. The people

Suchitra Vaze, Director of Product, Growth, Bengaluru, designed the round and owns the decision; she needs a hire for two squads she covers herself. Unsaid: she has twice told the Chief Product Officer that her round is the loop's best instrument.

Anirudh Wagle, Chief Product Officer, Mumbai, wants the seat filled before the 1 December freeze and prefers "someone who can present to the board". Unsaid: he met Tejal at a conference in August and told her to apply.

Ritu Khandelwal, Head of Talent, Gurugram, is measured on time-to-fill and offer acceptance, and wants a proctored test licensed from Ekaksh Assessment Labs. Unsaid: a declined offer costs her number more than a mediocre hire does.

Pranjal Kotak, Head of Data Science, Hyderabad, built the dashboard and wrote the mix memo; he scored Kabir 2 of 5 on structure. Unsaid: he never read the release note, and mix was the first explanation he tested, not the last.

Niamh Corrigan, Senior Data Scientist, Dublin, found the artefact and thinks the firm has a definitions problem, not a hiring problem; she interviewed at 11 am Indian time, 5:30 am her own. Unsaid: two quarters of trying to move card metrics onto Dhanak's own events, and Kabir is the best argument she has had.

Arunima Ghoshal, Senior Product Manager, Pune, the internal finalist, has told a mentor she will look outside if passed over again. Unsaid: her squad's next two quarters depend on her staying.

Kabir Dholakia, Group Product Manager, Bengaluru, holds an offer at ₹78 lakh fixed from Chetak Commerce Exchange and would take ₹74 lakh "if the data function reports into product within a year". Unsaid: he left his last firm after losing an argument over a definition.

Putri Hartono, Growth Marketing Lead, Jakarta, the fourth panellist, rates communication heavily. Unsaid: she took two of the calls after 9 pm local, between flights.

7. Voices

From Kabir's interview, typed up by Suchitra:

"Before I pick a metric I need to know who can change it without telling me. Your activation rate has a step change between June and July of eight points. Nothing in a consumer funnel moves eight points on the first of a month unless somebody shipped something, and the thing most likely to have shipped is a definition."

From Niamh to Pranjal, 6 October:

"The bank's note is three lines on page nine. But our dashboard has been comparing 60-day April with 30-day July, and the whole diagnosis sits on that comparison."

Pranjal's reply to her, eleven minutes later:

"Rebuilding six months of history on a different window is a two-week job I do not have. Let us not rewrite the story because one flag changed."

From Anirudh to Suchitra, Saturday 7 November:

"Board offsite is on the 24th and whoever we hire presents the growth plan. Tejal would be ready for that. Is the other fellow going to argue with the CFO about definitions?"

From Putri, on the panel thread:

"I may have been unfair to Kabir. It was 9:40 at night here, he spent twenty minutes on data lineage, and I scored what I could follow. I would score him differently in the morning."

8. The options as Suchitra sees them

Option A: Tejal Munshi. The panel's highest total at 64 of 80, strongest on structure and communication, ready for the 24 November board offsite, inside the band at ₹70 lakh, first-year cash ₹75.95 lakh. Against her: the diagnosis she delivered so fluently is the house view, and the house view rests on a comparison that does not hold. Her numeracy mean of 3.25 is her lowest dimension; Niamh scored her 12 of 20.

Option B: Kabir Dholakia. He found in twenty minutes what the organisation had held unread for three weeks. Highest numeracy at 4.75, lowest communication at 2.50, offer lapsing Wednesday. He wants ₹74 lakh, ₹2.00 lakh above the band, and the data function under product within a year — which would put Pranjal, who scored him 12 of 20, under the man who disassembled his memo. He never sized the opportunity, and growth here is a job of persuading eleven people a quarter.

Option C: Arunima Ghoshal. Cheapest on paper at ₹55.00 lakh and productive in a fortnight, best judgement score at 4.25, tightest panel agreement with a spread of 2. Against her: a band exception, a backfill that takes her true first-year cost to ₹97.00 lakh, and nobody able to separate what she worked out from what she knew. If the round cannot tell reasoning from recall, Suchitra wonders what else it cannot tell.

Suchitra has written all three as a choice among candidates. Reading her notes at eleven at night, she can see two other things the evidence might be about. The round may have measured the panel rather than the candidates: four interviewers, four implicit theories of analytical strength, no calibration, one of them scoring at 9:40 pm. And the ₹7.16 crore in Exhibit 5 may be the smaller number on the page, because an organisation that compared a 60-day window with a 30-day one for four months will do it again on another metric next quarter. Nobody is being hired to fix that.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The recommendation is due at 9 am on Monday 9 November. Kabir's offer from Chetak Commerce Exchange lapses on Wednesday 11 November; his recruiter will not extend. Headcount approval expires with the freeze on 1 December; a role unfilled by then returns to the pool until the planning cycle that closes in March.

The band is ₹58 to ₹72 lakh fixed. Anything above it needs the Chief Financial Officer's signature, and two such exceptions have been refused this year; anything below the floor needs a written exception from Anirudh. The internal promotion cap of 25 per cent is a policy Ritu's team published in April and has applied to nine promotions since. The 8.5 per cent search fee is contractual. Niamh has three weeks of regulatory work before the quarter closes and cannot take on a metrics rebuild. Ekanta Bank's next file-format release is due in February 2027, and Dhanak has no veto over it.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What did the round actually measure in each interview? Separate what it measured about the candidate from what it measured about the panel and the question paper.
  2. Work through Exhibits 1 and 2. With forty-five minutes and no data dictionary, what would have told you the June-to-July step was suspicious?
  3. Exhibit 3 was offered in support of the mix explanation. Read it with its footnote: what does it establish, what does it rule out, and what does the missing data cost?
  4. Tejal's ₹12.80 crore and Arunima's ₹7.16 crore are both arithmetically correct. How should an interviewer score a correct calculation on an incomparable baseline, and how does a candidate avoid that trap?
  5. Arunima knew about the window change before she walked in. Is a round that rewards institutional knowledge broken, or measuring something real? What would you change to find out?
  6. It is Monday morning: one name to give, a lapsing offer, a band she cannot clear, a board offsite on the 24th. What does Suchitra do, in what order, and what does she tell the board about the two sizings and the four weeks in which nobody read the memo?

At 11:40 pm she opened a blank message to Anirudh, typed "My recommendation is", and stopped. She looked again at Exhibit 4a: 64, 57, 63. Three numbers close enough that the ordering was noise, from an instrument she had built to be the loop's most reliable, measuring a question whose premise her own organisation had got wrong. She deleted the line and sat with the laptop open.
exp20v2-craft.interview.analytical:
Analytical and Metrics Rounds

Choosing a metric, diagnosing a funnel drop, sizing a market under time pressure: what the interviewer is actually listening for.

1. A Tuesday in August

On Tuesday, 18 August 2026, Sudha Venkataraghavan, a group product manager at Vasant Fresh Network, sat down in a glass room in Bengaluru with the last candidate of the day. Vasant Fresh is a fictional quick-commerce company delivering groceries in roughly fifteen minutes, in a category whose best-known players include Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart. It had received 1,140 applications for two associate product manager posts, and fourteen candidates had reached the analytical round. Sudha had forty minutes to learn whether the person opposite could reason with numbers while someone watched.

The candidate was Vinay Tandon, a second-year ISB MBA student. Sudha gave him a sanitised version of a problem the company had met a week earlier. Tarun Vaswani, the data analyst on her team, had noticed that weekly orders had fallen from 5,48,800 to 4,76,770 with no change in app traffic. Nobody yet knew why. Sudha asked: "Orders are down. What do you do?"

Vinay's first sentence was, "I would look at marketing spend." He had named a cause before establishing what had moved, where, or by how much. If he recovered, Vasant Fresh would gain someone who could find a leak worth lakhs in an afternoon; if not, it would hire someone who produced plausible stories faster than they could be tested.

This page follows that conversation. Its argument is simple. An analytical round is a test of whether you can say out loud what a number is made of, in small steps, with arithmetic that is right, before you say anything about why it moved.

2. The idea

An analytical round is one stage of a product-management interview loop. It takes one of three forms: a metrics question asks you to choose or defend a measure of success; a diagnosis question gives you a number that has moved and asks why; an estimation question asks you to size something with no data in front of you.

These test one skill: decomposition, breaking a quantity into parts that can each be reasoned about. The physicist Enrico Fermi is remembered for asking students to estimate, say, the piano tuners in Chicago by chaining plausible guesses. The funnel, a sequence of steps with some fraction dropping out at each, entered product vocabulary partly through Dave McClure's 2007 "AARRR" framing (acquisition, activation, retention, referral, revenue).

The problem this solves is that confident storytelling is cheap and measurement is not. "Orders fell because of competitor discounts" cannot be checked; "orders fell by 72,030, all of it in UPI payments, from one date" can be acted on. The sentence Sudha would repeat in any meeting: tell me what the number is made of before you tell me why it moved.

3. How it works, step by step

Sudha's scoring sheet was a sequence. First, clarify: what is the metric, over what period, against what comparison? "Down" could mean against last week, last year or forecast. Second, check the movement is real, a step usually left implicit: a tracking event may have broken or a dashboard may be double-counting. Third, decompose: write the metric as a product of parts. Orders equal sessions (one opening of the app) times the fraction of sessions that become an order, and that fraction splits along the funnel. Fourth, cut the part that moved by stage, platform, city, payment method, new versus returning users, and date. Fifth, hypothesise, tied to what changed. Sixth, size each hypothesis in orders. Seventh, recommend what to do tomorrow and what would change your mind.

Figure 1. The diagnosis sequence. The dashed arc is the common shortcut that skips verification, decomposition and cutting.

4. A worked example, line by line

Back to Vinay. Prompted ("what would you want to know first?"), he asked for the funnel. Each step rate is the share of the previous stage that continued; the cumulative column divides by the 40,00,000 sessions at the top.

Vinay compared this with the latest week. Sessions were again 40,00,000 and the first three step rates were unchanged, so checkout starts were still 6,86,000. Orders were 4,76,770, so payment success was 4,76,770 / 6,86,000 = 69.5%, against 80%. The loss is 5,48,800 − 4,76,770 = 72,030 orders, 72,030 / 5,48,800 = 13.125% of the earlier week. Payment success fell 10.5 percentage points (80 − 69.5); orders fell 13.125 per cent. They are different statements.

Figure 2. Bar lengths are drawn to a common scale (12.5 px per lakh). The first four bars are identical in both weeks; only the final bar shrinks.

The funnel has located the problem at one stage out of four, which is the most useful single thing a diagnosis can do. The next cut is by payment method. Tarun split the 6,86,000 checkout starts:

The whole loss sits in UPI, the instant-payment system run by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). UPI success fell 15 points, or 15 / 80 = 18.75% in relative terms.
